Meditation on the Reality of the Self.
The Jewel Garland of Meditative Concentrations (Dhyānaratnāvalī)

For the sake of peace, one should meditate on the white [deity]. Then, having always arisen at dawn, the yogi should contemplate the one who is all-pervading, possessing a divine form, situated within the lotus of the heart, like a wise sage.
One who is not yet awakened should meditate upon Śiva, Sadāśiva, within the lotus of the heart.
Meditation on the Reality of the Self.
Having four arms and four faces, seated upon a square lotus,
this is known as the *ātmatattva* (the principle of the self), which possesses the luster of refined gold.
In her left hand she holds a sacrificial ladle and a water-pot, and in her right, a rosary of lotus seeds.
Knowledge is meditation on reality.
Resembling a blue lotus, he is blue in color, possesses eight facets, and is endowed with eight arms;
[he holds] a discus, an arrow, a lotus, the *cinmudrā*, a conch, a bow, and a water-pot.
And I requested protection from him who holds [the gestures] in his right and left hands;
he has one face with a gentle countenance and is proclaimed as the essence of knowledge (vidyātattva). || 2 ||
p. 2) || Meditation on the Śiva-principle ||
Resembling pure crystal, encircled by a serpent as its sacred thread, this is indeed remembered as the Śiva-tattva, possessing five faces and four arms. (3)
In the right hand, a rosary of lotus seeds; in the left, a trident and a water-pot.
This is the meditation on the *nivṛtti-kalā*.
Nivṛtti is proclaimed as having the luster of gold in its true essence, adorned by the moon of her four faces, and holding a vajra, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus.
The Chapter on the Contemplation of the Ritual for Consecration (Pratiṣṭhākalādhyāna)
Resembling pure crystal, she has one face and four arms;
holding a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, she is adorned with jewels of consecration.
Meditation on Vidyā and Kalā.

She has the color of jewels, hair like a conch-shell or the moon, three faces, and four arms; holding a spear, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, she resembles the blazing fire of knowledge.
Meditation on the Peaceful Form of Kālī.

Four-faced, four-armed, black in color, and possessed of great strength; holding a banner, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary of beads, and a lotus; she is peaceful and wears the sacred thread across her entire body.
Meditation on the Kalā beyond Peace (Śāntyatīta).
Resembling pure crystal, she has five faces and four arms; holding a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, Śāntyatītā bestows boons. (8)
Meditation on the Principles (tattvas)
The earth element is yellowish-white and bow-shaped; water is white;
that called fire is red and triangular; and wind is black and hexagonal.
The white [element] is well-purified as that called space (vyoman); the yellow [element] is fragrance; taste resides in the red [element];
then touch is the black [element]; and sound has a white luster.
The generative organ is the color of young grass, while that called the anus resembles a seat;
the feet have a dark-blue luster, and the hands are yellowish or perhaps without luster.
The tongue has various colors and a sky-like luster, and likewise it is red;
the skin, flesh, and ears are black, while the mind is of a variegated color.
Ahaṅkāra is reddish in hue; Buddhi resembles kāśīśa (green vitriol);
that which is called Guṇa has the luster of indranīla (sapphire); Vyakta is likewise red.
Passion (rāga) is red; that which is called Niyati is blue; the light of Vidyā and the Moon is [white];
that which is called Kāla is of mixed color, while that which is called Kāla is like the color of the dark-blue [cloud].
The Māyā-vidyā [tattva] has the luster of yellow orpiment; Sādākhya is situated within Rakteśvara and has the appearance of crystal; and the Śakti-tattva has a white radiance.
The Śiva-tattva is proclaimed to be like pure crystal;
one should contemplate all manifest things, beginning with space and ending with the earth, as being characterized by the forms of "a," "i," and "u."

4) || Meditation on the Worlds ||
Kālā, Kalādyā, Anantādyā, Bhuvanākhyā, Raviprabhā, and the eight beginning with Sūkṣmā are blue-hued; Nivṛtti and the others possess the radiance of the established state.
They have four arms and three eyes, adorned with crowns of matted hair;
they likewise hold a skull, an eye, a bow, and a trident, as well as a vajra.
Meditation on the Colors of the Deities.

Space (ākāśa) is white in color; that which begins with the letter 'a' is deep blue; that consisting of the letters from 'ka' to 'kṣa' is red; and the radiance beginning with the letter 'a' is yellow.
Meditation on the Footprints
Everything beginning with Vyomavyāpin is the western [face] named Sānnidhya;
it is the Brahman-seat (pada) of a red luster, consisting of the sequence of Viṣṇu, Rudra, and so forth.
Resembling nine colors of blue and praised by sounds, words, and so forth,
those mantras beginning with Īśāna are the phonemes (varṇas) as they will be described hereafter.
Meditation during the Sandhyā periods.
One should meditate upon the Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, Raudrī, the red, the white, and the black goddesses at dawn,
midday, evening, and twilight, respectively.
The Meditation on Brāhmī
Clad in red garments and adorned with red ornaments. || 14 ||
p.
5) || Meditation on Viṣṇu ||
White, white—adorned with all ornaments. || 15 ||
The Meditation on Raudrī.
One should contemplate one's own body as having entered into the enjoyment of the circle of light [emanating] from the petals of blue lotuses;
this is the supreme twilight of the wise, the fourfold heart-essence.
O slender one, the power of Śiva, though undivided, attains multiplicity—
red, white, and black— like the fibers of a lotus stalk.
One should visualize the white and black door-frames at night;
the heart, the bindu, and the aperture of Brahmā—these are situated in the higher realms in successive order.
The first three [periods] are joined with the sattva and other [guṇas], while the fourth is devoid of qualities;
for the yogi of breath, the two twilights are as red as the sun and the moon.
That which is the supreme awakening to Śiva is called the highest *sandhyā*.
[This is] the meditation on the *Gāyatrī*.
Having abandoned all these gods, headed by Brahmā, one should worship Virūpākṣa, who possesses the luster of molten gold and resides within the sun,
with joined palms.
Meditation on the Staff-Bearer (Daṇḍin)
p. 6) This is Daṇḍin Dvātya.
|| The Meditation on Piṅgala ||
On the left side is Piṅgala, who holds a staff;
on the left is Pratihāra, who likewise holds a staff made of wood and has a dark complexion.
Meditation on Gaṇapati
Raktapadmā—Śiva. || Contemplation of the Guru ||
The crown of matted locks is the supreme teacher;
it is abundant meditative concentration.
Thereafter, one should prepare the seat: a lotus upon a lion-throne, with an abundant [pedestal] placed in the center, square and supporting everything.
The Meditation on Vimalā and Others
One should visualize [the seat] as pure, essential, worthy of worship, blissful, and unsurpassed,
shaped like a lion’s foot in the corners starting from the southeast.
Meditation in the Lotus Posture (Padmāsana)
In the center of that is a red lotus, adorned with petals in the eight directions.
[This is] the meditation on Dīptā and the others.
And upon the filaments (kesara), one should assign the eight Śaktis beginning with Dīptā;
from the east to the northeast, they should be situated in the center, facing in all directions.
The six [limbs] are characterized by the form of the flame of a blazing lamp. This is the meditation on the Sun (Ādityadhyāna).
The white lotus, together with the heart and so forth.
One should meditate upon the Saumya [weapon],
which resembles a mass of lightning, a scripture with fierce fangs and a terrifying appearance.
[Somāni]
Soma has a face distorted by a *kumuda* [flower];
his radiant form is characterized by fierce meditation.
Fierce, with a red and terrifying face, two hands holding a lotus and the gesture of fearlessness,
his countenance formidable with fangs, matted-haired, and clad in red garments.
One should meditate upon Caṇḍeśvara, who holds a chisel and possesses the splendor of a lotus;
[this is] Gaṇapati.
I praise the pot-bellied one...
O Sarasvatī!
White, white, [she who is] self-born;
with lotuses in her left and right hands, she possesses the splendor [of Lakṣmī].
The red one, the lord of the three [times], who is...
[the supreme].
The Gaṅgā
Mahākālī, seated upon a makara throne, holding a lute.
To Kṛṣṇa, the threefold...
[and] Yamunā.
To the dark-complexioned [deity]...
[the gatekeeper of the weapon-mantra].
Four-armed and four-faced, with a radiance equal to a blazing fire,
he grants boons and holds a mace, a spear, and likewise the gesture of fearlessness along with a trident.
One should meditate upon the King of Weapons (the *astra-rāja*) situated in the middle of the threshold (*dehalī*);
[this is for] Brahmā, the Lord of the Site (*vāstvadhipati*).
[He should worship] Gaṇeśa, seated upon a swan, [holding] a water-pot, in the direction of the wind (the northwest), and then in the north, with the form previously described.
In the northeast [is] Mahālakṣmī of the aforementioned form, who increases the Guru;
she is Ādhāraśakti.
Seated upon the Tortoise-stone below, having the form of the Milky Ocean,
[she rests] on the seat of Ananta.
The earth, the jasmine flower,
[the bank],
and the seat of Ananta are said to be of the same nature as yellow orpiment and the mud-born lotus.
Ananta.
Then, having pervaded that space, he saw the omnipresent Lord Ananteśa standing there,
white in color, with four faces, eight arms, and twelve eyes.
One should recollect the support of the earth as described for the fourth maṇḍala:
*dharmādi*.
Its four corners are formed by the goddesses Prabhūtā, Dharmā, and the others;
they stand in the form of lions, possessing the brilliance of the sun's rays, and are auspicious, appearing yellow and black.
Gazing at one another, they were surrounded by many lions;
their faces were terrible with fangs, they had three eyes, and their forms were fearsome.
The forms of Śiva in the ages of Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth, are without sandals;
they are placed in the corners starting from the southeast and ending with the northeast, in due order.
Non-dharma and so forth.
One should visualize those [deities] known as Adharma, Ajñāna, Avairāgya, and Anaiśvarya,
possessing variegated forms and colors, as the guardians of the directions.
One should contemplate the black and white [forms] as having such a nature;
below the seat and above it, one should visualize them as red and white.
In the south-western direction and in the region of the north-east, there is the supreme [deity] consisting of Māyā and Vidyā.
The Lotus Posture.
At the tip of the ruby is a string of pearls;
the blue lotus petal is the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara), and the white lotus is the essence of pure knowledge (Śukla-vidyā).
Then one should worship the heated [vessel] with the Vāmā and other Śaktis.
The eight Śaktis, beginning with Vāmā, who possess hands like lotuses and radiance like the rising sun, are located in the filaments starting from the east.
One should visualize the spear as white as cow’s milk, with its pericarp being *manonmanī*;
at the tips and stalks of the petals is the white solar disc of the sun.
Brahmāvat, situated in the center of the solar disc, [is there];
upon the tips of the filaments, however, is the lunar disc, white and radiant.
Viṣṇu, situated in the middle of the lunar orb, [should be meditated upon].
One should remember Rudra at the tip of the pericarp, within a mandala radiant with red light;
he stands in the midst of fire, adorned with a serpent as a sacred thread.
In the center, resembling a jar filled with milk, is the curved pericarp;
there, seated upon the mandala of Śakti, is the covering of the [deity].
The Seat of Śiva.

One should meditate upon the seat of Śiva, beginning with the earth and extending to the edge of the crooked [universe], as an all-pervasive throne; one should contemplate the Śakti on that seat of Śiva, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.

One should contemplate the form of Śiva’s body, which is free from division, as being two-pronged with its pedestal, resembling the radiance of the rising sun, and situated within the portion of the *liṅga*.
[The section] on the thirty-eight kalās.

One should arrange the limbs for the sake of accomplishment through the immediate differentiation of the Kalās: Īśāna as the head, Tatpuruṣa as the face, Aghora as the heart, Vāmadeva as the private parts, and Sadyojāta as all the limbs.

The five digits beginning with Śaśinī and the forms beginning with Brahmā are the Śaktis; they bestow fearlessness and boons, and likewise hold nooses and goads. Śaśinī is [located] above... [and] Śiva is partless (niṣkala).
With hands [holding] the earth and other crooked things...
[and] a sword, a shield, a bow, arrows, a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), and a human skull.
A water-pot, a rosary, a lower garment, and the gesture of granting fearlessness.
Bearing the Supreme Lord with his right and left hands;
or else,
[bearing] an axe, a sword, a trident, and a thunderbolt-fire in the right [hands].
In the left [hands], he holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), a bell, a serpent, a noose, and likewise kusha grass.
The power that withdraws the fire reduces the fetters to ashes;
it is the illuminator of those established in the stages who abide above Mahāmāyā.
One should know that the power which causes agitation to the Nāgas and rends all things is the noose; it is called by me the "noose-triad" known as the impurity of karma.
Her form consists of the resonance of the bell, which purifies the body of the mantra;
she is the fearlessness of all worlds and indeed the protective power.
The attainment of even enjoyment for oneself is a restraint that serves as a check;
thus, the natures of beings are manifested by noble persons through their own selves.
One should abandon [the body] with weapons in hand;
in this way, one should contemplate the body as consisting of knowledge during the growth of the *liṅga*.
The Eye.
The eye, the object of expression, the root-binding, and the piercing—
this is Īśāna.
The world, which has the appearance of crystal, is being swallowed by him;
that is Tatpuruṣa.
Wearing yellow garments, [with a crown upon his head],
[he is] Aghora.
Three-eyed, with the moon upon his crown, having a distorted face,
adorned with a garland of skulls— Aghora, the granter of all desires.
Vāmadeva.
The left [face] is red, holding a *su*...*dhārin*,
[namely] Sadyojāta.
With a white sacrificial ladle and offerings such as perfumes and flowers,
one should worship Sadyojāta, who has a single white face and hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
likewise, one should worship those [faces] beginning with Īśāna, situated in the five directions, who possess a serene appearance.
[He should be visualized] with a black form, eight hands, and faces in all directions, adorned with every ornament;
or alternatively: in his left [hands], a snake, a rosary, a blue lotus, and a citron.

The hands of the Lord hold a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting mudrā, as well as a spear; he is of reddish luster, possesses divine eyes, and his nature consists of both vision and action.
The three mandalas, beginning with Fire, which consist of the three principles (tritattva), are the support;
they possess faces as described for the limbs beginning with the Heart, and are joined with the hand-held implements and so forth.
Or, according to the teaching of Yogaśiva, one [should worship] a single [deity] with a hand holding a trident; [this applies to] the heart and the other [limbs].
The heart is like the moon, the head has the luster of refined gold,
the crest is the color of vermilion, and the armor is radiant as a horn.
Seated in the lotus posture, wearing a crown of matted hair adorned with the sun and moon,
they have three eyes and four arms, and are decorated with all ornaments.
Facing Śiva, the Śaktis are endowed with tridents and the gesture of fearlessness.
Then [he saw] the four-faced one, as well as Astrarāja, the fanged Piṅgala, and the Lord,
who possess many faces beginning with the heart-mantra, and who bestow boons and strike fear.
Or else, one should likewise visualize them in the mind as bearing tridents and lotuses. [This is] the Weapon [mantra].
The lords of the vidyās and the others are white in color; those beginning with the heart are like black, red, and the moon, and like the moon, yellow, crimson, and fire.
[He visualizes himself] with five faces and ten arms, holding a trident, a shield, and a sword as his implements;
in his right [hands] he holds a rudrākṣa rosary, and in his left, a scent-vessel and a small bell.
He carries the sun and lotus in his hands, has three eyes in every face,
possesses sixteen years of age, and is adorned with all ornaments.
With a mouth and face of terrifying form, with wide-open eyes and provided with fangs—
[this is] the Lord of the Eightfold Knowledge (Aṣṭavidyeśvara).
The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) all have four faces, ten arms like those of Śiva,
crescent moons upon their crests, reside upon lotuses, and bear various weapons.
Holding a sword, shield, bow, and arrows, they possess a water-pot and a rosary;
their hands are endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and they hold a trident and a lotus.

The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), in order, are golden, fire-colored, blue, horn-colored, moon-colored, lion-colored, red, and black; they possess the colors of their respective vehicles and have their hands joined in the *añjali* gesture.
They should be meditated upon in sequence starting from the east as having one face, matted hair,
three eyes, and being endowed with a spear and a trident, adorned with crescent moons as their head-ornaments.

he has three eyes and is [the one who is] ...ka.

The Lotus Sūtra (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra)
The discus, with the luster of a conch shell... [repeated syllables] ...the discus.
I bow to the hundred-spoked wheel in the heart and head; I worship the wheel that is dark-blue, powerful, and has a neck like a bull; I praise and prostrate before the wheel in the form of a person.
One should meditate on all [the goddesses] with hands in the añjali gesture and holding lotuses in their hands in the east, their heads marked by the vajra and other symbols; this is the fifth vow.
A certain distinction is stated regarding the unmanifest (avyakta) and the face-linga:
the deities beginning with Ananta are on the tips of the petals, and the lords of the Gaṇas are on the ears of the pedestal.
Upon the stone, the weapons of Lokeśa should be worshipped on the feet of the pedestal, together with their respective retinues, according to the distinctions of their individual pervasions.
Salutations again and again to the glorious feet of the Teacher, together with His Śakti;
salutations again and again to those who are the cause of the constant awakening of the matured self.
Having first purified the Seat of Knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), which bestows all-encompassing wisdom and is presided over by the Lord,
one should invoke her who resides upon the Seat of Knowledge with mental, verbal, and physical prostrations: "O Vāgīśvarī!"
One should invoke the Goddess into the triangle;
there, Vāgīśvara arises together with the Śiva-fire produced therein.
p. 19) || Śivāgni ||
Seated upon a white lotus throne, with four faces and four arms,
possessing a long beard, he is the embodiment of Brahmā, adorned with a crown of matted locks.
Holding a *sruk* ladle, a *maṇḍala*, and a staff with beads, with his lotus-like hands free from impurity;
or else—having a body slightly reddened, possessing three eyes, and endowed with arms bearing the weapons of Śiva.
Meditation on Śivāgnivāgīśī.

I salute Śiva, who is ever intent upon the enjoyment of the oblation offered there, who is desired by all, who resembles a fire consuming its fuel, and who is superior even to Bali and the gods, as previously described.
May there be auspiciousness.
The Sixteenfold Form.
Soma-Āskandeśvara, Candraśekhara, Vṛṣavāhana, Naṭeśvara, Gaṅgādhara, and Tripurāntaka.
Then there is Kalyāṇasundara, Ardhanārī, Pāśupata, Kaṅkāla, Keśavārtha, and after that, Bhikṣāṭana.
The grace of Caṇḍeśa, the southern [aspect] which destroys Time (Kāla),
the emergence of the Liṅga, and the sixteenfold forms of the various manifestations— these are the divisions.
The Meditation on Somāskanda.
Kṛṣṇa, whose left leg is bent and resting upon the lap of his mother, holds a deer and the gesture of fearlessness in his right hands, and carries a battle-axe and a bracelet in his left hands.

I worship Guha, the Lord of the Cave, who is accompanied in the center by the Goddess whose other foot is slumbering while leaning upon his left arm, and who is joined by Skanda, who holds two lotuses in his hands. 1.
Meditation on Candraśekhara
With a broad face and eyes, possessing a gentle and amorous expression, his hands bestowing fearlessness and boons, his body marked by the lunar disc upon his crown,
with straight limbs and even feet, he stands in the *sthānaka* posture, glowing like coral.
Holding an axe and a deer, he stands upon a lotus seat. || 2 ||
Meditation on [the deity] mounted upon a bull.
On the right side, he should hold a staff and a bracelet upon his hand placed on the head of the Lord of Cows (Kamadeva);
on the left, I shall describe him as holding half [the moon] and a black axe in his other pair of hands;
with a bull behind him, serene, endowed with three eyes, and wearing a crown with braided locks.
On the left is the Lord Īśa, accompanied by Gaurī, joined with the Vijaya mountain, and mounted upon his bull.
|| Meditation on Naṭeśa ||
He has one face, four arms, and three eyes; in his left [hands] he holds a *dhattūra* flower and the moon, while his right hands extend toward a peacock feather and an upward-pointing lotus.
He wears a *svastika* and earrings on the left, and holds a *ḍamaru* drum, the Ganges, and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*).
I bow to Naṭeśa, whose matted locks are disheveled, who stands with a body smeared with ashes that shine like the night.
p. 21) || Meditation on Gaṅgādhara ||
He placed his sinless left hand, embraced by the Goddess, upon her right hand; O Caṇḍikā, he was speaking pleasant words nearby,
and with his right hand he was firmly joining the pure Gaṅgā to the tip of his matted locks above.
I worship Paśupati Gaṅgādharesha, who holds a black antelope in his left hand. || 5 ||
The Meditation on the Burning of Tripura
I praise the burner of Tripura, whose face is uniquely smiling, who possesses the brilliance of ten million suns,
who holds in his palms a black axe, a bow, and an arrow,
and whose right and left feet are raised upward.
He stood there, the supreme lord of the quarters, with the moon as his crest-jewel and three eyes.
The Meditation on Kalyāṇasundara (Auspiciously Beautiful)
I bow to Him who has a crown with the young moon shining like a jasmine flower, who wears a dark blue garment,
and who holds the lotus-hand of the Daughter of the Mountain resting upon His left thigh;
who holds an axe in His raised right hand, and who is attended by the Lotus-born Brahmā standing before Him.
I worship the auspicious deity with a smiling face, who is supported by Viṣṇu on his left side. || 7 ||
The Meditation on Ardhanārīśvara

Bearing the form of both male and female in his body, with the reddish luster of the moon, matted locks, and a serpent-earring, wearing a tiger-skin garment upon his forearm, and treading upon a bull with his feet, he stands with [the goddess] on his right.
In the left [hand], he holds a dark blue lotus with its stalk; his lotus-feet are straight—this is the meditation on Pāśupati.
With a curved brow, red and thin, and three eyes, he holds a trident and the gesture of fearlessness, as well as a hand-drum (ḍamaru) in his left;
thus adorned with the crescent moon on his crest, he bears the Pāśupata weapon in his left hand.
I worship the Lord Pāśupateśa, who, with his right hand joined in añjali, bestows grace upon Arjuna—who is endowed with firm devotion—using that weapon which shines like ten million suns. 9.
The Meditation on the Skeleton

Having a reddish luster, a smiling moon-like face, and a crown; with his left staff-like arm holding the three eyes and a lotus hand bearing the skull-tambourine (*kaṅkāla-vīṇā*) of the Hundred-Sustainer (Brahmā);
holding a staff in the right [hand], and in the other [the fourth] a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), positioned respectively on the right and left sides.
I worship Lord Kaṅkāla, who incessantly holds a ṭaṅka and a black antelope.
Meditation on the Meaning of the Lion's Roar (Haryarthadhyāna)

On his right side is [the form] with the luster of coral, wearing a crown of the moon, adorned with ashes and rudrākṣa beads, holding a chisel and a hammer, endowed with an eye situated on the forehead, and richly clothed in deerskin;
on his left side is [the form] with a dark-blue luster, joined with a mountain-crown, and beautified by yellow garments.
I bow to Hari, the bestower of boons, who holds the resplendent Pāñcajanya conch and is joined by a hand granting boons.
The Meditation on the Lord of Alms-Gathering (p. 23).

White in luster and with auspicious eyes, holding a hand-drum and a sprout of *dūrvā* grass in his right hands, and a trident and a skull-cup joined together in his left; wearing excellent sandals upon his feet, bearing matted locks and the crescent moon, and carrying a deer in his right [hand] and [the moon] in his left.
I worship the Lord of the Alms-round, who is truly endowed with the qualities of the [three] vehicles. || 12 ||
The Meditation on the Grace of Caṇḍeśa.
Three-eyed, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, resembling a crystal gem, holding an axe and a black antelope skin;
with the beauty of one leg bent while the other rests upon a lotus pedestal;
bearing a garland of flowers in his two hands together with the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī); seated upon a bull—[I meditate on him].
O Caṇḍanātha, [I seek] your grace—the one with the parasol, praised by pleasant sounds, and [bestowed upon] Caṇḍakaṇa. 13.
Meditation on Dakṣiṇāmūrti

May the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who dwells upon the four elements, eternally manifest before me— he who stands with one foot placed upon the earth and the other raised above it, holding in his lotus-like hands a serpent, the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyānamudrā*), the flame of fire, and a book, O my supreme Guru! 14.
The Meditation on Śrī Kālanātha
With three hands, he displays a well-honed axe, a stainless trident, and a noose;
with his other left hand, he manifests his own primordial power as Gaurī.

With his left foot slightly bent, his stainless [feet] having destroyed the garland of the sun's rays, and his feet worshipped by the gods—may that auspicious Śrī Kālanātha, whose form is free from blemish, be served. 15.
Meditation on the Emergence of the Liṅga.

One should meditate upon the Lord, whose measurement is determined by the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), who has a crest of matted locks upon his linga-form, and whose hands rest upon his hips; he is dark-complexioned, holding a deer and the gesture of fearlessness in his left hands, while in his right hands he holds an axe and an immeasurable foot-ornament; he is crowned with a diadem and accompanied by Brahmā and Acyuta.
One should meditate upon the pure Haṃsa-kola situated below the obstruction, arising from the Liṅga. || 16 ||
The meditation on the sixteen planets is completed.
|| Meditation on the Goddess ||
He should have eyes like the moon and fire,
and hold a lotus, the gesture of granting boons, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary of *japā* flowers, and a bracelet; he should be adorned with ornaments of snow and possess a variegated face.
Whose essential nature is the supreme jewel shining upon his lofty crown. || 1 ||
The Supreme Goddess is dark-complexioned, two-eyed, and two-armed; she stands in the *tribhaṅgī* posture with her right and left feet bent;
she holds a blue lotus and a water-pot at her breasts, while her other hand hangs down.
Furthermore:

Dark-complexioned, holding a blue lotus, radiant with a crest-jewel and a jeweled earring, skilled in the use of weapons such as the rosary-bead, sweet-voiced, and with her hand raised holding a white lotus.

I bow to Gāyatrī, whose face is red, who is most playful, who brings others under her control, whose eyes are like lotuses, who dwells within the temple of Śiva’s desire, and who is the beloved of the Lord of Dance.
Once again:
The equal bending of Śambhu’s power is described as that which is without eyes, the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and the excellent ground;
it is indeed the hanging lotus from the right hand, with its face possessing the essence of the mind in a state of modesty.
The meditation on Vardhanī.
She has two eyes, possesses a white complexion, and is endowed with four arms;
she is adorned with a basket-shaped crown and decorated with necklaces and armlets.
She should smear her fingers with the sacrificial thread and upper garment,
and she should mark her breasts with saffron or worship her face with it upon her ear.
Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess Vardhanī in the midst of the water, holding a noose and a goad, and bestowing the gestures of granting boons and protection from fear;
One should place [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and worship it; I bow down.
Meditation on the Six-Armed Goddess.
With a dark complexion and three faces, likewise with six arms holding curd-mixture (cāmikṣā),
adorned with all ornaments, and possessing good fortune and two sandals.
Holding a pomegranate fruit and a lotus in his left and right hands respectively,
as well as a rosary and a noose, and likewise displaying the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons.
Thus, with worship, I bow to that which is indeed the very form of meditation.
Meditation on Naṭeśadevī.
She has two arms and a beautiful face, is endowed with two eyes,
wears a crown adorned with a casket, and possesses dark blue locks of hair.
One should visualize the Goddess, whose hips and breasts are broad, who holds a single lotus in her left hand, while her right hand holds a blue lotus, and who is adorned with all ornaments.
Having meditated upon the Goddess, who is clothed in fine silk, adorned with a garland of bilva fruits,
and seated upon a white lotus throne, I bow down to her.
The Goddess:
The goddess is yellow in color, seated upon a lion, holding a trident and a mirror in her two hands; she wears a basket-shaped crown and is adorned with pearls and other ornaments.
Having meditated upon the Goddess adorned with all ornaments, I bow down to her. || 8 ||
The Goddess is seated upon a red lotus throne, white in complexion with a smiling face;
she has one face and four hands, and is radiant with a crown and tiara.
Holding a noose and a goad, granting boons and fearlessness,
her hips are closely joined, and she is adorned with pearl necklaces.

"I pay homage to the goddess Mahādevī, who is worshipped by gods and asuras and is highly honored by the wives of the sages. Having meditated thus, one should worship the Great Goddess with this mantra.
The Goddess should meditate upon the goddess Manonmanī, who resembles pure crystal.
I worship her who has four arms and three eyes, adorned with dark-blue locks of hair, possessing a beautiful smile and a lovely face, and holding a noose and a goad.
The meditation on the *manonmani* [state] of the *kukkuṭayāli*.
Then, one should visualize the goddess with her head facing south, her beautiful feet turned toward Gomukha, her two arms holding water at the end [of the gesture],
her yoni directed toward the *arghya*, and possessing a white, excellent *liṅga*.
He established the nature of Sadāśiva and Manonmanī. || 11 ||
The power of vital breath.
Red in color, seated within a red lotus with spreading petals,
with red lips formidable with passion, possessing three eyes that easily carry the memory [of the deity],
holding in his six hands a citron, a sugarcane, a noose, a sprout, a bow, and an arrow, as well as a skull-cup.
I bow to her who, though possessing the body of a child, holds the power to protect the entire great earth.

From him who holds in his lotus-hands a noose, a bow of sugarcane, a sword, and another goad, as well as five arrows, and who is accompanied by her who has three eyes and rests upon a skull at the corner of his mouth— she who is rich with full breasts; from that one who stands upon a red lotus with petals glowing like red bodhi, whose lineage is rooted in the red water-lily...
May the Goddess, who has the hue of the rising sun, the supreme power of life-force, be the bringer of happiness to us. 13.
The Four-Armed Goddess.
O four-armed one, adorned with a crescent moon, whose breasts are full, red as saffron dye,
holding in your hands a sugar-cane, a noose, a goad, and flower-arrows— salutations to you, O sole Mother of the World! (14)
Vāgīśvarī (The Mistress of Speech)
Vāgīśvara is indeed the Lord of the Sacrifice (Yāgeśvara), abiding as Bindu and Nāda;
Bindu is declared to be Vāgīśvara, and likewise Nāda is Vāgīśvara.
One should know him as having five faces, three eyes, four arms, and two feet; he is white in color and displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
She holds a rosary in her left hand and a *kūrca* (bundle of kuśa grass) in her right hand;
she is described as Vāgīśvarī, and after her follows Vāgīśa.
O Eight-Armed Goddess!
Her body is white in complexion and in the full bloom of youth; she possesses two breasts adorned with high-set necklaces;
her face bears the crescent moon and she has eight arms; she is radiant and beautiful, graced by a jeweled crown.
O bearer of the fear-dispelling goad, noose, and mace; devoted to the fire, the serpent, and the *japā* beads;
with golden jewels upon your ears and beautiful earrings; seated comfortably on a lotus throne clothed in the garments of night!
May there be auspiciousness; I bow at the feet of Śaṅkara. || 16 ||
I bow to her who has the luster of the dawn, who is three-eyed, adorned with a jeweled crown and a beautiful red forehead-ornament;
she shines with nooses, goads, lower bows, and arrows held in her lotus-like hands;
her body is draped with a necklace of large pearls shimmering upon the slopes of her full and lofty breasts.
I take refuge in the Sovereign Lady, whose hands hold a clinging lotus and who wears beautiful red garments.
p.
29) || Annapūraṇī ||

I salute the Goddess Annapūrṇeśvarī, who wears her hair as a garment, is adorned with pearl necklaces, possesses the weight of full breasts, has a beloved waist-belt, and holds a cup filled with divine nectar and food.
The Jewel of the Mind
Resplendent like the rising sun, she is the state beyond mind (manonmanī).
The Form of the Goddesses.
And each of these supreme goddesses, possessing individual powers, becomes fourfold at the time of their manifestation:
as Bhavānī in the form of enjoyment, as Kālī through the wrath of Viṣṇu, and as Mahiṣī and Durgā.
O Goddess!
Seated upon the pedestal in the center of a red lotus throne, with crimson locks of hair falling down to her ears,
beautifully draped in fine red garments, and possessing a face as lovely as the petals of a red lotus.
The goddess was adorned with a beautiful garland of red flowers, anointed with red sandalwood paste, and her body was likewise smeared with it. || 21 ||
O Goddess!
She whose body shines with a white complexion, who delights in white garments and the essence of nectar;
she whose eyes possess the fragrance of white flowers, and who radiates the splendor of a white lotus face. || 22 ||
Kāmāri (The Enemy of Desire)
She who is the left-hand consort of the Enemy of Kāma (Śiva), seated upon a lotus throne, bestowing desired boons, with bracelets and a crest-jewel upon her hands;
her limbs adorned with the luster of the *kadamba* flower, she whose glance protects the world and whose breast is marked by the crescent moon. (23)
O Goddess!
She who sports with the orb of the moon as her face, who is intent upon the gestures of granting fearlessness, the goad, and the noose;
she whose two breasts are prominent and radiant with a necklace, and who beautifully wears a crown of jewels and gems.
[She is] the dwelling on the left side of Śiva, the conqueror, who protects people and illuminates the world. || 24 ||
Manonmani (She who transcends the mind)
O Great Goddess Manonmanī, Śaṅkarī, Bhramarāmbikā,
Kālī, Karālikā, Aṅkāli, Kālāgni, and she who takes any form at will!

O you whose body is adorned with earrings, necklaces, crowns, bracelets, and armlets; O you who wear earrings and have skulls, arrows, and tridents as your ornaments; O you who hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and the mace!
O you who possess the forms of the discus, conch, bow, sword, noose, and goad, resplendent with golden garments and excellent ornaments, O lady with beautiful hair!
O Śaṅkarī, who shines with every ornament, O mistress of life, O sole protectress of all the worlds, O Śaṅkarī, salutations again and again! || 25 ||
The Commander-in-Chief.
I bow to the daughter of the Moon, who is yellow-hued and holds a lotus, adorned with divine garments and ornaments,
with her left hand hanging down, the daughter of Mahendra, wearing garlands of Mandāra flowers;
she whose speech is honored by the gods, moon-faced, standing to the left of the Lord of Gods.
I worship the goddess Senā, who is adorned with divine ornaments, who has two eyes, and who is posed in the *tribhaṅgī* stance. || 26 ||
O General!
The right foot is bent and the left foot is extended;
the right hand holds a blue lotus and the left hand is extended downward.
Red in color, with wide eyes, blazing with a diadem and crown,
adorned with all ornaments, he possesses the very form of Devasenā.
Yoginī
On the left side [of the deity] is the Yoginī, endowed with two arms;
she holds a blue lotus in her right hand, while a bracelet hangs from her left.
And likewise, seated in the lotus posture, the yoginī should practice meditation. || 28 ||
Meditation on Vallīśvarī
[Visualize] Śyāmā, holding a blue lotus, her ears radiant with jeweled earrings,
her right hand hanging down, her crown and tiara standing high;
she is joined with [her consort] at their mutual glances, stands on the left of him who was born from the Śara reed-thicket, and wears a garland of forest flowers.
One should meditate upon Vallīśvarī, whose face is like coral. || 29 ||
The left foot is bent in the *vallī* posture while the right foot is extended;
the left hand holds a lotus, and the right hand is hanging down.
Golden-hued, large-eyed, and wearing a golden-colored crown.
(32) It is joined with the bodice of the station (*sthānakañcuka*) and has the nature of the great creeper (*mahāvalli*). || 30 ||
On the right side is Bhoginī, endowed with the color of jewels;
she holds a *kaṭindika* in her right hand and a white lotus in her left.
Seated upon a lotus throne and adorned with all ornaments, one should worship Skanda’s form, which is described as being like the moon and Varuṇa.
Vallīśvarī
On the right side of Skanda is the auspicious Śyāmalā Vallikā,
adorned with a crown and tiara, possessing two eyes and joined hands.
With the left hand holding a lotus, the right hand is bent;
with the right hand extended, he stands firmly on his right foot.
She had golden earrings in her ears and was adorned with all ornaments;
she was dressed in white garments and decorated with white garlands.
"Seated in the *baddhaparyaṅka* posture, endowed with the two [qualities], and with a slightly smiling face"—thus is meditation described;
this is called the form of Vallikā. (32)
Dark-complexioned, with two eyes, one face, and two hands;
wearing a crown set with the nine jewels, and holding a blue lotus in his left hand.
In her hand she holds a water-pot, and she is exceedingly beautiful;
she wears a garland of jasmine and campaka flowers and is adorned with every ornament.
Likewise, one should meditate upon Vallikā on the right side of Skanda. (33)
O General!
Having two hands, two eyes, two feet, and one face,
he wears a crown of pearls and gems, and holds a blue lotus in his right hand.
On the left side of Skanda are a bracelet on the left hand, yellow garments,
a garland of *pārijāta* flowers, and a blue lotus.
Having meditated upon the form of the army, let them worship it with repeated salutations: "Namo namaḥ. || 34 ||
Bhadrakālī.

With a dark body, red garments, and arms like flames, she possesses the splendor of the suns of the eight directions; holding a trident, a hand-drum, and a sword, with a skull-bowl fashioned as a *ḍamaru* in her left hand,
another bell, a shield, and a plough together with a moving [implement], she is fierce in appearance and three-eyed.
This immeasurable triple world is the form of Cāmuṇḍā; O Bhadrakālī, I bow to you. || 35 ||
One should meditate upon Mahākālī, the destroyer of all enemies, the one uniquely worshipped by all the worlds,
whose abode is dark and terrifying, and who resembles a dark cloud.
With terrifying fangs, she possessed three eyes resembling the crests of flames from the three sacrificial fires;
her ornaments were formed by eight serpents, and her body filled the eight directions.
She has a triangular form, rides upon a lion, possesses a single pot-bellied breast,
and is adorned with a thousand arms, staffs, and a thousand weapons.
She possesses the splendor of a garland of tinkling bells hanging down as far as her ankles;
she is the supreme Śivā, intoxicated by drinking the blood of all her enemies.
It destroys the desires of adversaries and bestows sovereignty upon others.
Having thus meditated upon Mahākālī, who holds a trident, a skull, and a noose, and who takes away the life-breaths of enemies, one should recite the mantra: "Be present here! (35).
Kaṅkāladevī
She has one face and three eyes, is adorned with matted locks and a crescent moon,
and holds a trident and an axe in her hands, O Lord.
One should meditate upon the four-armed Goddess as bestowing fearlessness and boons, holding in her hands a rosary of elephants' tusks, a garland of severed heads, and a necklace of nine jewels.
She who laughs with loud, boisterous laughter, who holds the medicinal herbs as the mistress of the cremation ground,
and who is surrounded by bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, brahmarākṣasas, and dānavas.
One should worship Kūṃtyāmāṇḍī, who is adorned with kūśmāṇḍa fruits, who possesses great strength,
who is dressed in red garments and jewel ornaments, who holds a large skull-bowl in her hand, and who is auspicious.
Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess, who effects the great dissolution along with her millions of attendants and others, the wise one should recite the name-mantra.
The Name of the Presence of Blood.
She who has one face and two eyes,
and who holds a trident and a chisel.
She has a red face, a red body, and wears red garlands.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, possessing a terrifying face with a loud laugh,
she has nine sounds at her feet and is attended by hosts of attendants at her sides.
She who wears garlands of elephants, skulls, and serpents;
whose limbs are adorned with the ashes of the cremation ground; the destroyer of all rākṣasas.
His wife was dressed in red garments, adorned with red clothing,
formidable with her finger-ornaments, and accompanied by a loud, boisterous laugh.
Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess, the destroyer of enemies, || 37 ||
Bhadrakālī.
And Kālī, who likewise has four arms and possesses a dark blue form,
holds a trident and a skull-cup in her hands, while others hold a ḍamaru drum and a noose.
O Bhadrakālī, [one should meditate upon] her own form as being endowed with upright hair, terrifying with fierce fangs, and either seated or standing. (38)
She has a dark complexion and wears red garments; her eight lotus-hands on the left side hold a flaming trident, a vetāla, a sword, and a hand-drum (ḍamaruka),
while those on the right side hold a serpent, a noose, a discus, and a sword joined with fire.
This is the form of Cāmuṇḍī, the subduer of all; O Bhadrakālī, salutations to you! || 39 ||
p. 36) || Meditation on the Goddess Reṇukā ||

In his left hands he holds a trident and a skull-cup, and in the other [right] hands he bears a sword and a drum with three cords; he has three eyes and is resplendent, adorned with the eight ornaments of a serpent.
He resembles millions of Rudras at the end of an eon, wearing various blazing ornaments.
I take refuge in the venerable Reṇukā, whose left foot is supported by Dakṣa and remains asleep. || 40 ||
With a body the color of the morning sun, with hair like fire, holding a casket, a hand-drum, a trident, a sword, and a skull-cup in his hands,
and having serpents for the flames of his eyes, he is seated upon the throne of a heroic lion.
I worship Goddess Reṇukā, the mother of the entire world. || 41 ||

We approach and worship Goddess Reṇukā, who holds a red-colored severed head and a sword in her hands, as well as a trident, a skull-cup, and a hand-drum; she who bears a spear, a noose, a mace, and a sword. (42)
Cāmuṇḍī
She has four arms and three eyes, possesses the form of the dark-hued goddess Kālamekhala,
has a face made terrifying by her fangs, and is clothed in a tiger skin.
She holds a sword and a trident in her hands, is auspicious with a skull and the gesture of granting boons,
adorned with a garland of tinkling bells, and has the form of one mounted upon a corpse.

One should meditate upon the youthful Śakti, who has drunk from the breast of Śiva-Śakti that is adorned with serpents; having meditated thus on this Śakti, O Cāmuṇḍī, one should contemplate the form.
p. 37) || Cāmuṇḍī ||
Reddish in luster, clad in yellow garments, with a lotus-face and adorned with a crescent moon, she is endowed with divine rubies and distinguished by ornaments of various jewels;
she shines with beautiful flowers, is worshipped by the entire host of enemies, and has eyes as broad as bilva leaves.
I meditate upon Śaṅkarī, who is Cāmuṇḍā, whose weapon is a severed head, and who is a river of nectar for the enemy clans. || 44 ||
|| Durgā ||
She was well-dressed, with dark blue hair shaped like the petals of a blue lotus,
possessing beautiful breasts and a lovely face, and adorned with all kinds of ornaments.
Holding a conch and a discus with her right hand, she bestows fearlessness;
the goddess rests her left arm upon her thigh, she who effects the destruction of the Daityas.
Having meditated upon Durgā—who is equipped with a breastplate, who stands upon the head of a buffalo, and who is joined with her protective retinue—I bow down to her. || 45 ||
The Meditation on Eight-Armed Durgā.
Having one face, with flaming hair, red eyes, and eight arms,
he is endowed with a dark blue complexion and likewise possesses terrible teeth.
One foot is placed by him upon the head of Mahiṣa,
while the other is raised and placed upon Mahiṣa’s waist.
And I shall describe [the form] of Mahiṣa: from the tip of the trident, he has arisen with two hands, holding a skull and a sword along with the trident.
One should place the bow and arrow, as well as the mace and the discus,
at the tips of the hands on the left and right sides of the body.
Having meditated upon Durgā, who adorns herself with all fears, I bow down to her. || 46 ||
Meditation on Kāmāriśakti.

She has a dark complexion and wears red garments; her two eyes emit blazing flames. She possesses eight sacrificial altars, and in the tips of her hands she holds a trident, a vetāla, and a sword, along with a hand-drum (ḍamaruka) in her left hand and a skull-cup.
In her other [hands] she holds a shield, a noose, and a plow together with a goad; she is fierce and has a mad appearance.
I meditate upon this form of Kaumārī, the bringer of peace who brings the three worlds under her control. || 47 ||
O Goddess Reṇukā!
Holding in her lotus-like hands a skull-bowl, a trident, a sword, a bow,
and a drum, she has three eyes and is radiant with the eight ornaments of serpents;
resembling millions of suns at the end of an eon, she is adorned with various shimmering jewels.
One should take refuge in Śrī Reṇukā, whose feet rest upon the ground with her legs tucked up by her right side. || 48 ||
|| Meditation on the Fortress ||

I take refuge in Goddess Durgā, who resembles gold, whose beauty is enhanced by the crescent moon, who rests upon a conch, who holds a formidable trident in her hand, who has three eyes, who sits upon a golden lotus, who is clad in yellow garments, and who is gracious. 49.
The Meditation on Mūkāmbikā
O you who bestow bliss, whose protective flame shines like a bandhūka flower in the central corner of the root-lotus,
and who steals the luster of the beloved of Videha with the blaze of your flames!
I meditate upon the Blessed Mother Mūkāmbikā, who is cherished by Śiva, who wears blue earrings, who is clad in a blue upper garment, and who dwells in Kolpura. || 50 ||
Mahālakṣmī
With her left and right hands, she holds a *śrīphala* fruit and a lotus;
she is being approached by two golden jars from which great prosperity (*mahāśrī*) emerges like elephants.
Mahālakṣmī has two eyes, the appearance of saffron, one face, and four arms;
she wears a crown and a tiara, and is endowed with full hips and breasts.
The goddess, seated upon a white lotus-throne, possesses two arms; she is adorned with golden ornaments, wears excellent white garments, and rests upon a white lotus.
Having meditated upon Lakṣmī, who grants fearlessness and boons, who is adorned with all ornaments, and who always pacifies Rudra, I pay homage to her. || 52 ||
Mahālakṣmī has four arms and two eyes, is adorned with a jeweled crown,
possesses a yellow complexion, and is embellished with all ornaments.
In the right hand is a lotus, and in the left hand is a bilva fruit;
on the two sides of the two hands, they display the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
I bow to Lakṣmī, who is meditated upon as bestowing the consecration by means of two elephants with pot-like frontal globes on her left and right sides.
p. 40) || Mahālakṣmī ||

Those [goddesses] who sit upon lotus-thrones, with broad hips and eyes as wide as lotus petals, with deep-spiraled navels and shoulders weighed down by the weight of their breasts, wearing white garments and upper cloths;
they are established by divine splendors, lordly elephants, and golden jars adorned with clusters of jewels.
She, who holds a lotus in her hand, dwells eternally in my home, which is endowed with every auspiciousness.
The Meditation on the Lotus
The lovely stalk is like a ruby, possessing a luster equal to a blue lotus;
the sprout has the appearance of coral, and the radiant petal is beautifully colored.
One should visualize the filament as golden in color, with a string of pearls at its tip;
in its center, one should meditate upon the birth of Lakṣmī, resembling the color of a lotus.
O Mistress of the Supreme Niṣkala!
Wearing white garlands and garments, and anointed with white perfumes and unguents,
she rests her left hand upon her left knee and holds the *vīṇā* mudrā in her right hand.
O Goddess, having meditated upon her who is seated on a lotus-throne, adorned with all ornaments, and who is the supreme, partless, formless reality, [I offer] salutations again and again.
O Mistress of the Pārijāta Tree!

I shall meditate daily upon Him who is adorned with white garments, unguents, and ornaments, whose body is as bright as the moon-crested Lord, and who holds in His hands a book, a jar of nectar, a lute, and a garland.
Mātaṅgī.
I meditate upon Him who sits upon a jeweled throne, possessing a beautiful voice like that of a parrot, with limbs as dark as a sapphire, holding a lotus and a crescent moon in His hands,
playing the lute; He wears white water-lilies, a yellow garland, shimmering dust [on His body], and red garments.
Mātaṅgī, her limbs adorned, overcome by the intoxication of honey-wine, with her hair shining with various ointments. || 58 ||
Manonmani (She who transcends the mind)

I consider you, O Great One, who possesses a divine and super-divine form such as that of the Mother (Mātṛkā), to be truly great; I honor you, the source of all mantras, who are accompanied by the Siddhas.
I honor you, the Great One, the Vidyā born of Manonmanī, for you are indeed the beautiful one who pervades all.
I pay homage.
The Youthful Supreme Goddess.

May she who is worshipped by the networks of the dawn’s rays, who holds a rosary and a book in her hands while her other hands are auspicious and hold a blue lotus and a white lily, and whose nature is eternal auspiciousness— may that young maiden dwell within my heart.
Śakti-lakṣmī (The Goddess of Power and Fortune)

Śrī Śakti Lakṣmī, who has the color of fresh gold, whose six upper arms are adorned with a pair of lotuses, a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows, and who is beautified by well-applied perfumes, garments, and garlands.
O Sovereign Lady of the Unborn’s Womb!

Yellowish-red and radiant with two [hands], wearing a noose as her garment and holding a lute and a thunderbolt in her hands, she bears the crescent moon upon her crest; she is three-eyed and possesses the great form of Artha.
The Meditation on the Wish-Fulfilling Cow, the Sovereign of Non-Existence.

I meditate in my heart upon Amṛteśvarī, who is adorned with white garments and fragrant unguents, who holds a book and a rosary in her two arms, who is graced by a digit of the moon, and who has assumed the form of the wish-fulfilling cow. (63)
O Bhuvaneśvarī!

I worship Ratneśvarī, who possesses the luster of a thousand rising suns, is adorned with red garments, and holds a noose, a goad, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands.
The Fortune of Good Luck (Saubhāgyalakṣmī)

Adorned with variegated garments and ornaments, anointed with fragrant unguents, possessing the hue of excellent jewels, and receiving worship with delightful white flowers, others offered a ladle of rubies and a golden vessel that was difficult to hold, to the Supreme One.
The Meditation on Vārāharatneśvarī
I praise her who is blue in complexion, holding the Earth, the Rod of Punishment, and the Vajra in her arms;
whose face has waves of light from her fangs, who possesses three eyes, and whose crown is embraced by the serpent Maṇḍa and the blood-stained sword.
The goddess Sarasvatī.
Resembling pure crystal, with a radiance equal to the orb of the sun,
possessing a luster like a white kunda flower, she is auspicious, having reached the state of the navel of the smile.
One should meditate upon the four-armed Goddess, adorned with pearl necklaces,
holding a rosary and a goad in two hands, and bearing a book in [the other] two hands.
Adorned with a white garment resembling a mirror, she possessed beautiful breasts and a waist like the altar; her crest was fashioned in the shape of a crescent moon.
She is endowed with matted locks and a skull-bowl, her face resembling the full moon,
and adorned with bracelets made of gold, jewels, and other precious materials.
Illuminating the three worlds with her armlets, girdle, and other ornaments, she possessed a neck like a conch shell and lovely red lips, adorned with various decorations on her left side.
One should meditate upon Sarasvatī, who has three eyes, is adorned with golden anklets,
is the dawn of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahma), and is fully absorbed in the desire for knowledge.
Sarasvatī.
I shall worship the Mother of the World, Śāradā, of pure radiance—
the Goddess seated upon a white lotus-throne, possessing three eyes and adorned with the moon.

Having meditated upon the form of Bhāratī—clad in white garments, four-armed, wearing a crown of nine jewels, and holding a book, a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, and likewise a red lotus—and having worshipped her, one should say: "Salutations to you. (68)
Sarasvatī.
They have four arms and three eyes, and are likewise white in color;
they hold a rosary in the right hand and a book in the left hand,
while with the [other] right hand they show the *pada* and with the [other] left hand a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*).
And one should worship Sarasvatī, who is adorned with pearl necklaces and all ornaments, by means of that which brings all the worlds under its sole control.
Sarasvatī.

Her radiant body is anointed with glorious sandalwood paste; she is adorned with white garments, a garland of jasmine flowers, and shimmering earrings; she is decorated with a brilliantly shining necklace of pearls;
she holds a book that resounds with the sound of divine knowledge and wears a rosary of rudrākṣa beads.
May Vāgdevī, the mother of the three worlds, dwell for a long time within our lotus-like faces. 70.

One should always worship this Goddess Sarasvatī— the self-born mother of many worlds, the bestower of desired fruits, adorned with three forms, possessing three eyes, and the embodiment of sacred knowledge— by means of that which is worthy of praise.

Out of devotion, I have approached this beloved sacrificial cow, whose hoof-prints are colored by the shade [of her presence] near the footstool, and upon the tips of whose hooves the sprouts of jewels set in the crowns of the Asuras and Asura-lords are reflected.
She who possesses the luster of jasmine, the moon, and snow,
endowed with four arms, holding a crystal rosary with one hand, and likewise a white lotus, a parrot, and a book with another.
May the goddess of speech, who shines with a luster resembling jasmine, the moon, a conch, crystal, and gems, and who is ever-pleased, dwell forever within my mouth. 73.
O Bhuvaneśvarī!
She who possesses a luster equal to the rising sun, who has surpassed the fresh *japā* flower and the crescent moon as her head-ornament,

who wears a crown of light, who is three-eyed, whose earrings shine with various gems, who is as beautiful as a lotus, who is adorned with necklaces, triple-strand chains, and a girdle, and who is made variegated by bracelets of excellent jewels and her own radiance— [I bow to her].
I bow to Ambikā, who holds a noose, a goad, and an ankusha, and who displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
O Goddess Annapūrṇeśvarī!

The virtuous remember the beloved of the enemy of Smara— she who is as fair as the rising orb of the thousand-rayed sun, who bears the weight of pearl ornaments and a lute hanging from her breasts, and who holds in her hands a ruby ladle and a vessel of honey.
The Single-Syllable Lakṣmī Mantra
Golden-hued, clad in white garments, displaying the two gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with her hands, she holds an elephant trunk raised up and a golden jar filled with nectar.
Obeisance to Lakṣmī, the single-syllabled one, who is radiant with all ornaments. [This is] the meditation on the Sovereign of Supreme Light.

She has four hands holding a noose, a goad, a boon-granting gesture, and a gesture of fearlessness; she is three-eyed and radiant; she wears red garlands and garments, and is beautifully adorned with red clothes.
We worship, saying: "I bow to the supreme light of red color. || 77 ||
Siddhalakṣmīḥ

One should worship the goddess known as Śuddhalakṣmī, the sovereign of excellent jewels, who possesses a golden luster, is adorned with deep red ornaments, holds a ripe talaṅga fruit and a boon-granting gesture, wears variegated garments, and is exceedingly beautiful with fine unguents.
|| Meditation on Tūyīmba ||
Adorned with flowers of the *punnāga*, *ambuja*, *jāti*, *campaka*, and *bakula*,
she holds a bow made of sugarcane, arrows of radiant splendor, and a noose and goad.

In the center, within the abode of the infinitely coiled serpent that is emerging, in the auspicious *kalpa* of *dara*, in the *nāda* whose nature is the essence of the flavor of sound— there, with the nine *nādas*, one should worship the Mother of the Veda.
The Meditation on the Goddess.

Adorned with jasmine, blue lotuses, *vakula*, and *campaka* flowers, as well as white gems, water-lilies, and *punnāga* and *mallikā* blossoms; beautifully decorated with necklaces and garlands, and sprinkled with excellent white perfumes and unguents.
Holding a noose, a goad, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, she is well-worshipped by the God of gods and the God of the gods.
O Goddess Jyeṣṭhā!
The goddess, accompanied by a maiden and a son, joined by two *khārjukāka* birds,
wearing red garments, and adorned with a pearl necklace.
Then, having made the wife of Kali— who is adorned with all ornaments and has a crow as her vehicle— the object of meditation, one should remember the mantra as follows.
Jyeṣṭhā.
She is mounted upon the hand of one whose banner is a crow, seated comfortably on the lap of Kāla;
at her sides are her daughter and son, as well as the jewel and the bull-leader.
The boar-faced one is red in color, with a luster like that of a bull's gem;
there is a bull on the right side and likewise a gem on the left side.
Salutations, salutations to the wife of Kali, who is adorned with every ornament. || 82 ||
|| Meditation on the Chariot ||
The supreme guide should visualize the chariot as having the form of a person:
the two feet are the wheel-base (pādacakra), and the region of the knees is the pin (kīlaka).
The thighs are said to be one *tala* in height, the region of the hips two *talas*,
the region of the navel three *talas*, and the abdomen likewise four *talas*.
The fifth [seat] is the location of the heart, as well as the [seat] beginning with Stambhaka;
the remainder is said to be the mouth, [to be covered] with a variegated cloth or a hide.
A cord, a tube, a stretched thread, a waist-string, and a small bell;
ornaments of gold, silver, iron, bronze, and copper.
Having meditated upon him as having a horse for a vehicle, with a cord and a fine iron plowshare,
endowed with all ornaments, and beautified by his adornments.
The chariot had the form of a man and was the vehicle of Śiva-Śaṅkara. || 83 ||
The Meditation on the Seven Mothers.
Brahmī has four faces, is yellow in color, possesses eight arms,
is endowed with eight eyes, and is seated upon a swan vehicle.
He wore a diadem and crown as well as diamond earrings;
he was clad in yellow garments and beautifully adorned with a yellow parasol.
She grants fearlessness and boons, possesses eight garlands and a shaven head, holds a vajra and ornaments, and is resplendent with all kinds of jewelry.
Having thus meditated upon that which is described as being of such a form, possessing the nature of Brahman, (verse 84).
O Māheśvarī!
Endowed with five colors and possessing ten arms,
he has fifteen eyes and is equal in radiance to the five colors.
She holds a skull-cup, a goad, a staff, an umbrella, and a mallet;
she is endowed with a crown of matted hair and adorned with serpent ornaments.
Wearing white garments and beautifully adorned with a white parasol,
she is mounted upon a bull and wears serpent-earrings.
In her right hands she holds a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, a sword, and a hand-drum;
in her left hands, a fire, a skull-cup, the boon-granting gesture, a shield, and a goad. 85.
Having likewise meditated upon Māheśvarī adorned with all ornaments,
and Kaumārī, who is red in color, six-faced, and has twelve eyes;
He is joined by two enemies as arms, likewise has a peacock for his vehicle,
wears red garments, and is beautifully adorned with a red parasol.
A spear, a discus-bearer, a sword, a noose, and likewise a bell;
a cock, a thunderbolt, a shield, the boon-granting gesture, a bow, and a goad.
Having meditated upon the form of Kaumāri, who is adorned with gold ornaments and all manner of beautiful decorations, one should worship her with the mantra. || 86 ||
p.
49) || To Viṣṇu ||
He has a black complexion, two eyes, one face, and four arms;
he wears black and yellow garments and is seated upon the throne of Garuḍa.
Adorned with a beautiful and splendid black umbrella, decorated with pearl necklaces,
and with golden earrings upon her ears, she holds the conch, the discus, the mace, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Having meditated upon this form of Viṣṇu, endowed with all ornaments and adorned with every kind of jewelry, one should worship it with the mantra. || 87 ||
O Vārāhī!
The face has the form of a boar, blue in color and four-armed;
it is joined with a horse as its vehicle and is beautifully adorned with a blue parasol.
He wears blue garments and is adorned with blue jewels;
likewise, he holds a staff with a blade, as well as a sword and a shield.
Then, having fashioned and meditated upon Vārāhī—who pierces the earth and the netherworld (pātāla) and is adorned with all ornaments—one should worship her with the mantra. || 88 ||
Māhendrī.
[He beheld] Indrāṇī, golden-hued, with one face and four arms,
mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, and beautifully adorned by a dark parasol.
Adorned with golden ornaments and endowed with a thousand eyes,
[he holds] a thunderbolt, a spear, a mace, and a sword, and is radiant with a crown set with jewels.
Having meditated upon the form of Mahendra, adorned with jeweled earrings. || 87 ||
Cāmuṇḍī
Having fangs and a face with three eyes and eight arms,
she is mounted upon a tiger and possesses a body the color of smoke.
She was enriched with the great beauty of a blue parasol, adorned with all ornaments,
wearing golden earrings on her ears, and set with golden bands.
She wears matted locks, a topknot, and a crown, and bears a garland of skulls;
in her right hands, she holds the gesture of fearlessness, a trident, a bracelet, and a sword.
In her left hands she holds a noose, a skull-bowl with a bell, and a shield;
one should meditate on Cāmuṇḍā in this form, adorned with all ornaments. (90)
Goddess Durgā.
Holding a conch, a discus, and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands, clothed in fresh garments and endowed with great strength,
she stands with feet firmly planted upon a lion, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
O Kāmākṣī, the source of the universe!

I worship the Goddess, the source of the universe, who possesses auspiciousness and welfare; she whose hands grant fearlessness and boons, who holds a goad and a foot, who wears a crown and earrings of gold and jewels, who bears the hero’s spear, who is adorned with every ornament, and whose eyes are the embodiment of Dharma and Kāma.
(p. 51) || Meditation on the Five Powers of the Devikūṭa of Īśvarī ||
O Ambikā, [one should meditate on] her holding a ṭaṅka and a deer, granting fearlessness and boons,
endowed with all ornaments, and standing with feet even. 93.
Gaṇāmbikā: The Mother of the Gaṇas.
With the upper half [of the body] like the sun and the moon, and likewise possessing the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and the excellent bowl (*pātravara*);
with one face and three eyes, he should be equal to the feet of the Gaṅgā.
Gaṇāmbikā has three eyes and one face; she holds the gestures of fearlessness and the granting of boons, as well as a noose and a goad, and she is accompanied by her foot. 94.
Sarasvatī.
Holding a lotus, a water-pot, and likewise granting fearlessness and the boon of boons;
having one face and even feet, his form is that of Gaurī-Śakti.
One should likewise [depict] Sarasvatī with a water-pot and a book, granting the gestures of fearlessness and boons, standing with feet even upon the center of a lotus flower. 95.
Meditation on Dvāraśakti Kālī.

[He holds] the noose, the goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons; likewise, with feet even, the belly slightly elevated, and deep [in voice], Viṣṇu resides within his own powers.
In his pure hands, he holds a divine noose and goad, as well as a book;
with feet evenly placed, he is most formidable, being the very power of the Self of Brahmā.
p.
52) || Meditation on the Earth Goddess ||
Then one should invoke the Earth-goddess, adorned with all ornaments,
having two arms and three eyes, and wearing a crown shaped like a basket.
She wore a golden sacred thread, had yellow eyes, and was in the full bloom of youth;
she was clad in yellow garments and possessed eyes like the petals of a white lotus.
With palms joined in reverence, or with hands adorned by blue lotuses,
[one should worship] Bhūmidevī, who is beautiful with all her ornaments, in her true form.
The Yamunā River.
He has four arms and three eyes, and is endowed with a skull and a trident in the right [hands],
and with the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and an axe (*ṭaṅka*) on the left side.
One should fashion him as being endowed with matted locks and a crown, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread;
and on his very right side, one should likewise fashion Yamunā.
Mahākālī
She has two arms and two eyes, is endowed with a dark complexion,
is seated upon a tortoise, and is adorned with all ornaments.
To the left of the full water-jar is a blue lotus in her right hand;
she is Yamunā herself, beautiful in all her limbs.
On the left side of the door, one should likewise worship the sage Mahākālya;
and on his left, one should worship Yamunā and Mahākālī. (100)
The Eight Bhairavas
Asitāṅga, Ururucchaṇḍa, Krodha, Unmattabhairava,
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra— these are the eight Bhairavas.
O Asitāṅga Bhairava!
Wearing matted locks of red flames, joined with the moon, red-bodied and composed of radiant energy,
holding a trident, skull-cup, noose, and *ḍamaru* drum, the protector of the world—
Nirvāṇa, whose mount is a dog, three-eyed, the tumultuous roar of bliss.
I pay homage to Vaṭuka, the lord of spirits and piśācas, the auspicious protector of the sacred field. || 1 ||
Rūrubhairavaḥ.
Nirvāṇa, non-conceptual, unborn, stainless, unchanging, the syllable *kṣa*, the syllable *huṃ*, possessing adamantine fangs, fire-eyed, fierce, in a state of madness;
uttering the sound *bhaṭ*, a devotee of the Nāgas, with a face knit in a frown, Bhairava, holding a trident in his hand.
I bow to the sword, the skull-bowl, and the hand-drum; I prostrate before Kṣetrapāla. || 2 ||
[The hymn] of Caṇḍabhairava.
Beholding him who bears a radiant white complexion, possessing twenty arms, five faces, and three eyes;
holding in his hands the gesture of generosity (*varada*), the moon, the royal parasol, silver, snow, nectar, a conch, a bow, a trident,
a sword, an arrow, a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), sand, a vajra, and a garland.
He who bestows all fearlessness, who holds a trident in his hand, who is joined with Bhujagi and Bhairavī, and who grants all spiritual accomplishments. || 3 ||
From the Krodhabhairava [Tantra].
I bow to the Lord who has three eyes resembling the rising sun, whose body is red like a lotus in bloom, who is smeared with ashes and other unguents,

and who holds in his hands the gesture of granting boons, a skull-bowl, the gesture of fearlessness, and a trident; he has a blue throat, is adorned with hundreds of magnificent ornaments, and shines intensely, dispelling the delusion of the ignorant.
One should always meditate upon the Lord, who is clothed in saffron-red garments like the bandhūka flower and who bestows fearlessness. || 4 ||
|| Unmattabhairava ||
One [hand] holds a khaṭvāṅga, another a serpent-noose, a trident, a skull, and a sword; in the left hand is a ḍamaru along with a bow (pināka);
he has the sun and moon as his crest-garland, is of deformed yet auspicious appearance, and wears all the sacrificial threads.
I bow to Kāla, the end-maker of time, the protector of the field who removes my fear. || 5 ||
[From] the Kapālabhairava [Tantra].
I bow to the Child, who resembles crystal, whose face shines with a water-pot, and who possesses divine ornaments, a girdle made of serpent-gems,
and anklets; who has a divine form, a radiant countenance, is most gracious, and has two eyes.
Or [he may be depicted] holding a trident, a mace, a skull-bowl, and a staff in his hands, and likewise [bestowing] fearlessness.
O terrifying Bhairava!
Three-eyed and red in color, adorned with all ornaments,
holding a skull and a trident in his hands, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
In his right hand he holds a trident, and in his left, the formidable khaṭvāṅga staff.
Clad in red garments, adorned with red garlands and unguents,
blue-necked and gentle, he was decorated with all kinds of ornaments.
He is described as having a blue girdle, a tuft of hair, and three eyes;
he is adorned with serpents, is fierce, and is decorated with a garland of heads.
With feet resounding with anklets, wearing a sacred thread,
adorned with garlands of small bells, he was of terrifying form and inspiring fear.
The Meditation on Saṃhārabhairava.
He has one face and three eyes, and twelve hands;
he holds a hand-drum, a goad, an arrow, a sword, and a trident, appearing terrifying.
The bow, arrow, skull-bowl, mace, fire,
and the boon-granting hand are likewise arranged as weapons on the left and right sides.
His form is characterized by a blue girdle and a blue upper garment;
he is adorned with blue unguents such as musk, as well as white perfumes and unbroken grains of rice.
A garland of white Arka flowers, attended by three crores of limbs, endowed with all ornaments, and proclaimed as the withdrawal (saṃhāra). || 8 ||
|| Bālabhairava ||
A hand-drum and a goad, together with a sword, a trident, and the gesture of fearlessness;
likewise, a serpent-noose, a skull-cup, a bell, and a pair of excellent garments. (9)
Having the luster of a frosty lotus-stamen, in the form of a child, naked, and possessing a splendor like that of the sun.

I bow down to this Vaṭukanātha, who wears a deerskin, a staff, and a skull, whose matted locks are adorned with waves of venomous serpents, whose eyes are long and wide, and who is fond of red garments and a girdle. 10.
One should meditate upon the Great Lord (Maheśa), who is as beautiful as a dark blue cloud, who wears the full moon and a garland of severed heads;

who possesses divine weapons, tawny hair, and terrifying fangs; and who, with his lotus-like hands, holds a drum (*ḍamaruka*), fire, a sword, a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, a serpent, a bell, and a skull-cup, while adorned with ornaments on his right side.
Three-eyed, and adorned with shimmering jeweled girdles and anklets. || 11 ||
Again, Bhairava said:

May Vaṭukanātha be victorious— he who holds a skull in his hand, wears earrings, carries a staff, has a young serpent of dark-blue hue as his sacred thread, and is the cause for the severance of obstacles to the sacrificial rites performed by practitioners seeking spiritual accomplishments. 12.
|| Rājabhairava ||
The Yakṣī Nagnarūpā is adorned with matted locks,
dark-complexioned, holding a staff, two-armed, and wearing a dark bodice.
Endowed with a serpent moon and his form encircled by earrings.
Adorned with a garland of small bells and decorated with serpent ornaments,
that which is known as Āpatoddhāraṇa is prescribed for the Rājasa type.
|| Tāmasabhairava ||
The glorious one, possessing eight arms, is naked, three-eyed, adorned with anklets on his feet, and stands upon a dog.
In his right hands, he holds a trident, a noose, a sword, and a khaṭvāṅga;
and in his left hands, a skull-bowl, an axe, a shield, and a bell.
Having meditated thus on the form, the ritual procedure for the Tāmasa [Bhairava] is prescribed;
[now follows that] of the Sāttvika Bhairava.
He holds a trident, a noose, a sword, a shield, and likewise a skull-bowl;
his hair stands erect, his eyes are beautiful, his eyebrows are curved, and he is possessed of great heroism.
With the upper body slightly contracted and adorned with serpent ornaments, the form of Bhairava is prescribed as being of the sattvika type. 15.
Once again:

I bow down to this Kṣetrapāla, who has the form of a naked man with three eyes and four arms, holding a serpent-noose, a trident, and a skull-cup; his hair stands erect and he is adorned with prominent fangs. || 16 ||
p. 58) || Again:
Śrīnātha, who is Brahmā and Rudra; the ray of the sun, the orb of the moon, and the forehead; the divine seat of bliss; whose conduct is manifold and who holds authority over all mantras;
the sound that is manifest in form, the flower of the host of planets, and the radiance of ten million suns.
I bow to the Kṣetrapāla, who manifests as various forms of Rudra and whose life-story encompasses the three worlds. || 17 ||
Bhairava’s [Chapter]
Adorned with naked serpents, wearing a girdle of tinkling bells, holding in his hands a skull-bowl, a trident, and a *ḍamaru* drum; possessing beautiful vessels in his hand,
with matted hair like flames, resembling fire, and crowned with the sun and moon.
Bhairava, who rides upon a dog and provides protection for the entire world and all living beings. || 18 ||
|| Bhairava ||

I pay homage to the one who has descended as Brahmā upon the path of Siddhānta and Yoga, who is established in the two families of Mantra and Tantra, who is surrounded by various hosts of sages, and who wears a serpent as his sacred thread;
I bow to the Protector of the Field (Kṣetrapāla), the end-maker of even Kāla, the Destroyer, who removes my fear. 19.
Bhairava has a white complexion and two eyes, is adorned with a crest of matted hair,
wears Vāsukī as a sacred thread around his waist, and is endowed with a garland of tinkling bells.

Having meditated upon the form of Bhairava as described in the ritual injunctions— his entire body smeared with ashes, holding a skull-cup and a trident, carrying a rosary and a staff, mounted upon a dog, and established in the state of Nirvāṇa— [one should worship].
p.
59) || The Skeleton-Bhairava ||
He is red in color, with two eyes, one face, and eight arms;
he is described as having a blue loincloth and being adorned with ashes smeared over his body.
He holds a sword, a trident, a hand-drum, a mace, a shield, and a skull-cup;
he is joined with a blue lotus and a lute, and is mounted upon a dog as his vehicle.
Having meditated upon Kaṅkālabhairava in this manner—
specifically as having six arms in his rājasa form and eight in his tāmasa form— [one should proceed].
The peaceful [deity] is prescribed as being of three types: two-armed and four-armed.
|| [This is] the Praise and Meditation.
Having praised you—the sky, the wind, fire, water, and the ether; you who are Brahmā, Janārdana, Aruṇa, Indra, the moon, and the primordial deity;
the joyful Lord of Siddhas and Yogis, the leading actor in the drama of cosmic play—[I bow] to you who dance through the beginningless cycle of the dissolution of the aeons.
The Lord Bhairava is victorious. || 23 ||
|| Contemplation on the Dog ||
The four Vedas are its four feet, Mīmāṃsā is its tail,
the six Śāstras are its heart, and that which is called the knowledge of Kalpas is its neck.
One should fashion two eyes from the Śiva-āgama and two ears from Jyotiṣa;
one should also fashion the witness of the world. Salutations to you in the form of a dog.
Thus, this very form of Bhairava is known as the form of meditation (dhyānarūpa).
[One should perform] the painting on the jar, the disc, and the cloth, as well as the hymn and its recitation.
One should recite this daily at the three times of day after performing japa, which bestows the attainment of fruits.
[The Meditation on Dakṣiṇāmūrti]
With limbs pale as ashes, wearing the crescent moon, and holding the *jñānamudrā* and a skull-cup,
