seated upon a tiger-skin seat, served by a multitude of the best of sages, most gracious, with serpents [as ornaments] and clad in an elephant hide— may the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti protect me forever. || 1 ||
Furthermore:
[He holds] a book with the color of refined crystal,
a rosary of *mārakata* gems in his right hand, and a tiger-skin garment.
He bears the moon and the sun in his matted locks; on his right side are the sun and the moon, while he sits beneath a banyan tree with his left foot resting upon the hoof of a horse.
The form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, which is served by hosts of sages and ascetics. || 2 ||
Furthermore—
near the banyan tree, seated upon a patch of ground, he was close at hand, the bestower of knowledge upon all the sages.
I bow to the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the teacher of the three worlds, who is capable of cutting through the suffering of birth and death. || 3 ||
Again:
His body is white in color, radiant with a crest of flame, and he holds a rosary as his weapon in his two arms;
his feet are served by immortals, and he possesses the form of a young boy with a lotus in his right hand. (4)

Furthermore: [I salute] Rudrākṣa, who holds fire in his hand, is accompanied by the Lord of Stars (the Moon), whose limbs are smeared with ashes, who is full of splendor, who has a lotus-seat, whose eyes are like fire, and who has the upward-flowing Gaṅgā as his companion.
I bow to the syllable Oṃ, the root mantra, fallen from the lips of sages, the essence of the Vedas, whose nature is Śiva;
I praise the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the master of Kailāsa and the sovereign of all the gods. || 5 ||
Furthermore:
his arms are resplendent with a mudrā, a book, fire, and a serpent; he has a serene countenance, is adorned with pearl necklaces, and shines with a crown radiant with a digit of the moon.
One should meditate upon the supreme Guru, the destroyer of ignorance, who is without beginning or origin, the Lord of Bhavānī, who dwells at Nyagrodha, as the refuge for one's desired goal.
The Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, whose body is fashioned white, who wears the sacred thread as his sole ornament, who holds the mountain-born Pārvatī in his hand, who bears a rosary and other attributes,
who is adorned with a sweet-sounding golden lute, who has an eye on his forehead, and who holds the peacock of the best of mountains in his hand.
Furthermore—
[he visualizes him] holding fire, a rosary, the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā),
and a book with his four faces, [the deity] who is praised by sages and seers. (8)
Salutations to You, whose nature is knowledge, ending with the exposition of the Vedas, scriptures, and so forth.
Again:
Having stepped upon that [world] with one foot and having placed another foot multiplied above it—[salutations to You].
May the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, my Guru, ever manifest before me with his four lotus-hands holding the seal of the exposition of the Vedas, the flame of fire, and a book. (62)
I bow to the one who bears the moon crested with the Gaṅgā, who sits upon a tiger skin,
whose body is white from the smearing of ashes, who dwells at the root of a banyan tree,
who has the lord of serpents as his ornament, and who holds a water-pot and a rosary in his palms.
I constantly remember Śrīkaṇṭha in my mind, who is ever attended at his side. || 10 ||
Furthermore— [she] has fire, jewels, and hair; holds a rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads of gnosis, a jar of nectar, and the *vidyā* [mantra], with the *jñānamudrā* at the tips of her hands.
May the three-eyed Lord with the moon upon his crest, the venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who has serpents for armlets, bestow grace upon me as I bow before him.
Furthermore—
[he is] the color of refined crystal,
holding a book in his right hand and a snake in his other [left] hand, with a rosary in his previous [right] hand.
Furthermore, one should bestow the Yugalāṅga-guhyavyākhyā-mudrā; the moon-bearer [Śiva] has his matted hair on the left, while the sun is on the right.
Seated at the foot of a banyan tree growing on a mountain, he placed his feet one upon the other; then,
becoming despondent, he recalled the luster of the anklets that had never left his feet.
The Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who is to be served by sages and gods.
Again—
with the embrace, with the hand holding a book, when the jar is filled—

I worship the embodiment of courtesy, who possesses the knowledge of mudrās and holds a rosary of rudrākṣa beads unlike those of others; who embraces the Daughter of the Mountain seated upon his left side, while she—dark-hued, holding a blue lotus, and radiant as the moon—embraces him in turn. 13.
Furthermore:
[He is] four-armed and three-eyed, with his crest adorned by matted locks;
moreover, in his two front hands, he holds a ring in the right one.
In the left hand he holds a book, and in both of his other hands as well;
or else, he holds a serpent-staff in the right hand and a trident in the left hand.
With his right leg extended and his left foot drawn into a circle,
he wears a garment of tiger skin and is adorned with all ornaments.
On that Mount Kailāsa, at the foot of a banyan tree,
Vasiṣṭha established a fire beneath it, with Bhṛgu to his right.
Bhāradvāja, Agastya, Bhārgava, and likewise Gautama—
one should thus meditate upon the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti within the heart.
The Meditation on the Twelve Ādityas.
Vaikartana, Vivasvat, Mārtāṇḍa, Bhāskara, Ravi,
Lokaprakāśika, Lokasākṣin, and Trivikrama.
Āditya, as well as Sūrya, Aṃśumālin, Divākara,
and Vaikartana— this is the meditation [on the Sun].
The form of Vaikartana, however, has one face and two hands;
he holds a golden lotus as his weapon in both hands.
Vivasvat is said to have golden ornaments and to wear garments of night.
The true form of Vivasvat, however, has two faces and four arms;
he is endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, and his two hands hold weapons and a lotus.
His garment shall be tawny and his ornament coral;
he is Mārtāṇḍa.
And Mārtāṇḍa is his own essential form, possessing three faces and endowed with six arms;
he holds the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, as well as a rosary and a water-pot.
One should likewise [offer] two lotuses, food, and ornaments to the Sun.
The true form of Bhāskara has two faces and four arms;
with two hands he performs a gesture of salutation, while his other two lotus-like hands [are held in specific mudrās].
He has a crimson luster, wears crimson garments, and his ornaments are made of blue gems. || 4 ||
Raviḥ (The Sun)
The true form of Ravi as well is endowed with four faces;
specifically, he has eight arms, holding a rosary and a water-pot.
He holds a trident, a noose, a goad, and a lotus, as well as the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons;
thus his weapons are described, and he wears beautiful red garments.
Having meditated thus upon the emerald ornament, one should worship it.
|| Lokaprakāśa ||
The color of the dyed [silk] is like the radiance of the Lokaprakāśa;
it is ten cubits long, has five faces, and a lotus measuring two cubits.
He holds in his right and left hands a trident, a goad, a staff, a rosary, a water-pot, an arrow, a bow, and the gesture of granting boons (varada-mudrā).
And bearing a blue gem upon his entire body, he is blue in color; he is the witness of the world.
I shall describe the World-Witness (Lokasākṣin): one should meditate upon him as having four faces and two hands, with his hands joined in the añjali gesture and wearing white garments.
Trivikrama, endowed with the wearing of rudrākṣa beads and adorned by the smearing of sacred ash.
The form of Trivikrama has two faces and four arms;
his two upper lotus-hands should be in the gesture of salutation (namaskāra).
Adorned with dark-red ornaments, wearing dark-red garments, and having a dark complexion—
[this is] Āditya.
The true form of Āditya has one face and two hands;
his pair of hands holds a lotus stalk, and he has the luster of a pomegranate flower.
In this way, the form of the eternal Āditya is indeed adorned with jewel ornaments.
[Sūrya]
The form of the Sun’s splendor has one face and eight arms;
it is endowed with two lotuses in its hands, as well as a bell, incense burner, and water-pot.
He grants fearlessness and boons, is endowed with a rosary of beads,
has a golden face, possesses a golden luster, and his ornaments are indeed made of gold.
Aṃśumālin (The One Bearing a Garland of Rays)
The form of Aṃśumālin has six faces and is red in color;
likewise, it has twelve arms, two of which are endowed with lotuses.
He holds a lotus, a sword, a shield, and a noose;
and in his right and left hands, he displays the spear, Bhairava, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons.
To Divākara.
Having the form of the sun, with two faces and four arms,
possessing the nature of bilva leaves, and having two beautiful lotuses like two water-lilies.
p. 67) A necklace and likewise ornaments joined with garments of saffron;
[this is] the meditation on the Sun.
Red in color and possessing two eyes, with a serpent as his sacred thread,
he is adorned with a jeweled crown and wears red earrings.
One should place Uṣas, endowed with a red luster and adorned with red garlands and unguents,
on the right side, and Prayūṣas on the other.
One should meditate on the deity facing the fire and having the form of the sun;
again—[one should meditate on him] with a white lotus... || 14 ||
Furthermore:
"By means of [the words] 'staff-bearer' (*daṇḍin*) and so forth, [we have] obtained food. (15)
Furthermore: [I praise] the Sun, the Lord of the beautiful worlds, the nectar, the essence of the Vedānta,
the auspicious one, knowledge, that which consists of Brahman, the stainless Lord of the gods, the sole knower of the world, who is himself [Brahman].

I eternally revere the Sun, who is Indra, Āditya, and the lord of men; the sovereign of the gods and the crest-jewel of the three worlds; whose heart is the very nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. (16)
Bhāskaraḥ (The Sun)
Having two eyes and two arms, with a face like a flame, he was the delighter of the Vasus,
endowed with many weapons, and adorned with all ornaments.
The deity seated upon a lotus throne, endowed with two powers, partless and free from transformation—that deity becomes Bhāskara. || 17 ||
The Sun.
Blazing, blazing...
[the sun]. The Sun.
He has one face and two eyes, two hands holding a lotus and a flower, wears earrings, stands with feet even, is red in color, and is captivating to the mind. (19)
I worship Śiva-Sūrya, mounted upon a chariot with a lotus-stalk for its pole;
he who holds a staff, who is both fierce and gentle.
Red in color, possessing such-and-such [qualities].
The Solar Disk.
One should meditate upon the solar disc, which resembles many red hues and is adorned with a golden rampart, for the sake of pacifying all diseases. 22.
The lotus of the Vasus, however, is in the heart-lotus and likewise has thirty-two filaments;
in its center resides Śeṣa, adorned with a thousand hoods.
In its center stands the deity, salutations again and again to Śiva-Sūrya;
[the two] twelve Ādityas.
Aruṇa, Sūrya, Sahasrāṃśu, Tathāpaha, Dātṛ, Viśva, Parjanya, Tvaṣṭṛ, Amitra, and Vāsava; || 24 ||
These twelve suns have two arms, granting boons with their lotuses;
they are the twelve Āditya-śaktis.
Ubha, Prabhā, Sabhyā, Prajñā, Medhā, Mālinī, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Śrī, Pratīkā, Antī, and Īritā— these are proclaimed as the twelve powers (śaktis) of the suns. || 25 ||
Candran: Moonlight.
White in color and possessing two eyes, seated upon a white lotus,
having two arms and holding a night-lotus, he is enveloped in a white garment.
Adorned with all kinds of ornaments and decorations, and embellished with strings of pearls,
it was further graced by a crown and a tiara encircled by a halo of light.
Kṛttikā on the right side, Rohiṇī on the left side— [this is] the moon.
Seated upon a variegated lion-throne, resembling jasmine and crystal,
endowed with a halo of light, having two arms and a prominent nose.
Whether seated or standing, Kumuda holds a lotus bud;
on his southern side is Rohiṇī, endowed with two arms.
With eyes like lotuses, radiant and resembling the filaments of a lotus,
he looked again and again.
Having the appearance of white cow's milk, with two arms and two eyes.
One should meditate upon the Moon, who is joined with a circle of rays, adorned with a crown of lapis lazuli, accompanied by Rohiṇī, and holding a night-lotus in his hand.
Then, having performed the worship, one should offer the eye-installation and the water for the guest-offering (arghya).
Furthermore: one-faced and two-eyed, white in color, with four arms,
seated upon a white lotus throne, and wearing excellent white garments.
He holds white perfumes and unbroken rice grains, as well as *jājī* flowers and nectar;
he is adorned with a necklace of pearls and has two hands holding a white lotus.
He has two hands holding a bow and arrows, rides a chariot drawn by seven horses,
and is dark-complexioned with Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī at his two sides.
Thus, the cool and vast [deity], joined with sixteen jars and adorned with all ornaments, appears in the form of the moon; homage to him! (4)
Furthermore:
two-armed, holding a white water-lily (*kumuda*), adorned with a halo of light,
having one face and two eyes, and wearing a necklace of pearls and jewels.
It rested upon her face, which was like a garland of jasmine and campaka flowers.
Seated upon a white lotus throne, possessing two powers and two flanks,
wearing white garments, and adorned with all ornaments.
The sixteenth is the jar, endowed with the nature of the full moon. || 5 ||
Furthermore:
[He sees himself] mounted upon a divine golden chariot, drawn by seven yellow horses;
it has a white-colored banner, a rope, and a white parasol with a fly-whisk.
(71) Adorned with white garments, in the center of that [altar] is a lotus-seat;
in the middle of the seat is a well-fashioned [image], and in the center of that is one in the form of the moon.
Furthermore:
one-faced, with two lotus-hands, two eyes, and peaceful in appearance;
wearing a crown of nine jewels and adorned with golden ornaments.
Salutations to you, who possess the form of the moon, adorned with the mark of fragrant sandalwood paste, a beautiful garland of flowers, and all ornaments.
The Meditation on Brahmā.
[He saw] Brahmā, yellowish in color, stout, with four arms and four faces, riding upon a swan, and holding a staff, a rosary, a sacrificial ladle, and a water-pot. || 1 ||
Brahmā has four faces and is yellow in color, adorned with four staff-like arms;
he holds a sacrificial ladle, a staff, a rosary, and kusha grass, and stands in the center of the solar disc.

In that very place, I worship the Lord of the upward direction (Brahmā), who likewise has the form previously described, and who holds a water-pot, a rosary of beads, and a staff of *kuśa* grass. || 2 ||
The beloved lord of the downward direction is yellow-robed and endowed with splendor;
he has four faces and eight arms, holding a spear and a rosary.
One should worship the sages, holding in their right hands a kusha grass stalk, a skull-bowl, a knowledge-mudrā, and a book. || 3 ||
Furthermore—its essential form is white in color, with four faces and four arms. (p. 72)
And likewise the staff, the entire rosary,
the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), the seat of the yoga-throne, and similarly the eight-eyed [image].
Furthermore, he was well-versed in the *Ṛṣipuṣpāñjali*, the four Vedas and their ancillaries,
the eighteen Purāṇas, and the six systems of philosophy, as well as the arts.
O Bhāratī, you possess a tongue endowed with the Mīmāṃsā and Yoga-śāstras;
you wear a crown of nine jewels and likewise ornaments of diamonds.
I salute the one clad in white garments, with arms crossed and wearing the sacred thread, who is joined with the solar disc amidst the gods and asuras. || 4 ||
Having thus meditated upon the form of Brahmā, one should worship with the mantra.
Furthermore,
the Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas were spoken from his eastern face.
I pay homage to the gods, asuras, and ṛṣis, and to the speech of Dakṣiṇa;
likewise, may the creation written here be [granted] by the northern face itself.
Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, whose form is Brahman, facing westward, with his lotus feet possessing the luster of a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali). || 5 ||
Meditation on Viṣṇu
Viṣṇu has four arms, bearing the mālī, the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus;
he resembles a dark blue cloud, and his hair is like the orb of the moon.
Furthermore: [he is] radiant with the color of gold, with a red face and red eyes.
Hari, whose hands and feet are raised in ease, who wears garments of yellow and green,
who is the essence of Śrī Viṣṇu and the Praṇava, and whose crown is as radiant as his face.
He has a water-channel and a sacred thread, the Śrīvatsa mark on his body, and four arms;
he displays the conch and discus, and holds the gestures of granting boons and protection.
He himself, having meditated upon the Supreme Self in the form of Viṣṇu—
endless, lotus-eyed, and endowed with a thousand hoods— [attained his goal].
Resembling a flash of lightning, mounted upon a tortoise, with palms joined in reverence—
Ananta, lotus-eyed, with one face and four arms.
Equipped with a bow and arrows, radiant with a diadem and crown,
adorned with necklaces and armlets, two-eyed, and clad in red garments.
I bow to the god who bears the conch and the discus, the protector of the lunar orb, who was fashioned by the gods and asuras, and who possesses a splendor equal to a handful of flowers. 4.
Having thus meditated upon the form of Viṣṇu, one should worship him with the mantra;
his form is blue in color, with one face and four arms.
He bears the descent of the conch and the discus, is adorned with golden rings and other ornaments,
has a mark upon his chest, and possesses the divine form of Lakṣmī.
With an embrace and with his hands, he grants fearlessness with his right hand;
he wears yellow garments and a sacred thread, and possesses a crown of gold and jewels.
Having meditated upon Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, one should worship him with the mantra.
|| Rāmar ||
O Lord of Sītā, best of the Raghus, resembling the radiance of the rising sun,
standing at the western gate with a crown variegated by the nine precious gems,
your chest radiant with a necklace, bearing a white parasol, adorned with golden bracelets and decorated with golden anklets— [I salute you].
Lakṣmaṇa paid homage to the god who was the husband of Urmilā and the son of Sumitrā.
Wearing a jeweled crown shimmering with playful gems— the abode of all auspiciousness— and holding a cluster of palm leaves, his face resembling the moon and his eyes as broad as lotus petals;
the Pārijāta tree for his devotees, the remover of the fear of worldly existence, seated upon the left side of Rāma.
I meditate upon Bharata, the lord of the lineage of sages, whose limbs are adorned with jewels and gold.
I worship Śatrughna, the long-armed one, whose limbs are adorned with various clusters of jewels;
and I worship Sītā, who resembles refined gold, whose face is like the moon, who is graced by strings of pearls,
whose breasts are embellished with musk and sandalwood paste, and who is arrayed in golden garments.
Her earrings were set with gems, and she sat magnificently upon the lap of the foremost of the Raghus.
I take refuge in the Goddess, my mother, who bestows the accomplishment of all goals for the worlds.
Before Rāma, he offered a pure wind as a golden sacred thread.

He who brings auspicious relief like a dark rain-cloud to the fire of Sītā’s grief, whose limbs are radiant with a divine countenance, who is a *pārijāta* tree for his devotees, and who is the Rudra of the Eon of Destruction for the race of demons.
One should meditate upon the son of Gaṅgā, whose complexion is like that of gold, with a joyful countenance, and holding a book.
Vīrarāmaḥ.
With his right hand, he brandishes a ten-faced, three-eyed, and uneven bow; with his left hand, standing firmly on the ground, he holds and whirls a single arrow.
His eyes reach to the edge of his jeweled earrings, his body is like a swarm of bees, and he shines with the brilliance of ten million suns.
May Vīrarāma, whose passion is bound by heroic glory and who is praised by the Lord of the Thirty-three gods, protect me. || 10 ||
O Vīrarāma, with his arms he holds a sword, a trident, a hand-drum, a bow, a crescent-headed arrow,
an axe, a conch, a discus, a scimitar, a plough, a mace, a club, a child, and a shield.

I bow to Rāma, who holds a rising fire in one hand and displays the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting with the other, while his left side bears a dark goad; I praise the three-eyed Vīrarāma, the remover of my misfortunes—may he protect me! || 11 ||
Rāma, wearing a jeweled crown and earrings, with a face like the orb of the moon, clad in garments bright as gold, holding a bow and arrow in four hands,
bearing a conch, a lotus, and the leaf of a forest tree, with a garland upon his chest— [I meditate upon him].
Then Sītā, endowed with auspicious marks, stood on the left side of Śatrughna and Bharata.

I worship, I worship Rāma, the Lord of the Gods, who is adorned with the splendor of all ornaments, whose auspicious marks are dear to his devotees, and who wears sacred ash, sandalwood paste, ointments, and a forehead mark.
*The Sixteen Names of Viṣṇu*
O Viṣṇu, one should meditate on Janārdana while taking medicine;
on Padmanābha while eating; and on Prajāpati during sexual union.
Today, at the confluence of the Prayāga, Nārāyaṇa and Śrīdhara will meet;
and in the battle, the wielder of the discus will face the prowess of his enemies at dawn.
In a dream, one should remember Govinda; in a terrifying situation, Madhusūdana;
in the forest, Narasiṃha; and on a mountain, Raghunandana.
One should worship Varāha in the midst of water, Jalaśāyana in fire,
Vāmana in a flowing stream, and Mādhava for all undertakings.
The man who recites these sixteen names at the three junctions of the day has no fear of any beings and shall be victorious in battle. (13)
The Meditation on Vīrabhadra
Vīrabhadra is three-eyed, blue in form, and four-armed;
likewise, he holds a sword and a shield within his two front hands.
Between his flanks and hands, there is indeed an arrow as well as a bow;
he is clothed in red garments and adorned with the anklets of a hero.
He was endowed with the sacred thread, possessed the other [hand] raised toward the Ganges,
had an earring set with a gem upon his ear, and was adorned with a garland on his head.
The *rājasa* [mudrā] consists of fierce eyes and likewise terrifying fangs;
the right foot is firmly planted while the left foot is drawn up.
"Accompanied by anklets on the feet and endowed with secret heroes"—when this is stated, O Vīrabhadra, the Bhoja [dance] is said to be of two kinds. (1)
Furthermore: three-eyed and dark-complexioned, adorned with a garland of heads,
joined with a crown of matted hair, and accompanied by the Gaṅgā and the moon.
One should place one foot firmly on the ground while the right foot is extended;
with the left foot hanging down, one should keep the body balanced.
In his left hand, he holds a shield, a battle-axe, a sword, and likewise a deer;
and on his left side, he likewise holds a shield and an axe.
On his left side, however, is Prajāpati,
adorned with all ornaments and embellished with every kind of finery.
Various types of *bhoga* have been declared; now listen to the various types of *vīra*. Furthermore:
it is endowed with eight arms and possessed of all auspicious marks.
In her right hands, she holds a trident, a sword, an arrow, and a doe;
and in her left hands, a skull-bowl, a shield, a noose, and a goad.
Dhyānaka and Vīradeva are said to be threefold in sequence.
Furthermore:
[he is] white in form, wearing all ornaments, and holding a lute placed across his body.

Holding a *ṭaṅka* axe and the skin of a black antelope in his two hands, wearing a garment of tiger-skin, with one eye half-blue, endowed with the three [eyes], and with matted hair bound upon his crown; (p. 78)
I bow to the lotus-foot of Sannatavīrabhadra; protect me! || 4 ||
Furthermore:

[one should visualize] Rudra, the incarnation of Rudra, with eyes like fire, hair standing erect, and excellent fangs; he is terrifying, with a fearsome bodily form, making a fierce and resonant roar, and his limbs are encircled by garlands of flames.

I bow to Vīrabhadra, the lord of spirits and ghosts, who is intent on discourse and debate, who carries a sword and a vessel, the sole protector of the world, the destroyer of Tripura, and the dark-hued one. || 5 ||
Furthermore:
upon her two lotus-feet [are] anklets that are brilliantly radiant with fine silk bands,
endowed with various divine ornaments, bearing the moon, and resplendent with the decoration of the lord of serpents.
I bow to Vāruṇavīrabhadra, the fearless; I worship you, O heroic deity. 6.
The Heart of the Universe.
Salutations to the one who holds a staff, a water-pot, and a girdle; to the beautiful and pure form that is not [merely] left behind;
salutations to the one whose hands are supreme in sustaining the three worlds, and who is the powerful protector of the Vedas.
The Sharabha.
Aghora and Śarabha likewise have one face and three eyes;
they are described as being blue in color, and each possesses sixteen arms.
Then, having placed a sword, a trident, a hand-drum, a mace, a discus, a goad, an arrow, and fire in the hands on the left side.
Holding a skull-cup, an axe, a staff, a noose, a bell, and a bow,
with his left-hand implements including a *khaṭvāṅga* and a snake-noose.
His matted hair was gathered upon his head, his entire body was covered in ashes,
a garland of small bells adorned his head, and he wore a sacred thread made of all [the elements].
He is joined with a red garment, and likewise possesses a red parasol and banner;
he has a distorted, boisterous laugh and the glory of seventy million attendants.
Having meditated upon Śarabha adorned with all ornaments, I pay homage to him.
[The Meditation on the Jewel]
The bell is said to be of various kinds, with a measurement of sixteen [finger-breadths].
Salutations to you in the form of the bell, which is elevated by twelve finger-breadths. || 1 ||
The Measurement of the Bell.
The stalk is elevated like the sun, and it is well-fashioned by Vasudeva;
at the tip of the stalk is a staff, likewise provided with the measure of eleven fingers (rudrāṅgula). || 2 ||
The enumeration of the elements, the measurement at the tip of the staff, the form of the bell, Nāla, Divākara, and Maheśvara as the staff itself.
"O Trident at the tip of the staff! O Sarasvatī, sound of the bell!"—with these words, one should worship the deities of the bell, saying "Homage, homage! (namo namaḥ). || 3 ||

Jvālādhvakeśī has beautiful fangs and two eyes; she holds a sacrificial altar, a discus, and an arrow, and is accompanied by the two [hands of] boon-granting and fearlessness.
To the left of the bull-god is a bull and a spear.
A bull of white complexion, with sharp horns and great strength,
possessing a divine form and exquisite beauty, resembling molten gold.
The Veda is its four feet, Agni is its horn,
the Sun and Moon are its eyes, and Rudra is likewise its mouth.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are said to be the form of the Bull;
Īśvara is the bracelet, and the Bull consists of all the Vedas.
The Bull upon the Couch.
In the Kṛta and Tretā ages it is complete; in the Dvāpara age, it is diminished by one quarter;
and in the Kali age, it remains as only a single quarter, being largely abandoned.
It is declared that Dharmadeva likewise faces the west;
having made his bed, he is called the knower of dharma who has Śiva as his vehicle.
The Bull.
He saw the bull of white form, with three eyes, stationed upon his own body-limbs,
the very embodiment of Dharma and the vehicle of the Supreme Lord.
A bull, possessing the form of a bull, with three eyes, his mind solely intent upon Rudra;
he is the very embodiment of Dharma, as pure and stainless as clear crystal. (8)
The deities of the divine liṅga and the bali offerings;
the eightfold form and the distinction of colors.
The [image] of the goddesses should be made of gold; that of Indra and the others, of silver;
that of the spirits (bhūtas) and so forth, self-manifested; and that of the attendants, of copper.
The arrows made of sarodru wood and other materials belong to the Vidyeśvaras;
these are declared to be the divine lingas for which offerings (bali) should be presented to the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and others.
To the divine emblems, the sacrificial offerings, and the deities.
The eightfold manifestations (aṣṭamūrti) distinguished by color are Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Paśupati, Ugra, Bhīma, Rudra, and Mahādeva; such are the eight forms. || 10 ||
Bhava is yellow in color, and Śarva is likewise reddish-brown;
Īśāna is white in color, and Paśupati is dark green.
To Rudra, [he gave] a gem of the color of a peacock's neck and a deer with a fierce appearance;
and to Mahādeva, a very terrifying crystal jewel.
Thus have the various colors of the eightfold form (aṣṭamūrti) been proclaimed. [Now follows] the meditation on the Goddess, the Liṅga, and the sacrificial offering (bali).
He has four arms, displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, as well as holding a noose and a goad;
he is the color of three-colored lotus filaments, stands on two feet, and wears anklets.
One should offer oblations to the Liṅga known as Devīka, which is adorned with a crown of matted locks and possesses the nature of the eightfold form (aṣṭamūrti). Thus it is proclaimed. (12)
The visualization of the human-limb offering.
Indra and Agni, Yama, Nirṛti and Varuṇa,
Vāyu and Soma, as well as Īśāna, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, beholding the world.
Having fashioned human-like figures for the world-protectors (lokapālas) and likewise their offerings (bali),
one should place an offering of grain-colored [substances] in front of them.
Meditation on the Self-Arisen Linga (Svayambhūliṅga)
Saṃvarta is red in color and occupies the petal of the eastern direction;
likewise, Caraka is dark-red and white in color, situated from the southeast.
And Kṛṣṇa on the southern petal of Kuṇḍodara,
and likewise Pīta and Dīrghakāya on the petal of Nirṛti.
The western petal is joined with Śyāma, who has short feet;
and the northwestern petal likewise belongs to the exceedingly red Siṃha.
The northern petal is joined with a blue elephant-faced [deity], and the northeastern [petal] is known as the face of Mekhavarṇa. || 14 ||
The mantra "vṛṣāṣṭavarṇam" is said to correspond to each respective petal of the directions. [This concludes] the meditation on the offering (balidhyāna).
Endowed with a fierce form, having two arms and two feet,
he holds a staff in his right hand and a skull-bowl in his left hand.
Having two eyes and red in color, he is remembered as the form of Bhūta. || 15 ||
One should offer the *svāyambhuva* bali, known as the "eight-fold being.
[This is] the visualization for the *ṛṣiliṅga* bali.
And the central necklace among the necklaces, beginning with the bull, is arranged clockwise;
the bull is in the eastern direction, and likewise the fire-god in the south-east.
To the south of the Mothers is Vīra-Vighneśa; in the southwest is Skanda;
likewise, Jyeṣṭhā and the others are in the petal of the northwest direction.
Durgā is in the north, and Caṇḍarūpaka is in the northeast;
the face of Bhāskara is in the east, and likewise Krapaya is in the northeast.
Then, having constructed the temple of Agni and likewise the abode of Pavamāna,
one should construct the entire assembly of attendant deities both inside and outside.
Likewise, one should worship Indra at the side of the Bhūtapīṭha;
the wise practitioner should do so in their respective places, starting from the southeast and ending with the northeast.
On the northern side of the door, Brahmā is proclaimed;
between Pitāmaha and Īśa, likewise, are the twelve Ādityas.
One should specifically install Bhāskara, Kṣetrapāla, and Śāṅkara between the discus and the fire, beginning with the asterism Aśvinī.
Having established [the fire] between the southeast (Āgneyī) and south (Yamya), it remains for seven nights;
the station of the ancestors (pitṛsthāna) is prescribed between the south (Yāmya) and southwest (Nairṛta).
Between Nairṛti and Varuṇa is the host of Apsarases;
and between Varuṇa and Vāyu is the station of the sages.
Likewise, the eight Vasus are between Vāyu and Soma;
and outside, between Soma and Īśāna, are the eleven Rudras.
One should worship either on the first pedestal, or on the eightfold pedestal;
then, having prepared the offering-pedestal, one should especially perform [the rites] in the four directions.
One should place [the deities] at the inner and outer seats;
the Piśācas, however, belong to the inner [seat] of all the gods, while [others] are on the outer seat.
To the south belongs that of the Yakṣas, and to the west that of the Rākṣasas;
to the north belongs that of the Gandharvas, and that of the Bhūtas is indeed in the northeast.
Above that, it is said, is the "pada"; one should place the petals of the eight śaktis there.
One should fashion the "agra-pīṭha" as a pedestal consisting of all the gods.
Then, one should especially offer oblations (bali) upon the pedestal situated in front.
[The Meditation on the Bali-Pedestal]
With five faces, equal countenances, and symmetrical nostrils and eyes;
with ten ears, ten arms, ten tridents, and ten [attributes] held.
