A single petal is the heart, of an intensely red color, with two feet; this is the pedestal for the offering to the spirits (*bhūtabalipīṭha*), the bearer of the offering. This is the visualization of the offering (*balidhyāna*).

We bow to the auspicious Rudra of excellent form, who has five faces and ten arms, whose body is intensely red, who holds in his hands the noose, the goad, the shield raised with the gesture of fearlessness, the trident, the sword, the arrow, the bow, and the discus.
With reference to the deities.
Āmoda, Pramoda, Pramukha, Durmukha, Avighna, Vighnakartṛ, Pakṣeśin, and Pañcaka.
One should know that the door is situated within, while the door-keepers face outward;
the sacrificial altar, the bull, and the trident should be facing toward the deity.
Āmoda is dark green in color, while Pramoda is black;
Pramukha has the luster of crystal, and Durmukha has the radiance of saffron.
Avighna has the luster of coral, and Vighnakartṛ has the luster of collyrium; thus, these six leaders of the bhūtas are distinguished by their respective colors. (22)
Having two arms and two eyes, likewise holding a ṭaṅka and a noose,
endowed with fierce fangs, of terrifying form and great strength.
Adorned with all ornaments, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, facing the palace, and possessing long fangs and a gaping mouth—[all this was seen]. (23)
In the east, south, north, and likewise in the west,
as well as at the five [corners] of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), a group of four [pillars] is said to be elevated.
Three parts are declared to be middling, while two parts shall be inferior.
The best [width] is equal to the height of the door; the middling is three-quarters of that;
the lowest for the sake of attainment is half the height of the door; its width is equal to its height.
Of the width, there are twenty parts of hāṭaketaka;
with one-third of that, one upamā, and likewise four jagatīs. (25)
Having made a projection (*kampa*) at the top of the water-course (*ādaka*), above that there should be a fillet-strip (*koṭipaṭṭikā*).
One should make the corner (*karṇa*) with one part out of four; the eaves-fillet (*udyapaṭṭikā*) should be made with that same single part.

Above the great fillet (mahāpaṭṭikā), the height [of the structure] reaching up to the top of the pillar-shaft (senadvaṃśa) is declared to be the best, with the pericarp (karṇikā) occupying one part at the summit.
It is renowned as Balipīṭha and is celebrated as the Ṛṣiliṅga;
indeed, all such liṅgas are remembered as being satisfied by the offering of bali.
The Bāṇaliṅga Offering Ritual (Bali)
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
Likewise, the Bāṇaliṅga is proclaimed to grant health;
one should offer oblations (bali) according to the sequence of worship starting from that [liṅga] in the east, and then from that [eastern one] in the east, using grain-colored [offerings].
One should perform the preliminary offering (pūrvabali) in due order; this is here called the divine liṅga (divyaliṅga).
[The offerings] for the Rākṣasa-liṅga are for the deities of the bali.
In the east, there is the host of Yakṣas and the host of Rākṣasas led by Bāṇa;
likewise, there is the host of Dakṣiṇyās, the host of Aṅgiras, and the host of Nairṛtas.
To the Kinnaras he gave the Gaṇas of Varuṇa; to the Pitṛs, the Gaṇas of Vāyu;
to the Dānavas, the Gaṇas of Soma; and to the Īśāna group, the mixed Gaṇas. || 28 ||
Thus, this is the group for the Rākṣasas; likewise, the offering of the bali is for the deities of the five enclosures and the gates.
One should worship Nitya and Nāma at the first door,
and one should worship Nandin and Mahākāla at the second door.
One should worship those with staffs and those with shaven heads at the third gate;
one should worship Āmoda and Pramoda at the fourth gate.
One should likewise fashion Gaṇeśa and Skanda in five forms;
it is taught that one should offer an oblation there at the location of the doorway.
The deities of the eight bali offerings.
Vṛṣa, Agnimātra, Vighna, Skanda, Jyeṣṭha, Durgā, Bhāskara, and Balibhuk— these are the eight deities.
The Measurement of the Bali Offering.
One should offer a measure of rice amounting to one-fourth of a prastha, as well as a sacrificial oblation (bali) of the same proportion.
Having especially performed the regular and occasional bali offering, one should perform the bali at the three junctions of the day; one should not perform it at other times. (32)
Now, in another manner, one should offer the bali for the sake of desired objects;
specifically, one should offer the bali upon the remains of the great sacrificial oblation.
One should offer oblations of sacrificial food and bali-offerings during the twilight rituals for specific purposes;
the size of that [vessel] is prescribed as being equal to a coconut for the highest [grade].
The measure for the *kapittha* [fruit] is the medium-sized sacrificial offering (*bali*);
the size of a hen's egg is the inferior sacrificial offering.
One should offer every kind of oblation (bali) measuring eight handfuls, two handfuls, or even just a single spear’s length.

The best portion is declared to be a mouthful (kabala), the middling is a mere fistful (muṣṭi), and the lowest is declared to be an oblation (āhuti); thus it is proclaimed that one should offer the bali.
The deities of the sacrificial pedestal for the offering to the gods.
Ambikā, Bhramarī, Durgā, Cāmuṇḍā, Kālarātri, Kaumārikā, and Ālikā-devī— [the practitioner] should offer the bali-oblation to Vanadurgā.
O Śaṅkarī, by the grace of Mahādevī, may all [the deities] presiding over the sacrificial seats of the gods accept [this offering].
In the east, Ākāśamātṛ; in the south, Bhūtamātṛ;
in the west, the five Astamātṛs; and in the north, Devamātṛ.
O Śraddhā, one should offer the bali-oblation to the unnamed Mothers at the front of the seat.
May Bāṇa, Rāvaṇa, Caṇḍeśa, Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Vṛṣa, and the others—all these devotees of Śiva—always accept this water of the grace of Sadāśiva. (38)
|| Meditation on the Banner Staff ||
On the pedestal is the deity known as Śiva in the form of a bull; the handle consists of Viṣṇu in the form of a bell-faced [deity];
and the garlands are the four-faced goddesses, while the form of the staff is the banner-staff adorned with its own colors.
One [form] has one leg, two faces, and six eyes; it possesses a garland of darbha-grass cords from the sacrificial fire-line;
its body is white in form, it has two arms and two noses, and it is seated upon a lotus throne in the form of a staff. (40)
The pedestal has the Earth as its presiding deity; the Lokapālas and others are its deities.

The mendicant’s staff, the secondary staff, the altar, the eight cords, and the garland of jewels and *darbha* grass have the Eightfold Form (*aṣṭamūrti*) as their presiding deity. I take refuge in [this] from the beginning of the worship until the final descent.
Having first worshipped Brahmā in the east, and Viṣṇu in the south,
Ananta in the north, and likewise Śaṅkara in the west.
Thus, for the worship of the one whose form is the banner (Dhvajamūrti), the following is prescribed:
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and likewise Varuṇa. (43)
One should install the deities of the seats (pīṭha) in the directions starting from the northeast, such as Vāyu and Soma;
having worshipped Rudra in the east, one should then worship Ananta in the south.
To the west, one should place Nāga, and likewise Śaṅkara to the north; to the southeast,
Nakṣatra, and Nirṛti as the guardian of the planets.
Having worshipped the Asura in the northwest and Dakṣa in the northeast,
and having honored Brahmā in the center, one should install the deities beginning with Daṇḍa.
The deities of the banner-cloth.
I perceive the bull, the bracelet, the umbrella, the chowrie, the auspicious trident, the moon, the feet of the virtuous Gaṇeśa, the power of Rudra, the bull,
the white silk cloth, the mirror, and the full water-pot.
The banner-cloth, the deity, the lamp, and the conch are to be protected. || 45 ||
The *pīṭha* has Pārvatī as its deity; the staff (*daṇḍa*) has Rudra as its deity;
the *iṣṭi* is joined with Skanda; and the secondary staff (*upadaṇḍa*) has Vināyaka as its deity.
The garland has Brahmā as its presiding deity; the foot has the Āyudha-deities as its presiding deities;
Vāsukī has the Rope as its presiding deity; and the bull has Janārdana as its presiding deity.
The two chowries are the moon and the sun, the parasol is Sarasvatī, the lamp is Śrī Mahālakṣmī, and the sound of the bell is the six-faced Kārttikeya. || 46 ||
Having thus worshipped the deities designated for the flagstaff,
[one proceeds to] the meditation on the nine planets.
Āditya has one face and two eyes, is red in color,
wears red garments, and is endowed with a red parasol and banner.
He indeed bears a red color, possesses seven horses, and is himself red as well.
He is seven *rajjus* in height, red in color, and possesses two arms;
he is born from a red lotus, is situated in the center of a circular [mandala], and stands upon a red lotus seat.
Likewise, facing eastward, he performed a circumambulation of the mountains;
and in the Kaliṅga country, there was a king of the Kāśyapa lineage. (47)
Having meditated upon the Sun born under the Viśākhā nakṣatra,
I bow to him who has one face, two moons, two eyes, and a white complexion.
He wore white garments and likewise possessed a white-colored chariot,
with a white parasol and banner, and ten horses of white color.
[He should meditate on] Kumuda, who has two arms, is white in color, possesses a cord of white dust,
and is seated upon a white lotus throne in the center of a square.
Facing westward and circumambulating the mountains, one should likewise proceed toward the southeast;
thus, in Varāṭa, there are ten kingdoms.
I bow to Soma, who belongs to the Ātreya lineage and was born under the constellation Kṛttikā;
who exists for the protection of the world, and whom I meditate upon—he who is red in color, two-eyed, one-faced, and four-armed. (48)
Wearing red garments and likewise possessing a chariot of red flowers,
he holds a red parasol and banner, and bears a spear, a trident, and a mace.
It is triangular in shape, situated in the center, and likewise facing southward.
And there is the Giripradakṣiṇa situated in the southern direction;
these five, beginning with Vijaya, were born of the Bhāradvāja lineage. 49.
I bow to Aṅgāraka, born under the constellation Aśvinī;
likewise, I bow to Budha, who has one face, two eyes, and a yellow complexion.
The chariot was yellow in color, beautifully adorned with a yellow parasol;
it was likewise draped in yellow garments and equipped with a bow and arrows.
Seated upon a heroic lion-throne in the middle of the arrow-shaped [mandala],
facing eastward, and likewise situated in the northeast direction.
He was the lord of Magadha, performed circumambulations of the mountains,
belonged to the Ātreya gotra, and his birth occurred under the asterism Śravaṇa.
Having thus meditated upon the wise one in this very form— having two eyes, yellow in color, with one face and four arms— I pay homage.
He wears yellow garments and has a chariot of yellow hue as his lord;
he possesses a yellow parasol and banner, and stands in the midst of the four-peaked mountain.
He should likewise be seated in a yogic posture, facing north,
and holding the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, as well as a rosary and a water-pot.
And in the northern direction, by way of the mountains in a clockwise circuit,
there is the Aṅgīrasa lineage of kings in the land of Sindhū.
He was born under the constellation Uttaraphalgunī as the preceptor of the gods;
such is his form, and thus I bow to Bṛhaspati. || 51 ||
He is white in complexion, produced from semen; he has one face and two hands, is endowed with a white garment, and possesses one eye and a single tusk.
He possesses a white parasol and a banner, is the lord of a white-colored chariot,
and is seated upon a variegated lion-throne in the center of a five-cornered pavilion.
Likewise, facing eastward with the mace and the boon-granting gesture in his hands,
he should circumambulate the Lord of the regions of the qualities and the mountains.
The Bhārgava lineage is likewise for one born under the constellation Jyeṣṭhā;
such a person resides in the eastern direction, as do the Rākṣasas and the preceptor-gods.
Thus, I bow to the Blessed One Śukra, who is of such a form:
having one face, two eyes, two arms, and a dark complexion.
He wore black garments, and his parasol and banner were likewise black;
his chariot was black in color, and his mandala was shaped like a bow.
The black lion-throne is situated in the center facing west,
and the trident-bearer holding a bow is stationed in the western direction.
The lord of the Andhra country, who performed circumambulation of the mountains,
belonged to the Kāśyapa gotra and had Revatī as his mother. (53)
Having thus meditated upon Śani, the rider of the donkey,
I bow to him— he who has two eyes, blue complexion, three hands, and one face.
He wears blue garments and is the lord of a blue-colored chariot;
his umbrella and banner are blue, and his mandala is that of a black winnowing basket.
In the center is a blue lion-throne facing south;
likewise, from the eastern direction, there are five [emblems]: the sword, the shield, and the trident.
I bow to Rāhu, who performed the circumambulation of the mountain, who belongs to the Jāmunī lineage, and whose birth was under the asterism Bharaṇī. || 54 ||
He has variegated colors, two eyes, two arms, and one face;
he wears variegated garments and likewise possesses a banner and a chariot.
In the maṇḍala, however, there is the shape of a banner, and likewise a variegated seat in the center;
and the lord of the forest region is situated in the northwestern direction.
Likewise, for one born in the Jaimuni gotra under the asterism Āśleṣā, the Lord [ordains] the circumambulation of the Vikṛta and the mountains. || 55 ||
Having thus meditated upon the banner (ketu) as being of this very color, I bow to it.
[The Meditation on the Weapon Deity]
He has three eyes, is red in color, with hair standing erect and prominent fangs;
he holds a skull-cup, a trident, a lotus, and a water-pot, and wears a garland of heads.
With thighs, hands, and two feet, with a face slightly white like that of Brahmā,
possessing great flames by the millions of millions, and shining with the brilliance of ten million rising suns.
Having constantly meditated upon the weapon-deity (Astradeva), who is a flame originating from Śiva and whose nature is that of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, during the rites of installation and festival; 56.
The pacifier of missiles and weapons, the destroyer of all sins,
the asura-slaying weapon of the gods, the trident with its sharp-edged tip, which brings an end to all the gods through illusion— may that beloved [weapon] held in the hand of Śambhu be auspicious.
He possesses a fire with three crests, has the form of wind and space, a splendor fallen from the blazing [sun], and the essential nature of the deity of the weapon. || 57 ||
The trident is at the tip of the bull, while the four-armed form of the weapon is at the elbow;
it is in the middle of the horns and in the middle of the left thigh.
Having meditated upon [the deity] as being present in all sacred fords (tīrthas), adorned with a deer-horn and clothed in a tiger-skin garment, one should worship him with the mantra. || 58 ||
He is the manifestation of power, three-eyed, three-headed, fierce, composed of the three qualities, and clad in red garments;
he has three feet, eyes of fire, and a body smeared with ashes.
The form that is peaceful and seated in bliss is known as the form of ash (bhasmarūpa). [It is characterized by] the drinking of tears of sorrow.
One-footed, with ten and eight hands, ten and eight tridents, five heads, and three eyes;
with wide-open mouths, endowed with ten ears, and blazing hair—[he is] the exceedingly radiant linga of the Fire-god.
He who grants fearlessness and boons, who is peaceful, whose form is lovely and infinite, who holds a deer and a rosary in his hands, and who is adorned with jewels upon his face.
I salute the one whose eyes are playful, who is adorned with the great Indra’s crest-jewel, whose roar is like the sound of the ocean, and who is white as a kunda flower or the moon. 61.
The Six-Petaled [Cakra] of the Six Supports.
The support is the four-petalled [cakra] at the root of the penis, possessing the splendor of the letters from *ru* to *sa*;
the Svādhiṣṭhāna is like many flashes of lightning and possesses six petals;
the Maṇipūraka is red-hued, has ten petals, and consists of the vowels beginning with *ma*.
With twelve leaves, [I perform] my vow for the removal of sins.

The lotus of the Ājñā-cakra is radiant, pure, and joined with the sixteen vowels including the two *mātrās* (the *visarga* and *bindu*), as well as the pair of seed-syllables *ha* and *la*; it is red in hue. Above that is a thousand-petalled lotus, brilliant and white.
The state of Sadāśiva consists of eternal bliss, and the belly of Annamayī is eternal.

In this [treatise], the meditation on the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa) at the *mūlādhāra*—known as the *mūlādhāra*, *svādhiṣṭhāna*, *maṇipūraka*, *anāhata*, *viśuddhi*, and *ājñā*—is described here. (p. 97)
And [he is] elephant-faced, red in luster, three-eyed, and large-bellied;
he has four beautiful arms holding a tusk, a noose, a goad, and a sweetmeat.
I worship Mahādeva’s son, the root, whose form is the mantra. || 63 ||
Svādhiṣṭhāna is Brahmā.
Having the form of gold, four-faced, wearing white garments and a sacred thread, with four beautiful arms holding a deer, a rosary, a water-pot, and a staff. 64.
I eternally worship the Grandfather (Brahmā), who is endowed with eight eyes;
[and] Viṣṇu at Maṇipūraka.
The Lord, who is the beloved of Lakṣmī, blue-hued, bearing the conch, deer, and mace,
is marked with the Śrīvatsa and resplendent in yellow garments.
Wearing a forest garland, a crown, and earrings at all times, he grants fearlessness to all the gods; he is the lotus-eyed one, free from ailment.
I bow to the irreproachable Viṣṇu, who resembles many suns;
[this is] in the Anāhata [cakra], O Rudra.
He has the luster of milk, a dark throat, three eyes, and the crescent moon;
he is the bearer of the Gaṅgā, four-armed, and holds a trident, fire, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The god who bears the Knowledge-Mudrā (jñānamudrā), whose tinkling bells are fashioned by Gaṅgendra,
who holds a white lotus and collyrium, and whose body is adorned with sacred ashes.
I bow to Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the creator of the dissolution of the universe.
In the one called Viśuddha, O Maheśvara.
Richly adorned with the splendor of a chisel, jasmine, and the moon, clothed in a tiger skin,
with the moon and the Ganges as the crest of his matted locks— he who is known as Maheśa, possessed of great majesty.
He whose eyes are the sun, moon, and fire; who has a dark throat and is free from ailment;
who resembles ten million fierce suns; and who wears a serpent as his sacred thread.
His left and right arms are enriched with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, along with a noose;
he holds an axe and a hand-drum, manifesting his own essential form.
I bow to the Great Lord of Gods, who is joined with Maheśvarī on his left;
[this is] the command of Sadāśiva.
Resembling pure crystal, endowed with the thirty-two marks,
seated upon a full-blown lotus, five-faced, and captivating to the mind.
He has fifteen faces, bears the moon upon his crest, and brings auspiciousness;
he is endowed with ten arms, possesses a variegated body, and wears a garment of animal skin.
His left and right hands are joined in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
[the remaining hands hold] a trident, a vajra, a sword, an axe, and a noose.
Bearing both the serpent and the fire, yet possessing a peaceful form;
endowed with the five coverings, he is devoted to the fivefold activity.
The deity who is the recitation of the five syllables, whose great body consists of the five mantras.
Endowed with thirty-eight kalās, devoid of beginning, middle, and end,
it is the Lord of devotion who seeks the goal of the Vidyās, and is joined with Bindu and Nāda.
I bow to the god Sadāśiva, who is adorned with all ornaments, the leader of the thirty-six principles, and who is united with Manonmanī. (68)
Existence-Consciousness-Bliss-Infinity.
In the supreme sixfold support at the crown of the head, within the thousand-petaled lotus,
one should contemplate the Guru-Nātha, the embodiment of compassion, resembling a hibiscus flower in hue.
Having two eyes and two arms, peaceful, clad in red garments and anointed with red unguents,
he eternally holds a red lotus and is radiant with a crown of rubies.

I bow to Him whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss; who is the power transcending the principles of reality, who bestows His own manifest form, and who is the guide upon the true path. 69.
The Joyful Meditation (Nandidhyāna)
Three-eyed and four-armed, endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons,
he holds a fierce tomara-weapon and a trident, as well as a rosary of beads.
One should thoroughly worship Nandin, who is clad in red garments.
[This is] the meditation on Nandikeśvara.
Nandikeśvara is red, three-eyed, and has matted hair; with his two hands, right and left, he holds a rosary and a trident. (71)
The Power of Joy (Nandi-śakti)
Seated upon a crocodile throne, possessing a body [adorned with] lotuses, having two eyes and two arms, and stationed atop Mount Meru;
holding a blue lotus in the right hand and a full water-pot in the left. (72)
Having meditated upon Gaṅgā, clothed in white garments and adorned with variegated robes, and having visualized Nandin on her right side, one should worship her. || 73 ||
O Nandikeśvara, grant me your permission.
O highly fortunate Nandikeśa, bestower of all desired fruits,
you ought to grant permission for worship by Śaṅkara.
By means of the power of Nandin’s authorization.
And Mahānandī, white in form, dwells on the left side of Nandikeśa in the Gaṅgā, bringing liberation to all the worlds. (75)
And you, O Mahādevī, ought to grant permission for the worship.
|| Mahākāla ||
One should meditate upon Mahākāla, who is black and three-eyed, holding a skull-cup and a trident in his left and right hands respectively, and possessing a formidable countenance.
He has four arms and three eyes; he holds a skull and a trident in his right hands,
and likewise, in his left hands, he holds a noose along with the gesture of fear.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
he is described as being black in color, having the very form of Mahākāla.
Power.
One should visualize the Yamunā situated upon a dark tortoise;
she is dark-complexioned, has four arms, and holds a water-pot in her right hand.
With the right hand, one should place the *rājñī* flower, and likewise the blue lotus in the left; in this same manner, one should place the fruit of the *nimba* tree with the right hand. (78)
Adorned with all ornaments, one should worship her for Yamunā;
O Mahākāla of great splendor, you who bring about the departure of all worlds! 79.
O Śaṅkara, you should grant permission for the worship;
[this is] the permission regarding the power (śakti).
O dark-complexioned one, you who possess a physical form, you are the Yamunā to the ocean;
O sole protectress of all the worlds, you are on the left of Mahākāla.
O Bhairava, you should grant permission for the worship of Śaṅkarī. [Bhairavānujñā]
He has one face, blazing hair, red eyes, and four arms;
he has two legs, rides upon a dog, and holds a broken sword and a skull-topped staff.
He was sky-clad, bearing a trident, and the protector of the temple of the deity. || 81 ||
And by the command of Devapūjāyateśa, Udghaṭī [was appointed];
Kuccikkol.
In this manner, the form of the opening is prescribed for the triangle;
then, having fashioned a circle, one should likewise color it with the syllable.
The gate-panels of the divine doorway represent the Sun;
the lower part has the Earth as its deity, and the staff likewise represents Kārkoṭaka.
The bracelet has Brahmā as its presiding deity, and likewise the discus has Viṣṇu;
the front part has Rudra as its presiding deity, and the upper part has Uddhāṭin as its deity.
Likewise, one should place the girdle in the difficult-to-access [intermediate] corners and the staff in those of great heroism;
Kālī in the middle corners and Bhairava above the front corners.
Engaged in the worship of the gods and other rites, one should perform worship at the two times of day;
and at the gate of the temple, to the south, [one should worship] Vijaya, who is black in color.

One should fashion a pillar that has two eyes, two feet, and two hands, equipped with a sword and a shield, adorned with golden ornaments, and provided with a divine doorway; such a one shall be the architect of victory. (84)
The Northern Quarter of the City.
On the northern side of the door, however, is Vijaya, who is blue in color,
adorned with golden ornaments, having one face and two feet.
One should know that for the pillar-shaped [liṅga], it has two hands, two eyes, a trident, and likewise an axe; this shall be the procedure for victory. (85)
|| Melpaṭṭi ||
Padaṅga is dark-complexioned, with one face and four arms,
holding a sword and a shield, as well as a skull-cup and a spear.
The wearing of a rudrākṣa necklace, a sacred thread, and white garments constitutes the procedure for the worship of the Sun in his true form. (86)
Kīṣaṃpaṭṭi (The Chapter on the Kīṣaṃpaṭṭi)
He has the dark complexion of a young elephant, is adorned with blue jewels,
wears yellow garments and a sacred thread, and possesses one face and four arms.
The trident, the hand-drum, as well as the staff and the noose, and the form of the serpent-iron—such shall be the procedure for worship and other rites. (87)
The Door-Slit.
Within the cavity of the Suṣira are the Moon and the Sun;
between them is the movement of the wind, and the three deities abide within that cavity.
The Protector of Heat.
On the right side is the *ghaṭṭa*, and likewise on the north is the *vighaṭṭa*; on the eastern part of the door-panel is the sequence beginning with the fastening (*bandhana*). (89)
Having granted permission for the worship of the deity, the door should be closed;
one should strike the door with the *poḍuhura* [mudrā].
For one with ears, however, it is red and pure on the back and sides;
its form is five-cornered and endowed with a single hand. || 90 ||
One may perform dance at the temple gates and other such places, and conduct worship of the deities with their permission,
[offering] to the presiding deities.
In the corner of Sadāśiva’s head is Rudra; in the corners of the ears is Rudra;
in the heart is the form of Viṣṇu; and in the corner of the hips is the Four-faced One (Brahmā).
In the corners of the feet is Vīra, the presiding deity of Vikarṇa;
[this is] Vaḍakoṭikku.
With beautiful ears, a blue form, and well-formed forearms and flanks on both sides, it is declared to be five-cornered and provided with a single hand. 91.
Having authorized the worship of the deities, protection is performed by way of the door of the deities;
[this is] for the presiding deities.
O Śaṅkarī, [place] Manonmanī in the front corner, Lakṣmī in the ear-corners, and Sarasvatī in the hip-corner. || 92 ||
At the corners of the base, Kali is the presiding deity of Vikarṇa.
[This concludes] the southern door-panel.
Stainless, in human form, four-armed,
[holding] a trident, a deer, a noose, and a sprout.

The upward-pointing crest-lock (*ūrdhvaśikhā*), the single foot-mark (*pāda*), and likewise the golden ornament (*svarṇābharaṇa*) are proclaimed as the characteristics of the *vimala* [initiation]. (93)
On the northern door-panel.
He is the divine person Subāhu, possessing a beautiful golden complexion;
his topknot is upright and even, and he has one face and four arms.
One should place the ṭaṅka-axe and trident, as well as the staff and lotus, along with the rudrākṣa and sacred thread, while standing on one foot. (94)
With the permission for the door-panels.
Subāhu and Vimala were appointed for the protection at Devadvāra,
and he was authorized to oversee the affairs of the gods and conduct the worship of the gods.
|| Kadavutarakka ||
O Lord of Pampāpura, who dwells in gold and silver, the master of the high and the low;
O Lord of the Universe, whose form is the end of the universe, you are the staff for the time of opening the door. 96.
The Kadavuśātta.

O Śambhu, who exists within all obstacles, O Lord of the universe, whose form is the cause of the world! Grant me permission to remove the bolted lock upon the door of my inner being, so that the sacred teachings may enter. (97)
To the sky-clad one, the hero, whose nature is divine splendor;
to the one who deluded the wives of the sages, and who protected the abode of the gods.
At the time of the worship of the gods, the door of the prison shall open by itself;
and having taken hold of that which is served by the Gaṇas, it shall likewise open evenly. || 98 ||
Caṇḍeśvaraḥ.

I bow to the lotus feet of Caṇḍeśvara, who wears the Śrī-kundalī as a crown, whose face is gentle with eyes of youthful age, who has makara-earrings on both ears, who wears a sacred thread, and whose arms are raised in the gesture of victory with joined palms like a mountain peak.
Furthermore:
two-eyed, two-armed, dark-complexioned, and holding an axe;
with hands joined in the añjali gesture at the heart, and adorned with all ornaments. || 100 ||
He is known as Caṇḍarūpa, endowed with a crown of matted locks;
he is the four-armed Caṇḍeśvara, possessing four faces and three eyes.
Carrying a water-pot, a trident, a rosary, and an axe,
he was adorned with a great serpent as a sacred thread and wore bracelets fashioned from it.
In the object of meditation, one who is bound by the rules of the pledge (samaya) and so forth [should visualize] the appearance of a fresh cloud;
and the sound is that of Caṇḍeśvara.
One should meditate upon Rudra-Agni, who is powerful, fierce, black as collyrium,
and terrifying; he is Rudra, possessing four faces and four arms, holding a trident and an axe.
With great flames issuing from his mouth, he is red in color and possesses twelve eyes.
Adorned with matted locks, a crown, and the crescent moon, wearing a serpent as a bracelet,
with a serpent as a sacred thread, and holding a rosary and a water-pot.
Salutations to the one seated upon a lotus-throne of ivory, whose devotion destroys the suffering of those bowed in prostration;
salutations to the performer of deeds, who dwells in the celestial chariot of Caṇḍeśvara.
Kṛṣṇa, the lord of the quarters of the world, was situated within the enclosure of Gaṇeśa.
Caṇḍaśakti (The Fierce Power)
She has two eyes and two arms, is dark-complexioned, and holds a rosary and a water-pot;
her breasts are bound together, and she wears a crown of matted hair.
In the same way, having meditated upon Śaṅkarī, one becomes the performer of fierce power. || 103 ||
The Meditation on Hanumān
Having the color of pure gold, blazing with eyes like fire, with a face resembling a lotus, always very gracious,
with limbs more beautiful than a mountain, and a face adorned with earrings;
I bow to the messenger of Rāma, the protector who brings victory in battle. || 104 ||
One should meditate upon the young sun, resembling a water-skin, the enemy of the gods, the remover of *darbha* grass;
O Lord of Gods, he praises your glorious and divine splendor, which is extolled by the foremost of the immortals.
Accompanied by Sugrīva and all the other monkeys, he is clearly manifest as one who delights in the ultimate truth;
his ruby-red eyes are adorned with jewels, and the son of the Wind is graced with yellow garments.
I bow to Him who wears a golden bracelet upon each of His two ears— resplendent with a sacred thread shimmering like a circle of lightning—
and whose face is radiant with a halo, while He bears earrings that are red-hued at their centers yet devoid of gold.
He who possesses six loincloths, is devoid of the best of monkeys, can assume any form at will, and is the lord of poets. 105.
I am he who removed the heat of Vaidehī’s intense grief, who is dear to the devotees of Viṣṇu,
and who stripped away the great pride of the formidable Rākṣasa lord in battle;
such as I am, [I always protect] us and the son of the Wind-god.
Garuḍaṃ!
They beheld him, golden-hued, with a uniform radiance free from blemish;
reddish-brown like saffron up to his ears, with blood-red eyes, and adorned with serpent ornaments.
He had tawny eyes, was Garuḍa, possessed a luster like gold,
long arms, broad shoulders, and was adorned with ornaments made of serpents.
On the head of Ananta is the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) Vāsuki;
Takṣaka and Arkoṭa are the two threads (sūtra), and likewise Haraka and Arkoṭaka.
In the right ear is Mahāpadmā;
Śaṅkha is in the region of the head, and Gulika is in the space between the arms.
Having thus meditated upon oneself in the form of Garuḍa during the three junctions of the day.
The Eight Auspicious Ones (Aṣṭamaṅgala)
The mirror, the full water-pot, the bull,
the pair of chowries, the śrīvatsa, the svastika, the conch, and the lamp— these are the eight auspicious objects of the gods.
The Power of the Eight Auspicious Signs (Aṣṭamaṅgala-śakti)
Umādevī, Dharādevī, Kāverī, and likewise Jāhnavī; Śrīdevī in Sarasvatī, and Śaśidevī in Dīpikā—these are declared to be the eight auspicious Śaktis among these [deities]. (109)
The Power of the Ten Weapons (Daśāyudhaśakti)
Vilāsinī, Virūpī, Dhāriṇī, Sundarī, Nirmalī, and Durmukhī—thus was the retinue of Haṃsavilāsinī arrayed. || 110 ||
These are proclaimed to be the powers (śaktis) of the ten weapons.
The Weapon Deity (Astradeva)
The pedestal, the lotus, the staff, the jar and the jar-mouth, joined with the *pālikā* and the lotus,
having the form of the three-fold leaf-light, consisting of all the gods, the trident-form— the weapon of Śiva; in the center Rudra,
and on the right and left [the deities] Vidhi and Hari, with the powers (*śakti*s) in the *pālikā*, the jar, Vighna, and Viśākha.
At the base of the staff is Caṇḍa, joined with the sun of his face;

possessing a splendor equal to the midday sun, bearing the moon, blazing with a terrifying loud laugh, three-eyed, adorned with serpents, holding a deer, radiant with tawny hair, and having a crown upon his head; [holding] a flame in his lotus-hand.
O Paśupati, I worship you who possess the form of a divine weapon, appearing with a mallet-like bell, a skull, and a face of most terrible fangs. || 112 ||
To Naṭeśvara.
He holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) and the hand-drum (ḍamaruka), as well as a serpent and a vessel of fire;
he is adorned with a snake-bracelet and wears a white sacred thread.
With one leg drawn up and the other raised, standing upon ashes,
with a serene countenance and peaceful, adorned with small bells on his feet.

Having placed Gaṅgā upon his head— which is joined with the support of the elements (bhūtadī), possesses the three syllables (tri-treṃ), has the luster of crystal, and bears the moon— he likewise remained thus for a long time.
One should worship the Lord, the King of Dance, accompanied by Umā;
[he is] Somāskanda, the Leader.
The deity Ṭaṅkakṛṣṇakaranda should have the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons;
his left foot should be resting on the ground while his right foot is extended downward.
On a single seat, however, there may be Śakti; in the middle is Bālakumāra;
and on the left of Umāskanda is Candracūḍakirīṭa and Śamīśvara.
Meditation on the One Mounted upon the Bull-vehicle (Vṛṣabhavāhana)
With the *ṭaṅka* (axe) and the deer, with the hand holding the *raṇḍa* (trident), and with the foot placed between the two *śaktis*, I worship Śiva mounted upon the bull. 115.
Śrī Balināyakaḥ (The Auspicious Lord of the Bali Offering)

With hands displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, holding an axe and a deer, possessing auspicious limbs, standing with feet evenly placed, moon-crested, and three-eyed.
May he have a crown with braided locks like the rays of the moon;
O Bhava, destroyer of worldly existence, I meditate upon Śrī Bali.
|| Pallakkuśokkar ||
With one foot hanging down on the left and the other resting on Śakti,
the God holds a chisel and a deer, and likewise displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
I worship the Lord, the master of the three worlds, who is accompanied by Umā. || 117 ||
The Horse’s Roar (Kudirai Śokkar)
Having made the form of the Lord who has the horse as his vehicle well-pleased— with his feet even, the mass of his hair bound by a bridle, and his arrows at rest— 118.
The Bull.
The entire [universe] and the partless [absolute] are the peak; the ear is space and wind;
the eye is the moon and the sun; and the nose resides within Śiva and Śakti.
Having made the face of all the gods, the tail [should be placed] between the two Brahmās;
the body-hair should consist of five limbs, and the circular seat-base (pīṭhaka) should be round.
And Dhvani is fierce.
Holding a hammer in the hand that grants fearlessness, with two hands in the boon-granting gesture, he is depicted as sleeping with his feet dangling, adorned with all ornaments. || 120 ||
The sacred thread of Śiva-Brahman, the fierce sound of the earrings—
this is Bhairava.
The sounding noose and trident, the skull, and the dog-vehicle;
Nirvāṇa, the fierce form, and the flame-haired Bhairava.
Having fashioned [the deity] with a serpent as a sacred thread, wearing a garland of skulls and the moon,
holding a staff and possessing fangs, his form being the deliverer from calamity.
The Teacher.

Dark-complexioned, with a body in the full bloom of youth, adorned with a thousand bee-like earrings; seated comfortably upon a lotus in the posture of yogic binding, with his left hand in the *puṣkala* gesture and his right hand in the *pūrṇa* gesture. 122.
Māṇikkavāsahar: The One Who Wears Jewels.
Having one face and two eyes, with two hands holding a flower and forming the *jñānamudrā*, his body is smeared and anointed with ashes.
Having meditated upon the God, who is adorned with a garland of rudrākṣa beads and graced with all auspicious marks, and who is called Māṇikkavācaka, one should offer [the mantra]. || 123 ||

I bow to him whose form is that of the Lord of Vātapurī, who has one face and two arms, holding a rosary in his right hand and a book and a mark of prosperity (*vibhūti*) in his left hand, wearing ornaments and a crown adorned with a rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads. 124.
p. 113) || Sundramūrti ||

The golden body, the pair of eyes, the face adorned with a smile, the crest-lock bound at the top of the head, the tip of the right hand’s forefinger joined with a bracelet, the left side [adorned] with ornaments,
lightning-like bracelets on both palms, and earrings as the flowers of the ears.
I bow to Śrī Sundareśa, who is the very essence of erotic beauty, the Brahmin of Śiva, endowed with all arts. || 125 ||
Asmar (The Stone)
I bow with my head joined to the feet of Śiva, who dwells in the rudrākṣa beads; whose face is gentle, whose ears are adorned with the beautiful marks of Śiva;
whose right arm holds a hand-drum, a trident, and a severed weapon; who stands upon a lotus; the wise one, the lord of the sun, whose chest is bowed in devotion. 126.
|| Sambāndhār ||
White in luster, wearing jeweled earrings and a topknot, with a gentle and serene countenance;
holding a long index finger in the gesture of threat (*tarjanī*) in his right hand and a vessel of milk in his left;
he is Nirvāṇa, Śiva, the object of praise for the lotus-born Brahmā, and the destroyer of the Buddhists.
I worship Śubhakara Jñānasvāmī, the eminent and auspicious poet of various Dravidian lands. 127.
The Buddhists.
I bow to the God who is an incarnation of the Buddha, who has two arms and one face, who displays the grace of his hands upon his thighs, and who wears a yogic cloth (yogapaṭṭa).
O All-God, salutations to you, the accomplisher of the destruction of Tripura;
you are the exposition of the Dharmaśāstra and the very nature of the Supreme Brahman. || 128 ||
For the sake of liberation through the isolation of gnosis (*jñānakaivalya*), one should meditate upon the Buddha;
homage be to you! [This is] the Banner-Staff (*dhvajadaṇḍa*).
He has three staffs, three faces, an autumn-like gaze, and eyes;
his body is made of darbha grass, he is the god of compassion, and likewise possesses four hands.
The wise and best of teachers should perform the meditation on the *śūlacakra* (trident-wheel), consisting of salutation and the posture facing westward, known as the *dhvajadaṇḍa* (flagstaff). 129.
The Gatekeeper.
Red in color, with two eyes, having a serpent as his sacred thread,
possessing a terrifying form, four-armed, and single-faced.
They all stood gazing upon the Lord who remained there, filled with wonder, holding a hand-drum and equipped with a staff weapon, possessing the very form of Dindiṇa.
The form of the shaven-headed ones is black in color, with two arms and two eyes;
it is equipped with the staff as a weapon and adorned with serpent ornaments.
The chariot drawn by elephants and the true form of the shaven-headed ones;
[this is] the meditation on Indra.
She has two arms and two eyes, endowed with a dark complexion;
in her right hand she holds a vajra, and likewise, in her left hand, the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya).
Clad in red garments, adorned with all ornaments, and mounted upon an elephant—this is said to be the form of Indra. (132)
She has two arms and two eyes, is red in color, and has a face turned forward;
she is seated, endowed with hair rising upward on her head, and holds a lamp.
Clad in yellow garments and adorned with all kinds of flowers,
he wears a white sacred thread and a white upper garment.
The *sruva* ladle indeed possesses a leftward flow, and likewise the *sruk* and *sruva* are on the left;
it is said that the vehicle is a goat, and the fire is described as being in the form of a ram.
Yama.
He has a form resembling the color of a black bee, with fangs like lightning;
he is two-armed, with red hair that is curled, and possesses a twofold grace.
The vehicle of Mahiṣa is equipped with a staff as a weapon;
it has two eyes, two feet, and is adorned with all ornaments. || 134 ||
O Prajāpati, the form of Yama has been described as having a terrifying appearance.
[Now for] Nirṛti.
He has two arms and two eyes, endowed with a dark complexion;
he is clothed in golden garments and equipped with a sword and a shield.
The form of the Rākṣasa is said to be joined with a human vehicle, possessing tusks and eyes, and adorned with all ornaments. (135)
Varuṇa-nirukti (The Etymology of Varuṇa)
White as a conch, a jasmine flower, or the moon, with two arms and two eyes,
he is endowed with all ornaments and resplendent with two earrings.
In the right [hand] the noose and the gesture of fearlessness, and in the left the face of a crocodile—
endowed with all these characteristics, such is said to be the form of Varuṇa. (136)
Vāyu (Wind)
He was black in complexion, had two eyes, and possessed the prowess of a spirit;
he had two feet, wore white garments, and likewise had two hands.
Carrying a bundle of kuśa grass in his right hand and a long sword in his left,
dressed in garments of mixed colors, he is mounted upon a young doe.
That which is known as the form of wind is said to be the shape of the wind [deity];
[this pertains to] Kubera.
She has two arms and three eyes, is endowed with a white complexion,
wears white garments, and is adorned with a jeweled crown.
With a mace in the right hand and likewise a treasure (nidhi) in the left, and mounted upon a horse as his vehicle—this is said to be the form of Kubera. (138)
Īśāna.
Four-armed and three-eyed, white in color and in the full bloom of youth;
wearing a white sacred thread, mounted upon a bull, and exceedingly peaceful.
His body is smeared with the ashes of Kapardin, adorned with the crescent moon,
and he holds a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, a deer, and likewise an axe in his hands.
Holding [the attributes] in the left and right hands, he is clothed in a tiger-skin garment;
he is described as having the form of Īśāna, or he may be held to have two arms. (139)
Brahmā.

Brahmā has four faces and is yellow in complexion; he is adorned with four staff-like arms, holding a sacrificial ladle (sruk), a staff, a rosary, and a small spoon (sruva); he wears a crown and has a swan as his vehicle.
Viṣṇu
Viṣṇu has four arms and wears a garland; he holds the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
He resembles a dark blue cloud and is seated upon Garuḍa.
All have two eyes and two arms, are adorned with crowns shaped like caskets,
have their hands joined in the gesture of reverence (añjali), or hold a lotus, and are endowed with fangs.
Likewise, [he holds] a discus, a trident, a sword, a goad, and a vajra-staff;
he has one face and two arms, with the [goad] in the left hand and the [staff] in the right hand at the waist. 142.
I worship Him who bears the powers whose forms are the powers of will, knowledge, and action.
[Ratha-dhyāna]
After the wheels, the sun, and the moon, it should consist of the nature of Brahmā;
after that, there should be the pedestal (pīṭha), as well as Viṣṇu, the mountain, and the elephant.
Among all the deities, the foot [should be placed] first, and after that the world;
likewise, the lunar mansion and the vital point (randhra) should be established, as well as the serpent and the binding of the thread.
The pinnacle is the partless void (*niṣkala-vyoma*), the limb of the Veda (*vedāṅga*) according to the chariot-cords (*rathasūtraka*);
likewise, the *ṛṣa* is to be received by the devotees through the five elements (*pañcabhūta*). (p. 118)
For one who performs that [rite], Rudra himself would be thus; therefore, one should meditate on him in this very manner.
One should describe him as profound, possessing the *śikhā* and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) of the Brahmins, endowed with all ornaments, youthful, and dark-complexioned.
The hand granting fearlessness, the hand on the thigh, and the hands in the gesture of salutation with palms joined;
[this is] the meditation on the Gopura.
The door is presided over by Brahmā, and likewise by Nīla and Viṣṇu;
Rudra is in the pitcher and the stalk, while the stone is for the sacrifice and the wooden parts.
All the gods and sages, as well as the Vasus and the Dhiṣṇyas, are present within the Śaktis;
and all the prescriptions of every Tantra are contained within the devotees and the Gaṇas.
Having adorned the Śṛṅgāra and commenced the Nakṣatra, one should likewise fashion the Gopura form and the Netra upon the head and the nose. (144)
|| Stūpi-dhyāna ||
The base, the sole, the heel, and the shank,
joined with the hair-line and the ridge, and connected with the neck and the three-fold joint.
The pinnacle in the region, the crown, the stūpa, and likewise the gopura;
the celestial chariot (vimāna) joined with the image, as well as meditation and invocation. 145.
p. 119) || The Meditation on Rāvaṇa ||
He had ten faces and was black in color, with eyes like the fire of wrath;
his form was most terrifying, with formidable fangs and a lower lip.
He has twenty eyes and twenty arms,
wears a crown of nine jewels, and likewise possesses ruby earrings.
He is equal to Mahābala, adorned with all ornaments,
and holds a discus, a trident, a staff, a rosary, and a sword.
In his right hands, he holds a vajra, a tomara, an arrow, and a goad;
and in his left hands, a bow, a water-pot, an axe, and a sword.
He should hold a noose, a spear, and a bell, and a shield with a serpent in his left hands;
and in his two Garuda-wing hands, he should hold the Vedas and a Brahmin.
Ālīḍha, Kānupāda, and Rāvaṇāsura;
Śeṣadhyāna, the five elements, Pañcāsya, and likewise Śvetasūtra and Puta.
Kālodanta, Jihvā, Nāsī, and Marutāni.
One should place Karṇa in the southwest (Nairṛtyā), Bhāraṇa in the west (Kubera), and Candra at the tail (Puccha); and one should assign the Vedas, the Oceans, and Śeṣa to the remaining positions.
The Meditation on the Tiger
The face, the teeth, the tongue, and likewise the facial hair;
Indra, Agni, and Nairṛti; the eyes, Kālī, and Bhairava.
Vārāhī, Raktacāmuṇḍī, Jyeṣṭhā, and likewise Āreṇukā;
the two ears are Prajā and Karṇa, while Brahmā and Viṣṇu constitute the tail.
The mouth is in all the scriptures, and the body is the deity of the sages;
the life-force, the god of love, and the Vedas—such is the nature of Vyāghra.
Thus, the wise and most excellent of preceptors [should assume] the form of a tiger.
The Meditation on the Mouse
The tongue, the teeth, the musical instrument, and likewise the mouth belong to Nairṛti;
the eye belongs to Day and Night, and the ear belongs to the deity Vāyu.
The sage should know that his body is the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), his hair the Vidyādharas,
his tail the serpent Ananta, and his four legs the four Vedas.
The individual soul (jīva) is Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and likewise the mouse;
[this is] the meditation on the Haṃsa.
The eyes are Dharmakīrti and the face is Parvatī;
the two feet are the Moon and the Sun, and the life-force is all that is stationary and moving. || 150 ||
The wise and supreme teacher should perform the meditation on the *haṃsa* according to the prescribed rule.
(p. 121) || [Now follows] the meditation on the elephant (*gajadhyāna*).
Śira is Vighneśa, Mastaka is Ṣaṇmukha, Jihvā is Daṃṣṭra, Ṣaṇmukha is Śuṇḍahasta, Itaraṅgī is Karṇa, and Durgikā is Kāmāri.
The eye, Arundhatī, Jyeṣṭhā, and likewise the bodies of all the worlds;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, the sages, and similarly the four-footed [animals]. (151)
The Meditation on the Lion
The face shall be Vīrabhadra, and the eye in the southwest shall be Agni;
the teeth shall be Aṣṭaśaila, and on the tongue shall be Kālī herself.

The wise and supreme teacher [should assign] the body-hair to the Ṛṣis, the Suras, the Yamas, and the Vāyus; likewise, the tail to the Śveta-s, the life-force (jīva), the vital breath (prāṇa), and Lakṣmī. Thus is the lion [mantra] described. 152.
Meditation on the Pavilion (Maṇḍapa)
In the right hands are a spear, a trident, a garland, and the gesture of fearlessness;
in the left hands are a vajra, a wheel, a noose, and a book.
One should meditate upon her who has the form of a pavilion—having one face and three eyes, seated comfortably, captivating to the mind, and adorned with all ornaments. (153)
The Meditation on the Sixteen Gaṇapatis:
O Lord of Obstacles, whirl the noose and goad until the end of the lineage.
I bow to Bhavānī’s dancing Gaṇeśa, who possesses five faces, has a lotus marked with three lines on his chest, is yellow in luster, and holds a wish-fulfilling tree in his hand. 154.
I bow to the youthful Lord of the Gaṇas, who holds in his hand a plantain, a mango, a jackfruit, and a sweetmeat, and who possesses the radiance of the rising sun. 155.

I bow to the daughter of the Mountain King, whose breasts are smeared with fresh saffron paste, who wears hanging garlands of jasmine and water-lilies, and whose beautiful feet are adorned with jeweled anklets.

The mass of his matted hair is the moon; his jewel is the fire of Smara’s arms; the purpose of his young eyes is the destruction of the gods; he is formidable with his bow; and from the churning of the ocean, the Kālakūṭa poison has emerged.
May Paraśiva, the Lord of All, protect us—he who holds the auspicious mountain, Hari, Sunda, Hāṭaka, Śira, Kāla, Nāśa, and Śūla upon his [elephant] Īṣāna, and who supports the worlds. 157.
Īśāna has a crystal-like luster and an upward-facing face; that face which has the hue of saffron is the eastern face, Tatpuruṣa; and the western face is Ghorānana, resembling a mother.
The face of Aghora is like the *japā* flower, while the face of Vāmadeva is likewise in the northern [petal];
the face of Sadyojāta, however, has a luster equal to cow's milk in the western petal.
Sumukha, Ekadanta, Vimala, and Gajakarṇika:
the first is the Child Vighneśa, the second becomes the Youthful,
the third is the Devotee Vighneśa, and the fourth is the Heroic Vighneśa.
The fifth is Śaktivighneśa, the sixth is Dhvajavināyaka;
the seventh is Piṅgalaudeva, and the eighth is Agviṣṭanāyaka.
The ninth is Vighnarāja, the tenth is Vipranāyaka;
the eleventh is Heramba, and the twelfth is Lakṣmīnāyaka.
The thirteenth is Mahāvighna; O Lord of the World, the fourteenth is [the deity] Nṛtta;
the fifteenth is named Nṛtta; and the sixteenth is Urdhvagaṇādhipa.
Bālagaṇapati (The Child Gaṇeśa)
I bow to the god Bālagaṇādhipa, who possesses plantains, mangoes, jackfruit, sugarcane, and sweetmeats in his hands, and whose splendor is like that of the rising sun. || 1 ||
The Youthful Gaṇapati

May that youthful Gaṇeśa protect you—he who holds in his hands a noose, a goad, a cake, a wood-apple, a rose-apple, sesame seeds, and a sweetmeat, and who possesses the luster of the rising sun. || 2 ||
Bhaktagaṇapati (The Lord of the Host of Devotees)
I worship the Lord of the hosts of devotees, who resembles the autumnal moon and who possesses a neck as white as coconut water and plantain milk-pudding. 3.
Vīragaṇapati
A *bhūtala*, a spear, an arrow, a bow, a shield, a sword, a *khaṭvāṅga*, a mallet, a mace, a goad, and a snake-noose.
I constantly remember the heroic, ruddy Gaṇeśa, who holds a trident, a tooth-axe, and a banner aloft;
[this is] Śaktigaṇapati.

I praise the Lord of the Śaktis, the dispeller of fear, who sits upon a green lotus embracing the Goddess, whose broad hips are radiant with ornaments, who is ruddy as the twilight, and who wields the noose and the goad.
Dhvajagaṇapati (The Banner Gaṇapati)

O Lord of the hosts of banners, do not forget her who holds a book, rosary, virtuous qualities, staff, and water-pot; whose hands are adorned with the splendor of liberation; who is moon-colored; and who shines with four faces upon the pillar of Ramā.
Blessed! || 6 ||
Piṅgalagaṇapati (The Tawny Lord of the Ganas)

A ripe mango fruit, a cluster of ripe blossoms, a stalk of sugarcane, sesame seeds, and sweetmeats—along with these, she holds an axe in her raised hand; this is Devapiṅgalā, endowed with the prosperity of the three worlds.
Ucchiṣṭagaṇapati (The Remnant Gaṇapati)
Who indeed would not seek protection from Gaṇeśa, known as Ucchiṣṭa, who holds a blue lotus, a pomegranate, a lute, rice, a bunch of kuśa grass, and a rosary?
To Vināyaka.
May the red-colored Vināyaka—whose tusk is marked by a noose and goad, who holds a radish fruit, and whose vehicle is a rat—destroy all obstacles for us. 9.
Kṣipragaṇapati (The Swift Lord of the Ganas)

One should meditate upon the swift Gaṇādhipa, who holds the noose of the *dantakalpalatā* (tooth-creepers), is radiant with the *pūrṇakumbha* (full jar) and *kuśa* grass, and possesses a face as beautiful as the *bandhūka* flower. (10)
Heramba Gaṇapati,
with hands displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, holding a noose, a tusk, a rosary, an axe, a goad,
a mallet, and a modaka.
May he who is named Heraṃba protect us—he who has the lion as his vehicle, whose face is like that of five elephants, and who is the lord of the Gaṇas, exceedingly white in hue. || 11 ||
Lakṣmīgaṇapati
O Nandin,

I shall delight in the two goddesses who are joined with a white lotus and a night-lotus, and who hold in their lotus-like hands a parrot, a citron, a lotus, a ruby-pitcher, a goad, a noose, and a wish-fulfilling creeper, while the white one holds a goad made of nectar.
From Gaurī and Tāpita, Lakṣmī arose; from Viśvahasta and Kamala, Gaṇeśa arose. || 12 ||
Mahāgaṇapati

He was accompanied by the goddess Nāyāntikā, who possesses a fair luster and is adorned with drops of nectar; she holds in her hands— marked with wheels— a white water-lily, a lotus, a citron, a goad, a sugarcane, and arrows, along with a jeweled pitcher, a rice-ear, and a water-pot.
May the great Gaṇeśa, whose body is crimson, bestow constant auspiciousness upon you. 13.
To Vighneśvara.
She who possesses three ornaments complete in her hands, which hold a conch, a sugarcane, a bow, a flower, a moon, an axe, a noose, a wheel, a goad, a single elephant, and a cluster of blossoms.
Victorious is Vighneśvara, who is fair as refined gold.
p. 126) || Nṛttagaṇapati ||

I worship Gaṇeśa, who dances on a single foot, whose trunk bears a noose, a goad, a sweetmeat, and an axe, whose fingers are adorned with well-fashioned rings, who possesses a yellow radiance, and whose hand holds the wish-fulfilling tree. 15.
Ūrdhvagaṇapati (The Upward-Facing Gaṇapati)
The god is seated upon a lion, possessing five faces and an elephantine countenance;
he has ten arms, three eyes, and a radiance as beautiful as the fruit of the jambū tree.
With her left hand, she held a leaf that was as white as a palace, filled with excellent modaka sweets, and possessed of beautiful teeth; she was endowed with great splendor.
[He holds] a serpent-noose, an axle, a thread, an axe, and likewise a mallet;
[he is] the auspicious, pot-bellied god, supreme with a noose, a goad, and a spear. 16.
Paraśu, Danta, and Ūrdhvanātha Gaṇādhipa—
these sixteen forms of Gaṇeśa extend from Bāla up to Ūrdhva.
During the arrival of a guest and at the time of marriage, as well as when viewing a painted image on a cloth,
a person should meditate upon Vighneśvara, who is being bathed and is reflected in the vessel.
To Vighneśvara.
With a noose, a goad, and tusks in his hands, holding a trunk-like hand and a pestle,
he has the face of an elephant, five arms, and two pot-bellied feet.
The dwarf Gaṇādhipa, Lord of Obstacles, mounted upon a mouse,
the dancing Gaṇapati.
The god who holds a noose and a goad, who has a tusk, a hand, and a fruit, who is lofty with his trunk-like hand, and whose belly hangs down—Gajanana. || 19 ||
With one foot bent in a dancing posture, the Lord of the Hosts of Dancing Forms—
Valambari Pillaiyār.
The elephant-faced Vāmana has an elephant's head, with a goad and a noose in his two hands, a tusk and gold or other objects in the other two hands, and a sweetmeat in his trunk.
Having made the left [hand] hold a jar of ghee, [this is] Gaṇādhipa with a protruding belly;
[this is] Nāgamukha Gaṇapati.

Possessing the color of saffron and four arms, with the face of a serpent and a crown adorned with a skull, holding a goad, a sweetmeat, and an excellent noose made of fangs—such is the true form of Gaṇanātha, resembling fire. (21)
Āliṅganagaṇapati (The Embracing Gaṇeśa)
Having touched the *liṅga* with his left hand and embraced [the goddess] with the other, he beheld the Goddess seated upon it— of pure complexion, with her beautiful thighs radiant like the sun,
her yoni suspended from the *aṇḍa*, and praised as she was embraced by the one on the left.
By others, she was seen as the mistress of her own beautiful retinue, like the sovereignty of the lord of the celestial hosts.
To the gracious Gaṇapati.

I praise the one with the countenance of an intoxicated elephant, whose color is white as a conch shell, who possesses full splendor and is gracious, and whose pair of ears are constantly moving. (p. 128)
I bow to the Lord of Creatures, the Son of Paśupati, who holds the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons in his hands, whose sacred thread is Vāsuki, and who is the King of Obstacles. || 23 ||
Vighnarāja (The King of Obstacles)
He has the face and tusks of an elephant, sharp fangs, and three eyes; he is indeed Brahmā, the ancient one whose form is all beings,
the supreme among the immortals, worthy of worship, red in color, and with beautiful hair.
I bow to the son of Paśupati, the Lord, the King of Obstacles. || 24 ||
To Śayanavighneśvara.

The youthful one who wards off the wind of obstacles, a sacrificial fire for the forest of impediments, a maddened Garuda for the swarms of Vighna’s brothers-in-law, a five-faced lion to the Lord of Obstacles,
a thunderbolt for shattering the lofty mountain of hindrances, and the source of the pot-born (Agastya) for the attainment of the destruction of obstacles.
May Vighneśvara, who reclines upon the coils of a serpent, protect me. || 25 ||
Lord of the hosts of spirits.
The color of saffron, holding a goad and a noose, with tusks like those of Acyuta, there shall be a pair of elephants;
with the face of a swift elephant and long, drooping lips, he is equal to the Bhūtas, the Lord of the hosts of gods. 26.
To Nairṛta and Vighneśvara.
In the south-western direction, one should worship Vighneśa, Gaṇeśa, who has a human form,
a large belly, a massive body, an elephantine face, and the countenance of an elephant.
Three-eyed and four-armed, with a serpent as his sacred thread.
The Lord of the Gaṇas is endowed with a basket and a crown, has protruding lips,
and holds a noose and a tusk in his right hands, while holding a goad and a sweetmeat ball in his left.

Endowed with a golden complexion, adorned with all ornaments, and accompanied by his vehicle, the elephant; whether seated or standing—the best of teachers should meditate upon this form of Vighneśa and worship it. || 27 ||
The Son of Umā
The elephant-faced one, the lotus born from the multitude of beings. || 28 ||
To Siddhivighneśvara.
He has one tusk, ears like winnowing baskets, and the face of an elephant; he possesses four arms, holds a noose and a goad, and is fond of wood-apples and sweetmeats.
Thus [is] Siddhivighneśa, the bestower of the perfect accomplishment of that task;
[and] Ṣaṇmukhavighneśvara.
He has the face of a six-tusked elephant, possesses twelve eyes and twelve arms,
and holds a Bhairava, the gesture of fearlessness, a trident, a noose, and likewise a goad.
A discus, a sword, a mace, a bow, an arrow, and a beautiful shield; likewise a crown and a tiara, all endowed with a red color.
(130) He is endowed with golden weapons and ornaments of nine kinds of jewels;
he has a snake as a sacred thread and likewise snake earrings. || 30 ||
Likewise, [one should visualize] Gaṇapati, the lord of the Gaṇas, adorned with all ornaments and possessing six faces.
Gaṇeśa should be of dwarf form, with ears like winnowing baskets and an elephant face; he should possess the form described as having the eyes of a Rakshasa and a terrifying body. || 31 ||
Meditation and invocation indeed ward off all obstacles;
they yield the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and auspiciously bring about the prosperity of the village.
It is said to bring about the increase of sons and grandsons, the augmentation of wealth, grain, and so forth, as well as good fortune, auspiciousness, and subjugation at the royal court. (32)
I bow to the victory established for Vighneśa in every undertaking.
[This is] the location for the installation of Vighneśa.
On a mountain peak, by a lake, or even at a cool tree and such; in forests, in groves of blossoming trees, or by the edge of a well, or in a temple of Śiva.
The wise man, having installed Gaṇeśa, should conceive of these [deities] as being present in the abode of Hari, in the place called Brahmā, on Mount Mandara, and in the temple of Skanda.
Meditation on Gaṇapati.
White in color, with a protruding belly, three eyes, and yellow garments;
wearing a serpent as a sacred thread and adorned with a crown of basket-shaped jewels.
Likewise, with the hand between the teeth, one should [hold] a *bilva* fruit.
Having meditated thus without distinction upon the Lord of the Gaṇas— who carries the kalhāra, the sesame seed, the modaka, the udyata, the ayuta, and the vaha— one should worship him.
To Vighneśvara.
Accompanied by his retinue and other attendants, adorned with a crown and a casket, he is red in color and has four arms; in his right hands, he holds a noose and a wheel.
The Lord, possessing a red complexion, holds a goad and a sweetmeat in his left hand; the tip of his hand, adorned with a serpent, is joined with the sweetmeat. (35)
One should constantly remember this form of Gaṇapati, the dispeller of all obstacles and impediments.
I praise the pot-bellied one, dark-complexioned... [and so forth]. || 36 ||
Gaṇapati
Seated upon a red lotus throne, [he beholds] the Lord of the [Mandala]. || 37 ||
To Vighneśvara.
He has the face of an elephant, three eyes, a dark complexion, and four arms;
he holds a sweetmeat ball and an axe in his left hands, and a tusk and a rosary in his right hands.
He wears a sacred thread made of nāgas and is adorned with all types of ornaments.
All undertakings are accomplished; obeisance be to you, O King of Obstacles! (38)
To Vighneśvara.
I meditate upon the Lord of the gods, the Lord of all worlds, whose essence is immortal nectar, whose feet are slightly bent, who is adorned with the moon upon his crest,
who is inconceivable, whose face is like gold and jewels, and who is fashioned with seven hands.
The entire body consists of impurity, possessing goads and having nooses for teeth. 39.
A pair of lotuses situated at the feet, resting upon a lotus-throne,
adorned with the ten Lords of Obstacles (Vighneśvaras).
Āmoda, Pramoda, Pramukha, Durmukha, Avighna, Vighnakartṛ, Bhakṣa, and Pañcahasta—[these you shall eat]. (40)
The elephant-faced lord of the Gaṇas—these ten are the leaders of obstacles.
[This is] the description of the ten kinds of Vighneśvaras.
Āmoda is dark blue in color, Pramoda is red,
Pramukha has the luster of crystal, and Durmukha is smoke-colored.
Avighna is yellow in color, while Vighna has the luster of red collyrium;
Bhakṣyaśi is pale white, and all five have beautiful small hair-tufts on their hands.
Gajavaktra and others are blue, while Gaṇeśa has the luster of saffron;
thus, the distinctions of color for the ten Lords of Obstacles (Vighneśas) have been proclaimed.
p.
133) || The Hand ||
Āmoda is eight cubits [in height], and Pramoda is endowed with six arms;
Pramukha is twelve, and likewise, the [height] of Durmukha is ten.
The four-armed and other obstructors, the seven who create obstacles,
the two-armed one fond of food, and the five-armed one— these constitute the group of five.
The elephant-faced Gaṇeśa has four hands, while the four-armed one [is also mentioned];
thus, the ten Vighneśas are fashioned from the hand itself.
Weapon.
A sword, a noose, a goad, a discus, a mace, a trident, and a sweetmeat;
likewise, a staff, an arrow, a bow, as well as a fruit and a lotus.
A slingshot, a mace, a shield, and a conch;
a spear, a mallet, a skull-topped staff, a thunderbolt, a serpent, and the gesture of fearlessness;
a water-pot, a goad, a brush, a skull-cup, and a rosary.
A book, a fragment of ivory, and likewise a fire-spoon and a pouring-ladle;
a Śāla-gāma stone, a conch shell, and one possessing the luster of all weapons.
Thus has the weapon of Vighnarāja been proclaimed. || 43 ||
The Characteristics of the Eyes.
Ugranetra, Samanetra, and likewise Raktanetra; Śāntanetra, Japannetra, Viśālanetra, and Sūkṣmanetraka.
This has been proclaimed as the characteristic of the eye of Vighneśa.
The various weapons of the ten Vighneśas.
The trident, the hand-drum, the sword, the mace, the shield,
the skull-cup, the noose, and the goad are proclaimed as the weapons of Āmoda.
Having placed the *modaka*, the mallet (*mudgara*), the *phaladanta*, and the lotus (*padmaka*) upon the pestle (*musala*), one should hold the weapon of Amoda.
The conch, discus, mace, and lotus; the javelin and the bhindipāla;
the bow and arrow, the khaṭvāṅga, the serpent, the noose, and the sweetmeat.
And the foremost weapon is said to grant success in all undertakings:
the Salākāgni, Sudanta, Daṇḍa, Vīṇa, and Vajraka.

[He holds] a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons, as well as a spear, Durmukha, a water-pot, a staff with a tuft of hair, and a rosary for the removal of obstacles.
The wood-apple (kapittha), the large and small sacrificial ladles (sruk-sruva), the tooth-stick of knowledge (jñānadanta),
the book, the sweetmeat (modaka), and the obstacle-maker (vighnakartṛ) are proclaimed as the weapons.
Sesame, sweetmeats, and tooth-sticks are known as the favorite foods;
likewise, the noose, the goad, the wood-apple, the cake, and the white lotus.
Having arranged it as "five cubits," it is proclaimed as the weapon.
The goad, the sweetmeat ball, the coconut, and the modaka—
these are prescribed as your weapons for the sake of Bhujagavaktra.
Having placed the mango fruit as the noose and goad, and the sweetmeat (modaka) as the red lotus,
these are proclaimed as the weapons of Gaṇeśa.
The Vehicle.
One should worship Āroda, Vyāghravāhan, Pramoda, and Siṃha;
furthermore, Gandhabherī at the head and Vṛścika for Durmukha.
One should worship, in conjunction with all others, from Vighna at the beginning up to Gaṇeśa at the end, as well as the vehicle of the mouse,
for both [forms] of Sarvavighneśa.
One should station Pramoda at the four-gated riverbank,
Pramukha at the edge of a well, and Durmukha in the great forest.
One should worship Hari in a beautiful place free from obstacles, and Vighneśa in a Buddhist temple;
one should eat what is offered and speak what is pleasing, and thus one shall become wise.
The best of installers should place the temples of Mātṛs in Kāra, those of the Durgā lineage in Gajastaka,
and the temple of Gaṇeśa in Skandālaya.
Endowed with all peace, he becomes like the Lord of All Obstacles;
thus has the characteristic of the ten Vighneśvaras been described.
O best of teachers, listen now to the procedure for extracting the mantra;
having performed meditation and invocation, one should worship Gaṇādhipa.
It bestows sons, prosperity, wealth, grain, and all forms of good fortune.
Having meditated upon Siddhivināyaka, who bestows the fruits desired by the mind,
and having worshipped the illustrious Gaṇeśa, the giver of success;
All undertakings are accomplished, even those merely conceived in the mind;
therefore, he is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Siddhivināyaka.
One should perform the worship of the Lord of the Host of Beings (Gaṇeśa) in all matters whatsoever;
at the commencement of studies, one should know that it brings auspiciousness and the acquisition of knowledge will certainly occur.
One should perform the rites for the gods, as well as the preparation for battle, with effort;
such indeed is the work of Karṣakaṇavināyaka.
The word *prati* [is used] at the three junctions of the day (*trisandhyā*), at the time of bathing,
during recitations (*japa*), in the forest, when there is fear of thieves, and in the midst of a great crowd.
In the midst of battle, in the middle of a fire, and at times of beholding the gods, one should meditate upon Vināyaka; even by merely recollecting him, there is great fruit.

At the time of installing the yantra and at the time of extracting the mantra, one should perform the ritual of the pillar and the consecration; however, in the case of recollection, one should remember Vināyaka.
Thus, for the sake of accomplishing all undertakings, one should meditate upon Siddhivināyaka; such indeed is the great fruit of the remembrance of Gaṇeśa.
I bow to the son of Umā for the sake of dispelling obstacles; I bow to Sarasvatī, who is like a jasmine flower or the moon;
I bow to the lotus feet of my venerable Guru; and I bow to Śiva, who is worshipped by Brahmā.
Hariḥ Om. May there be auspiciousness.
Likewise, Skanda, the wielder of the power of knowledge and the commander of the divine army,
as well as Subrahmaṇya, mounted upon an elephant and born from the forest of Śara reeds.
Kārttikeya, Kumāra, Ṣaṇmukha, Tārakāntaka, Senānī, Brahmaśāstṛ, Vallī, and Kalyāṇasundara.
Bāla, Krauñcabhettā, and Śikhivāhana—
these are the names of the Lords that a man should recite every day sixteen times.
O Great Sage, whoever recites this shall be completely liberated from all sins;
the meditation upon these representative forms is here called "invocation."
The first is Jñānaśakti, the second is Skanda,
the third is Senānī, and the fourth is Subrahmaṇya.
The fifth is mounted upon an elephant; the sixth is Śarakānana;
the seventh is Kārttikeya, and the eighth is likewise Kumāra.
The ninth is Ṣaṇmukha, and the tenth is Tārakāntara;
Senānī is declared the eleventh, and Brahmaśāsana is the twelfth of those two.
On the thirteenth day is Sundarī; on the fourteenth is Bālana;
the fifteenth is Krauñcahārī; and the sixteenth is Śikhivāhana.
Meditation on Śaktidhara (the Wielder of the Spear)
He has one face and two eyes, is adorned with four staff-like arms,
is endowed with a spear and a vajra, and his hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should meditate upon that peaceful, imperishable one who stands within the sacrificial pit, radiant with the ornament of earrings,
withdrawing his arrows, and mounted upon a peacock.
One [form] has two arms; in the left hand at the waist and in the right hand, he holds a Śakti who is the embodiment of the powers of will, knowledge, and action. || 1 ||
|| The Meditation on the Aggregates ||

I praise Skanda, the son of Kātyāyanī, who has the reddish luster of a lotus, who possesses two arms and one face free from ailment; I laud him whose hair is tied at the waist and whose right hand holds a loincloth and a staff, as he bows before the wish-fulfilling tree.
General-in-chief.
I bow to the blazing Āditya, who has twenty eyes and six faces, and a gentle smile;
who bestows well-being upon his beloved who embraces him with her lotus-like form on his left side;
and whose palm is placed upon the tips of her high thighs and breasts as she holds a shield and a trident to ward off fear.
In her heart, she holds a blazing spear, a wind-whip, a heavy mace, a cock, and a lotus in her hands.
Meditation on Subrahmaṇya
We worship Subrahmaṇya, who has one face and two staff-like arms, who is endowed with the gesture of fearlessness bound at his waist, and who resembles the youthful dawn. (4)
The Meditation on [the Deity] Mounted upon an Elephant.

I perpetually bow for the attainment of desired success to the Son of Īśvara, who has one face and two eyes, who holds a choice cock and a sharp spear with the gesture of fearlessness in his two left hands, who possesses the brilliance of ten thousand suns, and whose vehicle is the elephant Airāvata.
The Reed Forest.
Holding in his ten hands a spear, a shield, a sword, a banner, a cock, a javelin,
a staff, an axe, an arrow, the gesture of granting boons, the gesture of fearlessness,
and a bow; he is yellow, gentle, possesses twenty eyes, and rests upon a bed of peacocks and swans.
With these [verses], I meditate upon the worshipful six-faced one, born from the forest of reeds. || 6 ||
Kārttikeyaḥ.
O Kārttikeya, you who hold the boon-granting gesture, the vajra, and the shield in your three left hands, and the gesture of fearlessness, the spear, and the sword in the others;
you who possess the luster of the rising sun, are worshipped by the virtuous, and have six lotus-like faces—[salute him].
O Prince!
I meditate upon Kumāra, who holds a sharp spear and a sword in his two right hands, and his desired cock and shield in his two left hands;
he who is the lord of the vine (the mountain), whose eyes are like those of the gods, whose face is like the full moon, and whose body is as white as a jasmine flower or a cloud.
The Six-Faced One.
A spear, an arrow, a sword, a discus, a noose, and likewise the gesture of fearlessness;
a thunderbolt, a bow, a shield, a cock, a goad, and the gesture of granting boons.
And likewise, [the deity] with the peacock as his vehicle, endowed with all auspicious marks;
and Gajāyai and Gajavallī on the left and right sides respectively.
I bow to Sarvāyudhajaya, who is endowed with all ornaments and adorned with every kind of jewelry; his form is that of the six-faced one (Kārttikeya).
The Destroyer of Tāraka.
And on the banner of the boon-granting goad are bracelets, a bow, and a thunderbolt.
Holding the gestures of fearlessness, the noose, the sword, the mace,
the pestle, the spear, and the discus in his twenty hands, he is ruddy and resplendent like ten million suns.
It has the form of a shimmering star and is the cause for destroying the fear of friends.
Meditation on the General Together with His Army.
Holding in his hands the gesture of granting fearlessness, the goad, the spear, the trident, the gesture of granting boons, the thunderbolt, the noose, the lotus stalk, and the mace;
possessing two faces, twelve extended arms, and twenty lotus-like eyes.
I praise the commander of the divine army. || 1 ||
The Teacher of Brahmā.

We pay homage to Viśākha, the teacher born of the forest, who holds an excellent water-pot in his pair of left hands and a rosary and the gesture of fearlessness in his right; who is ten million times more beautiful than Cupid, whose eyes are like lotuses, and who has but one face. 12.
Kalyāṇasundara (The Beautifully Auspicious)

Holding a rosary of beads, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*) bound at his hip with his two hands; he is joined by the act of offering oblations according to the ritual procedure, performed with a *śruva* ladle resting upon his left thigh.

I take refuge in that one of auspicious form, who is adorned with every ornament, whose beautiful luster is like Viṣṇu holding a water-pot in his hand, and who is being praised by all the hosts of gods. 13.
Bālasubrahmaṇyaṃ (The Subrahmaṇya for Children)

I perpetually bow down to the youthful and exalted son of the Lord, who resembles the luster of a lotus, whose left hand rests upon his right hip, whose face is adorned with a beautiful girdle, and who bestows both youth and prosperity.
Meditation on the Piercer of Krauñca.

I praise the destroyer of Krauñca, the leader of the immortal hosts, who has eight arms and six lotus-like faces, holding in his left hands the shield, the noose, the spear, and the arrow, and in his right hands the boon-granting gesture, the thunderbolt, the sword, and the mace.
The Meditation on Śikhivāhana (Skanda)
I bow to the Lord who has the splendor of coral, whose face is singular, who holds a thunderbolt, a spear, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands;
the destroyer of the enemies of the world of gods, the bestower of freedom from obstacles, the son of Rudra, whose vehicle is the peacock.
The Six-Faced One.

He has ten faces resembling coral and twenty arms; his right hands hold a spear, an arrow, a sword, and grant the gesture of fearlessness, while his left hands hold a bow, a thunderbolt, a bracelet, a trident, a boon-granting gesture, and a lotus—such is the form of the Six-faced One.
Nṛttasubrahmaṇya (The Subrahmaṇya Invocation for the Dance)
We worship Skanda, who possesses a fearless, clashing spear, who is dark like the excellent *gaurīpuṣpa* flower, and who is the son of the Moon and the Ganges. 18.
