He has one face, displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, and as a youth holds a vajra and a śakti in his two boon-granting palms; he shines with a jeweled crown, has ears adorned with lotus petals,
and is established upon the first [elements]— water and wind.
|| Subrahmaṇya ||
The sacrificial thread should be two cubits long; together with the top-knot and the girdle, he should wear a loincloth and carry a staff, while the left [hand] touches the waist during recitation.
Having two arms and two eyes, he is Subrahmaṇya and handsome;
his right hand holds a lotus, while his other hand holds a spear. || 20 ||
The Meditation on the Skanda of Bāla (The Youthful)
Resembling the rising sun, possessing a mane of hair, and manifest in his own form,
he had four arms and two eyes, holding lotus-buds at his ears.
Adorned with all ornaments, he holds a water-pot before him;
joined with jeweled earrings, he holds a vajra and a śakti in his two hands.
He is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, accompanied by two spears,
adorned with necklaces and armlets, and likewise has a peacock as his vehicle.
O Subrahmaṇya!
Four-armed and two-eyed, holding lotus-buds at his ears,
adorned with crocodile earrings, and having two spears near him.
In the tips of his right and left hands, he holds a rosary and a water-pot;
or else, he is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and is provided with a waist-thread.
Whether it is joined with a peacock vehicle, or otherwise joined with a vessel,
or even in the form of a spear— this is said to be the characteristic of the three-eyed one (Śiva).
The Six-Faced One.

He who has six faces, whose vehicle is the peacock, who has three eyes, and is adorned with variegated garments; who always bestows boons with his hands, holding the spear, thunderbolt, sword, trident, the gesture of fearlessness, the noose, bow, discus, shield, cock, goad, and the gesture of granting boons.
One should meditate upon Skanda, the lord worshipped by the gods, who bestows the fruit of worship.
The Bālasubrahmaṇya Hymn.
Skanda has four arms and the appearance of a child; he is golden-hued, holds a spear and a cock in his hands, and is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 24 ||
O Prince!
Resembling a pomegranate flower, with the luster of a hunchback and the appearance of saffron,
he has one face and four hands, with a terrifying skull-bowl bound to his waist.
Holding a water-pot and a rosary, radiant with a crown and a casket, adorned with necklaces and armlets, and bound with a girdle as prescribed.
Adorned with the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), accompanied by the hidden hero (*channavīra*),
and endowed with all ornaments— [one should meditate upon] the youth who is the son of Śaṅkara. (25)
Nandakumāra.

[One should meditate on] Skanda Kumāra, the delighter of Sundarī, who has the color of saffron, possesses four arms, holds a spear and displays the gesture of granting boons, wears a bracelet, and has his right hands holding a vajra, a boon-granting mudrā, and the gesture of fearlessness. (26)
The Meditation on Kārttikeya

I bow to Kārttikeya, the son of Gaṅgā, whose womb was fire, born from the Śara forest; the embodiment of knowledge-power, the youth, the cosmic egg, the body of Skanda, Guha, the benefactor of the mountain, whose nature is fierce splendor;
the commander of the army, the fire that consumes the Tāraka demon, accompanied by the elephant-faced one, the six-faced one.
I bow to the God of gods, accompanied by the Subrahmaṇya peacock and the chariot bearing the banner. || 27 ||
The Meditation on the Youthful One (Kumāra)
May the world of the petals of power within the hexagon— the life-restorer of its mantra,
the crest-jewel of the Śaiva light— bestow upon the person the nectar that uplifts dharma,
the pure heart of the wise, and auspicious, radiant discernment.
I bow to the Lord Kumāra, the son of the God of gods, at Traikoṭācala. || 28 ||
Born from the tip of a conch shell.

I worship the son of the Lord born from Śaṅkhaṇa— the six-faced one adorned with golden earrings, shining with manifest lines of beauty, served by hosts of deities, and wielding sharp weapons and a bow.
The meditation on form as beautiful as a general’s array.
Yellow in color, with two eyes, one face, and two hands;
wearing a crown of nine jewels and likewise golden ornaments.
With Skanda’s left hand, [he holds] the right hand of Senānī,
joined with the index finger and joined with the little finger.
On his finger was a golden ring, and on his left hand was a bracelet;
Skanda’s right hand was joined with a white lotus.
[He gave] Skanda a golden crown, a necklace, and likewise ornaments;
[he gave] Skanda yellow garments and a night-watchman for the commander of the army.
With cumin, campaka, blue lotus, and trumpet-flower— thus,
with such a garland of flowers, one should worship Skanda, the bearer of the spear, as the commander-in-chief.
Adorned with all ornaments and beautified by every kind of jewelry,
[he saw] the deities beginning with Brahmā, as well as the four Vedas, the Śrutis, and the Smṛtis.
It is remembered as a rain of flowers accompanied by hosts of ṛṣis;
[it was offered] by yakṣas, kinnaras, gandharvas, siddhas, and vidyādharas to the gods.
And the sound of singing, instrumental music, and the like, as well as dancing and vocal music; and Skanda, the commander of the army, being massaged by Indra with his foot.
Indrāṇī holds a golden pitcher known as Gandhodaka;
Pārvatī and Rudra are the embodiment of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss (saccidānanda). || 30 ||
p.
146) || Subrahmaṇyar!

I bow to the one with the luster of vermilion, born from the forest of reeds, seated upon a majestic peacock, six-faced, the beloved of Devasenā and the daughter of Madhuripu, possessing twelve eyes; who holds in his right hands a spear, an arrow, a sword, a banner, a mace, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Holding a bow, a thunderbolt, a lotus, an excellent bracelet, and a trident in his other hands. || 31 ||
O Subrahmaṇya!
With a face as lovely as the moon and reddened with vermilion, his hands adorned with divine ornaments such as armlets and necklaces, bestowing the happiness of heaven and other realms,
holding a lotus, the gesture of fearlessness, a spear, and a cock, and anointed with auspicious red unguents— [I worship him].
We worship Subrahmaṇya, who bestows the attainment of desired goals upon those who bow down to him. 32.
The Meditation on the Son of Brahmā (Brahmasūta)
I shall describe the form of Indu, endowed with speech and body, possessing great splendor,
accompanied by its explanation and mudrās, and composed of divine syllables.
On the left and right sides, it is accompanied by elephant-creepers,
radiant with clusters of weapons and masses of splendor.
It bestows the fruit of all desired objects upon all practitioners;
it is adorned with every ornament and has a slightly smiling countenance. (33)
Skandaḥ
[He holds] the gesture of granting boons (varada) and has his waist girded; [he displays] the gestures of fearlessness (abhaya) and holds a spear and a vajra.
Skanda, who possesses a single body, is accompanied by a cock and a spear. (34)
Bālasubrahmaṇyaḥ!
Holding a water-pot and a rosary, displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, clad in a loincloth with feet evenly placed, and adorned with all ornaments.
His body is yellow and he is very serene; he wears a crown and jeweled earrings, a white sacred thread, and is compassionate and most venerable.
The commander-in-chief and chief of the gods is the son of Hara and the eldest of the deities;
he is celebrated as Subrahmaṇya, Kumāra, and Ṣaṇmukha.
The Fruit of the Sixteen Forms.
He established Skanda as a Brāhmaṇa through wisdom, endowed him with the splendor of progeny, and appointed him as the commander of the army, the sovereign lord, and the beautiful Subrahmaṇya priest.
The marriage while mounted upon an elephant, the son of the Śara forest,
Kārttikeya, valor, Kumāra, and abundant prosperity.
To the six-faced one, to his circle of kinsmen, to Rājasa, to Tārakāraka,
to Naravāhana, to Senānī, to Brahmaśāstṛ, and to Vaidyaka.
The knowledge of Kalyāṇasundara, the subjugation of kings, Bālaka, Dhānyaputra, Krauñcahārin, and Jayanta Śikhivāhana.
(148) Thus, [one worships] the sixteenth deity, who bestows victory over all worlds,
as well as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, union (sāyujya), and all prosperity.
To the God who removes all sins and bestows the attainment of union with Śiva:
Oṃ, salutation to Jagadbhū; salutation to Vacadbhū; salutation to Viśvabhū; salutation to Bhavadbhū; salutation to Rudrabhū.
One should worship the sixfold world-ground, which is the very nature of the Śiva-tattva, with faces toward the east and the other directions; for thus they truly become [manifest].
Thus, the sixteenth [chapter] is named "The Mirror of the Vase," and likewise [it describes] the painting on cloth, the form, and the ritual sequence.

May everyone follow my example; likewise, let them practice meditation in that same way for the sake of Dharma, wealth, desire, and liberation, as well as for union [with the Divine] and all forms of prosperity.
It destroys untimely death, dispels fear in the wilderness,
and wards off consumption, leprosy, and other ailments such as burning sensations and fever.
It destroys the fear of enemies of fire, brings everything in the world under one's sole control,
pacifies all poverty, and increases sons and grandsons.
I bow to Sarvakāryajaya; one should worship with sixteen meditations.
Having thus meditated upon Mahāsena and having paid homage again and again, [one should proceed].
O Lord of the gods of gods, whatever action— whether good or bad— I have performed according to my conduct, all that was supreme worship offered by Guha.
Having meditated, the wise person should cause all that fruit to ripen together with himself.
With devotion to that, one should constantly meditate, or recite the mantra three times a day.
Salutations to the lotus feet of the venerable Kumāraguru.
[He is] four-armed and three-eyed, and holds a skull and a trident.
In his right [hand] there should be the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and an axe (*ṭaṅka*), while on his left side he is fully endowed [with other attributes];
he is joined with a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmakuṭa*) and wears a serpent as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
On his very right side, one should likewise have Yamunā fashioned;
she should be two-armed, two-eyed, and endowed with a dark complexion.
Seated in the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana) and adorned with all ornaments,
he holds a full water-pot in his left hand and a blue lotus in his right hand.
On the Yamunā, [he saw] his own form, beautiful in all its limbs;
likewise, on the left side of the door, was the sage Mahākāla.
And one should worship Yamunā and Mahākālī to his left; this is the twenty-five-fold form.
The first [form] holds the moon; the second is with Umā;
the third is mounted upon the bull; and the fourth is in the form of a dancer.
The fifth is marriage, and the sixth is the wandering for alms;
one should know Kāmārī as the seventh, and Kālārī as the eighth.
The ninth [house] shall be Tripurāri, and the tenth [house] is the slaying of Jalandhara.
The eleventh is Gajāri, the twelfth is Vīrabhadraka;
the thirteenth is for the sake of Hari, and the fourteenth is Ardhanārī.
The fifteenth is Kirāta, the sixteenth would be Kaṅkāla,
and then the seventeenth would be Caṇḍeśānugraha.
The *Viṣāpahāriṇī* is recorded as the eighteenth,
while the form of the *Cakrapradāna* is the nineteenth.
From the propitiation of Vighna, there are twenty; Soma and Skanda make twenty-one;
Ekapāda is twenty-two; and Sukhāsana is twenty-three.
The form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti is proclaimed as the twenty-fourth,
and the form of Liṅgodbhava is indeed the twenty-fifth.
These various manifestations of Maheśvara have thus been proclaimed. [Now follows] the meditation on the Holder of the Moon.
With broad face and eyes, possessing a gentle and amorous expression, with hands granting fearlessness and boons, his body and crown like the orb of the moon,
his form upright and his feet even, standing in the *sthānaka* posture with the luster of coral.
Holding an axe and a deer, he stands upon a lotus seat. || 1 ||
Accompanied by Umā.

O Goddess, this divine form is joined with Śiva, who has a white luster and sits upon a comfortable seat; he holds a deer, an axe, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and possesses a face as beautiful as a blue lotus, together with Umā. 2.
Mounted upon a bull.
O Lord of the Earth, may you be gracious, with a curved goad and a water-pot in your right hand,
and holding a cowherd’s staff and a black axe in your left hand;
with a rosary at your back, adorned with three eyes, wearing a bound braid and a crown.
Worship that Lord who rides upon the bull, accompanied by Gaurī on his left, the bringer of auspiciousness. || 3 ||
The embodiment of dance.
O Śārdūla, whose feet shine as they rest upon the ashes of Śauryābhāsa, lifting Your left foot in the midst of garlands of flames; O Lord who dances upon the serpent,
You who perform service with Your feet, Your body smeared with ashes and adorned with garlands, You who are white with the moonlight of the left breast.
Having meditated upon Naṭeśa, who holds fire, a skull-topped staff, the gesture of fearlessness, and a hand-drum, I worship him. || 4 ||
The Meditation on Kalyāṇasundara (Auspiciously Beautiful)
One should meditate upon Him who has the luster of vermilion, three eyes, and four arms;

who is adorned with necklaces and armlets, clothed in divine garments, and wears a crown of matted hair and a bow; who is decorated with garlands and white water-lilies; and who holds Śiva and Pārvatī in His right hands—may He be grasped by all!
[He holds] a ṭaṅka and the lip of a black antelope; he is the subduer, with the moon as his crest-jewel...
O Pārvatī, [he is] joined by the goddess Śrībhūmidevī on his right hand, possessing the splendor of Lakṣmī.

One should worship the auspicious form, who is surrounded by the primordial elements, the ancient Fire, and Hari who is established there; who holds water in his left hand; who resounds with musical instruments, song, and dance; who is the first of all gods; who is praised by sages; and who stands with hands joined in the *puṣpāñjali* gesture.

The Alms-Gathering of Bhikṣu Āṭan I bow to the venerable Ārya Avalokiteśvara. In the city of Śrāvastī, there lived a certain householder who was wealthy, possessed of great riches, and endowed with abundant grain. He had a son named Bhikṣu Āṭan, who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by all. One day, while wandering through the city for alms, he saw a certain woman who was extremely beautiful, yet afflicted by leprosy. Her body was covered in sores, her limbs were withered, and she was emaciated and miserable. Seeing her in such a state, the youth felt great compassion and thought: "Alas! How pitiable is this woman; though she possesses a form that could captivate the world, she is now ruined by disease. Filled with pity, he approached her and asked, "O lady, who are you? Why do you wander alone in this manner? The woman replied, "Noble youth, I am a woman of the city of Śrāvastī. Though I was once beautiful and sought after by many, I have been stricken by this foul disease. I have no husband, no children, and no kin; I wander about seeking food and clothing. Hearing her words, the youth was moved by even greater compassion. He took her to his own home and provided her with food, drink, medicine, and clothing. He treated her with the utmost care, as if she were his own mother. Meanwhile, the householder, the father of Bhikṣu Āṭan, heard of this from his servants. Thinking it a disgrace to his family, he went to the youth and said, "My son, why do you bring this leper woman into our house? She is an object of scorn and will bring ill repute upon us! The youth replied, "Father, she is suffering greatly from disease and has no one to care for her. It is my duty to show her compassion. Do not forbid me. The father, being stubborn and driven by pride, would not listen. He expelled the youth from the house and forbade him from returning. The youth, however, remained steadfast in his resolve to help the woman. Driven away, the youth went to the forest and lived there as a mendicant. He continued to provide for the woman from afar, sending her food and medicine whenever he could. Eventually, through the power of his merit and the efficacy of the treatments, the woman’s disease was cured. Her skin became clear and radiant, and she regained her former beauty. When the youth learned that she was healed, he returned to the city. The father, seeing his son back and hearing of the woman's recovery, was filled with remorse. He welcomed them back and apologized for his harshness. From that time on, they lived together in happiness, the youth having fulfilled his vow of compassion. Thus ends the story of Bhikṣu Āṭan. May all beings be free from suffering. May they find peace and joy. May the teachings of the Buddha flourish forever. [Note: This text is a traditional Buddhist narrative intended for moral edification, illustrating the virtue of compassion (karuṇā) and the consequences of paternal pride.]
His lotus-foot, smeared with ashes like a tree on his body, is adorned with sandals and distinguished ornaments of rudrākṣa beads; his waist is encircled by the serpent Śeṣa;
his two hands hold a trident, a skull-cup, and another hand holds a damaru drum; and his seat is the deer of Dūrvā grass.
[He saw] the goddess Yānantāgni together with Vikīrṇakeśa engaged in wandering for alms.
The Meditation on the Enemy that is Desire.
Before him stood Śiva together with Umā, his body burning with supreme passion and his hands joined in reverence;
the sight of the other’s face was like the union of the Lord’s own countenance with another excellence.
The ender of time.
She has three eyes with the luster of the *bandhūka* flower, possesses eight arms, and holds aloft a trident in one hand, while the others hold a chisel,
an excellent needle, and a noose; she has terrifying fangs and a beautiful face,
with her left foot bent and its sole raised against the chest of Kāla.
One should bow to the God who is the end of Time, who is to be transcended, and who wears matted hair.
The Destroyer of Tripura.
(153) He is endowed with one face and possessed of four arms;
he holds a bow and an arrow, and carries a deer and an axe. || 9 ||
To the left [is] the god Tripurāntaka, accompanied by Umā; indeed, he is Jaladhara.
May there be for him a fierce axe, red in hue, holding the sprouts of the five *hariṇī* trees;

may he possess the wheel of honor worthy of being rested upon by the clouds in the east, bearing the sun within his matted locks, having the nature of fire, and bringing about the destruction of the elephant.
|| Gajasamhāra ||
Standing upon the head of an elephant, with his right foot placed above it and his left leg drawn up toward his face; with his hide draped over his back and raised tail,
holding a trident, sword, spear, horn, noose, shield, and skull-cup in his eight arms, he possesses a terrifying countenance and radiant splendor.
To the left is Gaurī Bhayāmukhī, who holds the hand of Hara above her head along with their son.
The Meditation on Vīrabhadra

White in complexion, wearing the remaining ornaments, holding a lute placed across his lap, bearing a chisel and a black antelope skin, clad in a tiger-skin garment with both hands, with eyes half-open, joined by the three [eyes], and with matted hair bound upon his crown; The final line of the verse is: *ardhonmīlanalocanaṃ triyayutaṃ maulījaṭābandhakam* (as provided above). (Note: The source text provided appears to be a fragment of a longer description of a deity, likely Śiva, characterized by these specific attributes.)
I bow to the lotus feet of Santata Vīrabhadra; protect me! || 12 ||
Hari: Half-meditation.
One should place Hari on the left side and Rudra on the right;
Hari as the bearer of the discus, and Rudra as the wielder of the trident.
Viṣṇu, wearing yellow garments, and Hara, wearing a tiger-skin garment.
One should meditate on Viṣṇu as being endowed with a crown, and Śaṅkara as being possessed of matted locks;
Viṣṇu should wear a garland of tulasī, while Rudra should wear a garland of bilva.
The blue Viṣṇubhūṣaṇa and Śaṅkara likewise as crystal;
his two feet upon the sandals, surrounded by all beings. (13)
Adorned with all ornaments, Viṣṇu is here in the half [of the body] of Śaṅkara.
This is the meditation on Ardhanārīśvara.
With the right foot bent and the left foot standing straight,
the man or woman in the middle of the body should adopt the three-fold bend (tribhaṅgikā) posture.
In the right hand of Hara is the trident, and likewise on both sides;
Pārvatī is on the left side, as well as a lotus and a waist-band.
One should meditate on Hara as white-complexioned and Umā as dark-complexioned;
Śambhu is clothed in a tiger-skin garment, while Maheśvarī is clad in yellow garments.
On the right ear of Hara was a serpent-earring,
and on his left ear, Umā wore golden locks of hair.
In the *bilva* garland of Rudra is the flower of the *jājī*;
likewise, O Śambhu, the matted locks and the crown of Śaṅkara are [the flowers] of Śaṅkarī.
(155) Adorned with every ornament and decorated with all jewelry,
Pārvatī stands here upon half of Śaṅkara, while all the gods join their palms in reverence. 14.
The Meditation on the Kirāta [Form of Śiva]
With red limbs and two arms, holding an arrow, with hair falling in locks, he stands possessed of a pair of fierce eyes; with a broad face and a wide chest,
adorned with pearl-like flowers on his ears, wearing a terrifying expression and a garment of tiger-skin.
One should meditate upon the supreme Kirāta, whose feet are bound and whose belly shines resplendently.
The Meditation on the Skeleton

His body is marked with ashes and his hands are adorned with a triple-tilaka shining with sindūra; he holds a skull-bowl in his left hands and wields a weapon in his right, beautified by garments of skin;
his hand rests upon a trident, and his crest is bound by the shimmering moon.
The vehicle moves through the city of Indra; it is surrounded by playful sport, O Goddess, amidst the medicinal herbs and spirits, beginning with the Bhūtas. || 16 ||
The Meditation on the Grace of Caṇḍeśa.
I meditate upon Caṇḍeśa, who wears yellow garments, has two eyes, and whose pair of palms are joined in *añjali*; he stands upon the divine seat between the two radiant Lords of Devas,
the Goddess and the God, who sit upon a throne of celestial bliss.
From Caṇḍeśa, the palm of Śambhu’s hand took hold of the crown for the sake of bestowing grace upon his son. || 17 ||
The Removal of Poison.
He should have a face resembling the sun and three eyes;
in his right hand he should hold poison, and he should grant boons.
Clad in red garments, possessing matted locks hanging down, endowed with a terrifying countenance, and having a form that removes poison. || 18 ||
The Bestowal of the Discus (Cakrapradāna)
One should know that within the city of the heart, when the hands are joined in añjali at the lotus feet of the Lord, there are twelve eyes;
one should behold the Kaustubha gem, the crown, the garments, and the excellent fruit [of the navel] adorned with a dark bracelet.
And one should see Viṣṇu, whose body is resplendent like the sun, standing amidst the lotuses.
[He saw] Ṭaṅka, Kṛṣṇamṛga, Varābhayakara, Cakraprasāda, and Hara. (19)
Meditation on the Propitiation of Vighnāntaka.
Vighneśa, red in color, accompanied by serpents, dark-complexioned, and three-eyed, holding a sugarcane,
a *kalpa* tree, a vessel of nectar, and a single staff in his hands, [is worshipped] with the mouth placed upon the lower lip;
may he grant the grace of the removal of obstacles.
The Meditation on Somāskanda.

His two arms shine like the rising sun, adorned with armlets, necklaces, and other divine ornaments, as well as garments and head-dresses; he is beautified by matted hair, a crown, and three glittering eyes;
on his left side he is joined by Gaurī, seated comfortably, while Kumāra stands in the center.
Thus bearing the form of the Lord of Umā and Skanda, holding [in his hands] the deer, the boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, and the axe.
p. 157) || Ekapāda ||

O Maheśvara, I worship Your single-footed form, which possesses the qualities of the Great Lord whose nature is white light, which is endowed with the bliss of the six hands and three eyes, and which bestows boons while holding a deer, a chisel, and a gesture of fearlessness.
Meditation in the Comfortable Posture (Sukhāsana)

One should meditate upon the Lord who has the luster of the dawn, whose ash is beautiful, whose eyes are like sacrificial ladles, who holds a deer, an axe, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons,
who shines with garments of saffron hue, and whose feet rest upon a comfortable seat.
Meditation on Dakṣiṇāmūrti

Standing upon the ground with one foot raised above the knee, he dwells constantly at the foot of a banyan tree, his body smeared with ashes, as he studies the Vedas; he wears a tiger-skin garment, holds a staff, a crystal rosary for recitation, and a rosary of *jñāna-mudrā* beads.
One should meditate upon the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti as Agni—white, three-eyed, and wearing tawny matted locks;
this is the meditation on the manifestation from the Liṅga.
The *liṅga* should be visible within; it should face downward toward the world of Hari (Viṣṇu). Above, it should have the form of a lotus-born swan (*haṃsa*) with beautiful splendors.
In its center stands the form of Śiva, resembling fire, clad in a garment of tiger skin.
O Ṭaṅka, you who hold the black antelope and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, born from the Liṅga, protect me!
Sundara, Somadhārī, Vṛṣārūḍha accompanied by Umā,
and Gaṅgādhara— these five are born from the one named Īśāna.
Ardhanārī, Hari, Ārdha, Somāskandeśa, and Vighnaka—
these five are the emanations from the faces of Puruṣa, [bestowing] the grace of the Discus.
Kāmahā, Kālahārī, Tripuraghna,
Vīraka, Jñānamūrti, and Gajāri— these six are among the Ghoravaktras.
The begging alms-round, the skeleton, Kirātārjunīya,
the snake-venom remover, and the dance— these five are on the left face.
Liṅgodbhava, Caṇḍeśa, Ekapāda, and Sukhāsana—
these are proclaimed as the fourth among the faces, namely Sadyojāta.
Thus, within the twenty-fivefold body and the vessel,
there is the nature of emanation and maintenance.
Bhikṣāṭana, Kaṅkāla, Vīrabhadra,
as well as Kalyāṇasundara and Candraśekhara.
Gangadhara— these five are proclaimed as the forms of creation; Bhikshatana, Kankala, and likewise Virabhadra are the forms of preservation.
The standing form is proclaimed as being mounted upon a bull with one foot raised.
The Form of Withdrawal.
Gajāri, Tripuraghna, Manmathasthitināśana, Kaṅkālahārin, and Dakṣiṇāmūrti. (p. 159)
Thus, this is called the fivefold form as well as the withdrawal.
The nature of concealment.
The Kirāta, the Dancing Form, Hari, Harya, and Viṣāntaka—
these five of the Liṅgodbhava are proclaimed as the manifestations of Tirobhāva.
The Form of Grace.
There shall be the removal of obstacles to the grace of Cakraprasāda and the bestowal of favor by Caṇḍeśa;
likewise, that which is called Somāskanda as well as Ardhanārī [are established]. (31)
Thus, the fivefold form is traditionally known as Anugraha (Grace).
The *ḍamaru* drum is the form of Sṛṣṭi (Emanation), Aghora is the form of Agni (Fire),
Bhujaṅga is the form of Sthiti (Maintenance), and Kuñcita is Tirobhāva (Concealment).

The granting of fearlessness and favor, the fivefold ritual acts which constitute its own form, the auspicious planting of the sprout, the hoisting of the banner, and the binding of protection— this is declared to be the pure heart-mantra.

The ritual of the procession accompanied by the festival of the vehicle, as well as the rite of the fire-oblation (homa) and the rite of the circumambulation with offerings, is proclaimed as the "rite of stability" (sthiti-karman).
One should perform the "mounting of the chariot" joined with the powder of *rajani*, as well as the festival of the black temple; this is proclaimed as the "dissolution" (*saṃhāra*).
The festival of silence, concealment, the journey of power, and grace—
all these are served by the people of devotion through the path of devotion.
The curiosity of creation and maintenance follows immediately after bathing and giving gifts;
one should bind the Mihira and Agaru [incenses], and it is taught that camphor is to be applied as an ointment.
Beholding the dance at dawn is declared to be a source of grace;
[this concludes] the fivefold daily ritual of the perpetual festival.
Worship, the offering of food (naivedya), emanation (sṛṣṭi), maintenance (sthiti), the Lord of Power (śrībalināyaka), incense, lamps, oblations, fire-sacrifice (homa), withdrawal (saṃhāra),
the concealment of the palanquin and other such items, the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla), and grace (anugraha) are thus described.
Thus, these five are eternally proclaimed as the rule and the sequence;
[this concludes] the meditation on Īśāna with the face turned upward.
He has ten arms, three eyes, five faces, and wears matted locks;
he holds a vajra, a trident, a sword, and a spear in his right hands, while displaying the gesture of fearlessness.
Holding a noose, a goad, and a hand-drum with his hands that grant boons,
he wears a crown of rubies and ornaments such as golden rings.
Gentle, with the luster of the color of crystal, he is Īśāna in the form of an image.
Meditation on the face of Tatpuruṣa, preceded by that [of Sadyojāta].
The Puruṣa has the appearance of saffron, with four faces and four arms;
in his right [hands] he holds a chisel, a trident, and likewise a hand-drum.
Holding a mace, with three eyes, gentle, and with a slightly smiling face.
A golden ring, a golden upper garment,
a pearl necklace, a crown, and ornaments of rubies and gems.
This should be the Puruṣa-mantra, whose essential nature is the form of the mantra;
[this is] the meditation on Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Terrible with fearsome fangs, possessing a countenance as radiant as blood,
he has eight arms, three eyes, four faces, and wears matted locks.
Wearing red garments and a red upper cloth,
his limbs are smeared with red sandalwood paste, and he is adorned with red garlands and other ornaments.
He holds a trident, a bhairava-skull,
and a sword in his right hands, while his left hands hold a serpent, a shield, and an arrow, appearing filled with wonder.
He has blue finger-rings and wears a serpent as a sacred thread;
thus is the fifth, the Ghora, whose nature consists of five forms.
Next is the meditation on Vāmadeva.
Born from Vāmadeva, he is red in color, four-faced, and four-armed;
he shines with anklets and bracelets, and wears a waist-thread and an upper garment.
He is red-sandalwood colored, wearing a golden sacred thread,
endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and holding a noose and a chisel in his lotus-like hands.
Three-eyed and possessing triple grace, he was adorned with earrings.
In this way, Vāmadeva would be the very embodiment of the mantra's own nature.
In the west is the meditation on Sadyojāta.
Resembling pure crystal, with four faces and four arms,
radiant with ornaments such as necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and earrings.
He wears a crown of gomedha gems and a white cloth as an upper garment;
he holds a shield joined with a sword, and his hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should know Sadyojāta as having the form of the one whose crest is the young moon.
Meditation on the Mouth of Pātāla.

I bow to that which is the beginning of the Vedas, possessing infinite forms yet devoid of attributes; who is worshipped with chowries, and by the *puṇṇāga*, *arka*, *puṣpa*, and *vakula* flowers; who is honored by the *nāgas* and *asuras*;
who is eternally radiant with millions of rays like a thousand suns; and who resembles Rudra at the fire of cosmic destruction.
I perpetually bow to that sixth face of Pātāla, which consumes its nourishment.
The Movement of the Five Faces.

Whether seated, reclining, dancing, mounted [on a vehicle], walking, or intoxicated; at the time of worship, he should be visualized as sitting comfortably, but at other times, as previously described.
The Colors of the Five Faces
Īśāna has the luster of crystal; Puruṣa has the radiance of saffron; Aghora has the appearance of collyrium; and Vāmadeva is like a jewel.
The Sadyojāta face, however, is white; it arises among the five faces.
Meditation on the Divine Liṅga
The earth is its pedestal, the water-bearing jar is its *liṅga*, space is its form,
the constellations are its flower garlands, the host of planets is its floral offering, and the sun, moon, and fire are its eyes;
it has the seven oceans in its belly, the mountain peaks for its arms, and the seven netherworlds for its feet.
I bow to the Veda, the scripture with its six limbs, whose faces are like the ten directions, and who possesses a divine liṅga.
The Meditation on Rudra.

We worship the beautiful-bodied Rudra, who is identical with Śiva, who has five faces, five necks, and ten arms; whose body is smeared with the blood of others, who holds a noose, a goad, a shield, and a sword, as well as a trident, a scimitar, arrows, and a bow.
The Meditation on the Lord of the Palace.
Two-armed and two-eyed, holding a pickaxe, a noose, and likewise an arrow;
endowed with fierce fangs, of terrifying form, and possessed of great strength.
Adorned with all ornaments and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
they all faced the palace with fierce fangs and formidable faces.
Meditation on Candraśekhara

Having one face and four arms holding a *vīṇā*, a *vedaka* fruit, a coral branch, and laughing; displaying the black antelope, the *ṭaṅka* axe, the boon-granting gesture (*varada*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*);
adorned with three eyes and clad in white garments; with the moon upon his crown; accompanied by Gaurī and her son. (12)
The Origin of the Liṅga.
Having fashioned the *liṅga*, one should likewise represent Brahmā in the form of a swan standing upon it,
and Viṣṇu in the form of a boar beneath the base of the *liṅga*.
With the palms joined at the heart, Brahmā and Viṣṇu should be placed on both sides of the liṅga;
in the middle of the liṅga, Candraśekhara should be fashioned as before.
Meditation on the One Who Bears the Crescent Moon as His Crest while Embracing [His Consort]
The God alone is accompanied by Gaurī, and the Innate One (Sahaja) is joined with Gaurī;
the two deities embrace each other, the Goddess with one hand.
That is declared to be the Tamāliṅga; thus it is said to be threefold. || 14 ||
Meditation on the Supreme Lord.
Holding a skull-cup in his hand, with a woman at his left side,
his matted locks cool as the moon, blue-throated and three-eyed,
with jewels made from the gems of serpents, and [adorned] upon his golden region...
The Meditation on Pārvatīśvara

Peaceful, seated in the lotus posture, wearing a crown of the moon, with five faces and three eyes, he holds in his right hands a trident, a vajra, a discus, a sword, and an axe, while in the left positions he holds [the gestures of] granting fearlessness and so forth.
I bow to the Lord of Pārvatī, who holds a serpent, a noose, a staff, fire, and a goad in his left hands; he is adorned with various ornaments and resembles a crystal gem. 16.
Meditation on Śiva
He has five faces resembling the moon and ten arms; in his right hands he holds a trident, a deer, a horn, a serpent, a vajra, and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya).
In his left hands he holds a noose, the gesture of granting boons (varada), a goad, and a jewel. Seated upon a white lotus, he is the very embodiment of Sadāśiva. || 17 ||
Meditation on the Linga of Food.
He has four arms and three eyes, adorned with matted locks and the crescent moon;
he is joined with a deer and a chisel, and is decorated with a garland of bilva fruits. || 18 ||
Having meditated on it as being without gender, one should worship it with the Sarvamantra;
this is the twelvefold division of the forms.
First is Mahādeva, second is Maheśvara,
third is Śaṅkara, and fourth is Vṛṣabhadhvaja.
The fifth is Śūlapāṇi, the sixth is Kāmāṅganāśana;
the seventh is Devadeveśa, and likewise the eighth is Śrīkaṇṭha.
The ninth is declared to be Īśvara, the tenth is Pārvatīpriya,
the eleventh is Rudra, and the twelfth is Śiva.
Having meditated upon these twelve divisions while recollecting the mantra, || 19 ||
The Meditation on Somāskanda.
Kṛṣṇa’s right foot is extended while his left is bent and resting in sleep; he holds a deer, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), an axe, the moon, and a bracelet in his left hands.
I worship Guheśa, who is joined by the Goddess whose other two feet are hanging down and asleep, and who is accompanied by Skanda and Soma, both holding lotuses in their two hands. || 1 ||
The thirty-sixfold division of the body.
Beyond that, Sadāśiva is the primary source from which the Liṅga arises;
he is also proclaimed as Candraśekhara and Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Next is Devārtiharaṇa, then Kālanigraha,
and likewise Kalyāṇasundara accompanied by Umā.
[Soma]āskanda, mounted upon a bull, and likewise Tripurāntaka;
for the sake of Hari, Ardhanārī and Kaṅkāla in his dancing form.
Bhikṣāṭaka, Kāmāri, Aghorāstra, Sukhāsana, Trimūrti, and Ekapāda; beyond these, Gaṅgādhara is considered supreme.
And likewise Caṇḍeśānugraha, the excellent Ādicaṇḍeśvara,
Gajaghna, the form of Brahmā, and similarly the form of Viṣṇu.
And Skanda, Śiva, Sūrya, Vighneśa, Kṣetrapālaka,
Bhairava of terrifying form, and likewise Āpamuddhāraṇa.
Kirātaka and Bhaiṣajya are said to be the thirty-six forms;
[these constitute] the form of Sadāśiva.

Five-faced, with ten arms, hands, and eyes, he holds in his right hands the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a trident, a thunderbolt (*vajra*), a spear, and a serpent, while in his left hands he holds a boon-granting gesture (*vara*),
a noose, a bell, a goad, and an axe; he is adorned by the beloved goddesses Pīta and Asitā.
I ever worship Sadāśiva, whose form bears a white face upon his heart.
The Origin of the Liṅga.
One should meditate upon the Lord, whose proportions are measured according to the sanctum, who has a matted-lock crest upon his linga-like head,

whose hand rests upon his hip, who holds a sacrificial ladle, and who is dark-hued; who displays the deer and the gesture of fearlessness in his left hands, while holding an axe in the other, whose feet and crown are immeasurable, and who is joined by Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
One should meditate upon the stainless Haṃsa and Kola situated above and below, arising from the Liṅga. || 2 ||
To the one whose crest is the moon.
His limbs resemble the color of the *aruṇa* gem; he has the moon as his crest-jewel and three eyes; he holds a deer and an axe, while in his left arms he embraces a spear and a consort;

he is endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons; he is adorned with necklaces and armlets; and his form is like that of the Moon-bearer upon the tip of a white lotus petal. 3.
Dakṣiṇāmūrti.

I bow to the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who is white as ash, who bears the crescent moon, who is radiant with the gesture of wisdom, a rosary, a lute, and a book, who is attended by the lotus-born Brahmā and the best of sages, who is most gracious, who wears a tiger skin on his left side, and who possesses a beautiful body.
The restraint of time.
Bearing an axe and a trident-lotus, the illustrious Kālanātha spoke these auspicious and beautiful words.
I bow to the auspicious god, who has the luster of vermilion and possesses three eyes.
Accompanied by Umā.
Seated upon a lotus in a blissful posture, with three eyes, his face joined with that of Gaurī at the junction of their lips,
with a gentle smile, his head crowned by matted locks and adorned with the crescent moon;
he embraces his consort with his left arm while holding an axe and a deer in his other two hands.
I worship Maheśa, who is accompanied by Umā, who is to be served, and whose right hand bestows fearlessness.
Soma-Skanda: A Dialogue on the Moon and the God Skanda.
With his left hand supported by Dakṣa...
[seated] upon a bull.
He is resplendent upon the head of a bull, possessing three eyes and a right arm; his left leg is placed upon the broad hand of the boon-granting gesture, while his right foot is slightly bent.
He stands with both feet evenly aligned, his right shank resting upon the other.
The god mounted upon a bull, holding an axe, is accompanied by a deer. || 9 ||
The Destroyer of Tripura.
I bow to the one with three eyes shining like coral; I praise him who, with his laughter, destroyed the cities of the demons.
The meaning of the word *hari*.
On his left side is Haryarthadeva, who has the luster of coral.
Ardhanārīśvara (The Lord who is half-woman)
I bow to Ardhanārīśvara, who assumes the forms of both male and female.
The Skeleton.
I worship the god Kaṅkāla, who has a reddish luster, a smiling face, a moon as his crown, and [is endowed with] ... || 13 ||
The Alms-Gatherer’s Song of Realization.
To Sārāga, however, [I offer] a blade of dūrvā grass; he holds a trident in his right hand and has placed its root— its stem being held in his throat— into the ears of the afflicted,
while with his other two hands he carries a skull-cup and a stainless damaru drum, his feet resting upon sandals.
I bow to the Lord of the Mendicant’s Alms-round, who possesses limbs that enchant naked women and is accompanied by hosts of Pramathas.
The Aghora Weapon Mantra.
Resembling a water-laden cloud, with terrifying fangs and three eyes, he is non-terrible (Aghora) yet bears serpents; clad in red garments and smeared with red unguents,
he holds an axe, a *ḍamaru* drum, a bell, a shield, an arrow, a bow, a trident, and a human skull.
I meditate. || 1 ||
The Triple Form (Trimūrti)

With one foot placed upon the hip of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, who stand on either side of her single lotus-foot, she is praised with joined palms for the sake of grace; she has two beautiful hips and her other foot is slightly bent.
She possesses three red eyes and holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a chisel, together with Umā, who holds a mallet in her hand.
One should worship the radiant one, whose crest is the moon, who occupies the station of the gods, who is accompanied by his three-footed [vehicle], and who is the triple-formed one.
Ādicaṇḍeśvara.
Golden-hued, with three eyes and the moon upon his head, holding a rosary in his upper right hand and an axe in his upper left;
bearing a fragrant trident and displaying the gesture of granting boons in the lower left,
with his feet resting upon the earth in the right and joined by the Goddess in the left.
I bow to the primordial Caṇḍeśvara, whose face is adorned with divine earrings. 17.
Brahmā.

Having a yellowish luster, four faces, and eight arms, divine, with a crown of matted locks, two eyes, and hands joined in the gesture of granting boons, holding a rosary and a vessel of fragrant water,
adorned with armlets and other ornaments, sweet-voiced, and decked in yellow garments.
I worship the Lord Brahmā, who is mounted upon a swan and accompanied by the creation.

One should meditate upon the Cause (Kāraṇa), who has a dark-blue luster, three eyes, and four arms; who is adorned with yellow garments, holds a discus and the gesture of fearlessness in his right hands, and carries a conch and a mace in his left hands; who is seated comfortably upon a lotus throne and is united with Kamalā.
I worship the illustrious Lord Viṣṇu, whose crown possesses the red luster of shimmering earrings. || 19 ||
The Form of Rudra.
[I bow to] the three-headed one, with the luster of the dawn, adorned by serpents, having a single lock of hair, blazing with a crown, the Lord who bears the moon upon his crest,
the sovereign of the gods; the God Rudra, who daily holds a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, and a lotus, while his lotus-like hands bear a rosary.
I worship.
p.
171) || Skanda ||
I bow to the Lord who has the luster of coral, who has a single face, and whose hands hold a thunderbolt, a spear, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness;
I praise Rudrabhū, whose hair is like that of a god, who slew the elephant-demon Gajāsura, and who has the peacock as his vehicle.
Śivasūrya: The Sun of Śiva.

I praise Śiva-Sūrya, who is seated in the lotus posture, whose body is red and who has three eyes; he holds a white lotus with his two hands, is adorned with red garments, unguents, and garlands, and possesses white limbs.
Vighneśvara (the Lord of Obstacles)
One-faced, three-eyed, elephant-faced, red in color, and four-armed; holding a sweetmeat (*laḍḍuka*) and a noose in his left hands, and a tusk and a goad in his other two hands;
with one foot placed down and the other leg raised and set in front.
One should constantly meditate upon Vighneśvara, who is short, pot-bellied, and has ears like winnowing baskets. || 23 ||
Kṣetrapāla (The Guardian of the Field)
One should meditate on the Lord who bears matted locks of red flames, has three eyes, and is endowed with fangs that are terrifying;
who holds in his hands, from right to left, a noose, a skull-bowl, a trident, and a *ḍamaru* drum;
who is naked, adorned with serpents, possesses beautiful eyes, is dark-complexioned, and has well-rounded glances.
With shanks as pure as a bell-metal drinking vessel, he is the protector of the field, auspicious. || 24 ||
Her feet are adorned with sandals; on her ankles are tinkling anklets;
in her hands she holds a trident, a skull-bowl, and a hand-drum; and her ears are adorned with earrings.

One should meditate upon that Bhairava, whose body is draped in a bodice, whose face is adorned with a tilaka, whose cheeks are framed by locks of hair, and who has assumed a form upon the surface of the earth. || 25 ||
He has a dark complexion, hair like flames, three eyes, and is adorned with serpents; his eyes are red, he has ten arms, and the moon is his crest-jewel.

He holds a trident and a *ḍamaru* drum, as well as a sword and an arrow in his right hands, while in his left hands he bears a bell, a noose, a skull-cup, and a bow, and wears a garland of severed heads.
I praise the naked, fierce one with formidable tusks, the burner of the Danujas, who possesses a terrifying form. || 26 ||
Rescue from Calamity
Resembling the rising sun, three-eyed, with blossoming and radiant locks of hair,
holding a trident, staff, and skull-cup in his pair of hands, blazing with earrings upon his ears,
clad in a bodice of tiger-skin, adorned with a garland of skulls, and casting a glance that reaches from his knees to the ends of the quarters.
I perpetually bow to that which, having taken the form of Karna, is the remover of calamities and the sacred thread fashioned by himself.
The meditation on the thirty-sixfold analysis of the six types of conflict is completed.
The Liṅgaliṅgodbhava, the Mukhaliṅga Sadāśiva,
the Mahāsadāśiva, and beyond that, the Umāmaheśvara.
He saw Umesh seated comfortably, as well as Somaskanda,
the moon-crested form, and Vrishantaka mounted upon his bull.
Bhujaṅga, Lalita, Bhujaṅgātra-sama,
Sandhyānṛtta, Sadānṛtta, Tāṇḍava, and likewise Jāhnavī.
The Gaṅgāvisarjana, the Tripurāntaka,
the Kalyāṇasundara, and likewise the Ardhanārīśvara.
The Gajāyudha, which destroys fever; the Śārdūlāhāra-vigraha;
likewise the Pāśupata, the Kaṅkāla, and the Keśavārthaka.
The wandering for alms, the slayer of lions, the one who bestows grace upon Caṇḍeśvara,
the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and likewise the bearer of the yoga-lute.
And Kālāntaka, Kāmāri, Lakubera, Bhairava,
Āpaduddhāraṇa, as well as Vaṭuka and Kṣetrapāla.
Vīrabhadra, Aghorāstra, and likewise Dakṣayajñahara;
Kirātaka, Gurumūrti, Aśvārūḍha, and Gajāntaka.
The slaying of Jalandhara, as well as Ekapāda and Trimūrtika;
and likewise Trimūrti and Ekapāda, as well as Gaurī granting her boon.
The nature of the gift of the discus, together with the play of Gaurī;
the removal of poison, as well as the Gāruḍa [mantra] and the burning [rite].
Likewise, [he described] the severing of Brahmā’s head, the destruction of Kūrma,
Matsyāri, Varāhāri, and the manifestation of the Prārthanā form.
Furthermore, there is the preeminence of blood-offerings, as well as the state of being a disciple;
likewise the Six-faced One (Ṣaḍānana), and similarly the one with eight or six bodies (Aṣṭāṣaḍvigraha).
p. 174) || Meditation on the Liṅga ||

This incomparable Linga, situated amidst the sages Śamadha and Nami, is formless, composed of light, stainless, free from impurity, exceedingly vast, free from disease, beautiful within, and possesses a great resonance. It is a lotus-like seat upon which another [deity] is established.
I bow within my heart to that which transcends the path of the mind and is praised by Hari and Hara. || 1 ||
The Origin of the Liṅga.
One should meditate upon the manifestation of the Liṅga within the inner sanctum of the divine temple. || 2 ||
Meditation on the Face-Liṅga (Mukhaliṅgadhyāna)

On the *liṅga*, one should visualize the four-faced Lord, whose upper face is stainless, with half an eye, wearing the moon, adorned with a crown of matted hair, bearing the Gaṅgā, white in complexion,
endowed with five shoulders, and having faces that are golden-hued, black, and red.
I worship that white triple-linga with clearly manifested surfaces, located in the directions beginning with the east. || 3 ||
Sadasiva.

Five-faced, with ten arms, hands, and eyes, he holds in his right hands the gesture of fearlessness, a trident, a thunderbolt, and a spear, while his head is adorned with a serpent; in his left hands he holds a boon-granting gesture,
a noose, a bell, a goad, and a chisel, and he is resplendent in yellow and black.
I always worship Sadāśiva, whose form bears a white face within his heart.
The Great Sadāśiva.
With a serene face, twenty-five-fold, wearing matted locks, possessing seventy-five eyes, and having earrings fashioned from his own cheeks.
I worship the supreme Mahāsadāśiva, adorned with fifty hands, endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, white-complexioned, and decorated with serpents. || 5 ||
Umāmaheśvara (The Great Lord with Umā)

I praise Umāmaheśa, who is red in hue, three-eyed, reclining and hanging down on his left side while holding the gesture of granting boons and a staff in his right; he holds a rosary and a trident, and is accompanied by Girijā.
Seated comfortably.
Peaceful, white, three-eyed, and endowed with elephant-like arms, his ears radiant with earrings;
holding a staff, a bell, a goad, fire, an axe, a serpent, and a boon-granting gesture, as well as the gesture of fearlessness; bearing his right foot while his left foot lies extended behind him.
I praise Him who is seated comfortably on the left with Gaurī, wearing a crown of the moon. || 7 ||
Accompanied by Umā.

One should worship in one's heart [the Lord] who is white-complexioned, seated upon a comfortable throne, endowed with power, holding a deer, a *ṭaṅka* (stone-cutter’s chisel), the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons; who has beautiful hands, lotus-like eyes, and bestows boons, accompanied by Umā.
Soma-Skanda: A Hymn to Soma and Skanda.
It has a single opening, possesses a source of water, and is joined with a cave. || 9 ||
Candraśekhara (The Moon-crested One)
With broad face and eyes, possessing a gentle and amorous expression, with even and slender feet and a stance the color of coral;
with hands in the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, adorned with a crescent moon upon his crown, holding an axe and a deer, he is the very embodiment of the Moon-bearer.
Meditation on [the Deity] Mounted upon a Bull.
I praise him who is mounted upon a bull, whose left side is joined with a face and a staff, and whose hand holds a bracelet—
[the one] near the bull.
On the head of the bull shines his left arm; he has three eyes, and his great thigh rests upon the hand of the boon-granting gesture (varada-mudrā);
his left foot is slightly bent, while his right leg is positioned in the *sthitapada* stance, reaching toward the other [side].
The god situated within the bull, the man, the sheep, the goat, the deer, and the axe.
Meditation on the Graceful Dance of the Serpent-Lord (Bhujaṅgalalitanṛtta)

One-faced, four-armed, and three-eyed, he holds a *dhattūra* flower and the moon in his left hands, while his right hand is extended with fingers like a peacock’s tail; his upper foot is raised and bent, and he wears a *svastika* earring on the right, holding a *ḍamaru* drum, the Gaṅgā, and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*).
I bow to Śiva, who stands upon the Bhūtas, graced by his arms moving gracefully in dance.
Meditation on the Dance of the Bow-Bearing Serpent-Frightener.
Holding in his lotus-like hands a staff with a serpent at its tip in the right and fire in the other, assuming the *sūcīmudrā*, standing in the *samapada* posture upon a pedestal,
restless, with hair tied in a topknot, three-eyed, and having Śiva as his crest-ornament with the Gaṅgā and the moon— [I meditate on him].
I bow to him whose city is the frantic dance of the serpents of fear, and whose garment is the tiger skin.
The Twilight Dance.
With one foot bent and placed to the left, while the other remains on the ground, he stands with his hands crossed in the *bhujaṅgaprāsārtha* gesture, turning away.
May the Actor, who reveals his joined *tāṇḍava* dance while standing gracefully and joyfully amidst the directions of the lotus-eyes of Ambā’s face, protect us through his performance. 15.

He has one face, four arms, and three eyes; in his left hands he holds a dhattūra flower and the moon, while his right hands extend toward a flame and a leaf. His upper foot is bent, and in his right [hands] he bears a svastika, an earring, a hand-drum (ḍamaruka), the Gaṅgā, and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya).
I perpetually revere the Tāṇḍava dance, in which matted locks are spread out as wide as the sides of the earth and its inhabitants. 16.
The Dance of Kālī’s Wrath (Kālitāṇḍava)
With her left foot slightly bent, its anklet recently adorned with shimmering luster, her moon-like face resounding with the tinkling of swinging golden bells, she—
whose radiant earrings glow with crimson light— puts an end to Kālī’s wild dance.
May Caṇḍikā protect the fierce one; may her counter-dance, which brings about prosperity, protect him.
Gangadhara.

[He] is peaceful, seated in a yogic posture, bearing the stainless moon, his body wrapped in a yogic cloth; he holds a chisel, a book, and a deer in his [left] hands, while his right eye gazes upon the minister [Mañjuśrī].
She, with her body hanging down and her hair tied in a topknot, pure and praised by the gods, carries [these items] on her right side.
I bow to the Lord of Gaṅgādharā, who is joined with Gaurī on his left and whose body is white with ashes. || 18 ||
The Dismissal of Gaṅgā

Seated upon a lotus, possessing a peaceful form and resembling a crystal gem, bearing an axe and a trident in his left hands while his right hand displays the gesture of fearlessness; with matted locks adorned by the rays of thousands of millions of suns,
he is performing the act of emission into the Bhāgīrathī, and is endowed with the other [form] consisting of the six dense wheels.
I bow to Gaṅgāvisarga, who is united on his left side with the beautiful Girijā.
The Destroyer of Tripura.

He has a reddish luster, a face like the full moon, and is dark-hued; he holds a deer and a bow in his left hands, while in his right hand he holds an arrow, and in the other left hand he holds an axe;
he wears the crescent moon upon his brow and is served by the gods, beginning with Gaurī, Candra, Hari, and Viriñci.
I worship the three-eyed God, the destroyer of Tripura, who was blinded by laughter. || 20 ||
Kalyāṇasundara (The Beautifully Auspicious)
I worship the auspicious god, whose crest-jewel is the young moon within a lotus, and whose face is white. || 21 ||
Ardhanārīśvara (The Lord who is Half-Woman)
I bow to Ardhanārīśvara, whose body possesses both male and female forms, and upon whose matted locks dwells the moon.
Gajārīśvara (The Lord who is the Enemy of Elephants)

Standing upon the head of an elephant, with his right foot [on it] and his left foot raised toward the face, holding a hide over his head with his two hands, his tail held aloft, blazing with a trident, sword, and horns; p. 179)

I worship the God, who holds a shield, a skull-bowl, and a noose in his left hands, who is endowed with fangs, whose splendor is red, and who is accompanied by the Goddess who bestows fearlessness and by Guha. || 23 ||
The Dispeller of Fever.
One should meditate on this [goddess] as having three faces with the eyes of Rudra, six arms, three feet,
and white in complexion; she holds a drum in her right hand extended forward and fire in her left,
while her two feet are placed upon a raised lotus seat in the *svastika* posture.
I worship the form of Jvareśa, smeared with ashes and bearing matted locks hanging down for years. || 24 ||
The Śārdūlaharaḥ (The Lion-Slayer) hymn.
With a pale yellow garment, three eyes, and adorned with curled locks of hair;
sporting a tiger’s face and a pair of hands holding a lotus in the left [hand] while the other is raised;
with his feet treading upon a needle, a mouse, a lizard, a rat, and a crocodile within that cave.
I bow to the Lord who holds a tiger and a serpent, while his other foot is drawn up in a tucked position.
Pāśupateśvara.
The primordial [deity] has a face with locks of hair, a red and slender body, and three eyes; he holds a trident and the gesture of fearlessness, or alternatively, a *ḍamaru* drum in his left hand;
he wears the crescent moon as a crest-jewel, and in his left hand he wields the *pāśupata* weapon.

I perpetually worship that Lord of the Pāśupatas, the Master of Peace, who holds Arjuna with his right hand joined in *añjali* and bestows grace with his left, shining with a weapon as radiant as ten million suns. (p. 180) 26.
Kaṅkālaśiva.
I worship him who has a reddish luster, a smiling face, and a moon as his crown, holding a staff-like arm in his left hand. || 27 ||
Meditation on the Meaning of the Word "Hari"
I bow to the Lord who grants all desires, whose left side has the luster of coral, and who is joined by a beautiful hand. 28.
The Alms-round of the Bhikṣu
I worship the Lord of the Alms-round, who has a white luster and auspicious eyes. || 29 ||
The deity Siṃhaghna.
One should meditate upon that state of Nṛsiṃha, who has the face of a lion, possesses eyes like the sun, moon, and fire, has flaming hair, excellent fangs, and is endowed with a pair of wings;
who is praised by the sound of "Sukha," holds the Vedas in his hands,
and stands with his two lotus feet adorned as he tramples upon the demon, crushing him with his feet.
I bow to the incomparable Lord Nārasiṃha, who bears a lotus-stalk, a trident, and a skull.
The Grace of Caṇḍeśa.
I bow to the three-eyed one, whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon, who resembles a crystal gem, and who holds a black axe;
whose beauty is enhanced by his left leg hanging down, and whose excellent feet rest upon a lotus pedestal;
who, seated upon his bull, bears a garland of flowers offered by his two devotees along with the daughter of the mountain and her consort.
I worship Caṇḍanātha, who possesses a beautiful parasol, whose ears are fierce, who is praised by the best of gods, and who is the Lord of the Fierce. || 31 ||
Dakṣiṇāmūrti: The Southern-Faced One.
Holding a jewel-casket containing fire in the tips of his hands marked with the *jñānamudrā*, though white in color,
he has one leg pendant and the other leg resting upon a corpse; he is three-eyed.
I praise Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who dwells upon the Girivara mountain.
Yogadakṣiṇāmūrti: The Dakṣiṇāmūrti of Yoga.
Holding the *cinmudrā*, a rosary, and an axe in his right and left hands respectively; with his left knee resting on the ground and his body wrapped in a yogic cloth (*yogapaṭṭa*);
with his right lotus-foot extended downward, accompanied by Sanaka and the other [sages], and with his feet placed upon the back of a *bhūta*.
I praise Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who is peaceful, possessed of the three eyes, serene, and accompanied by the king of mountains. || 33 ||
Vīṇā-Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
With limbs radiant with white luster, wearing a serpent-king as a sacred thread, bearing the moon, fire,
and a rosary of beads, his foot slightly bent while holding a shimmering golden lute, he stands upon the peak of the best of mountains.
The deity Dakṣiṇāmūrti. || 3 ||
The Meditation on the Ender of Time (Kālāntaka)
Blue in luster, with red eyes, bearing flaming locks of hair, possessing cruel fangs and being most terrifying,
[he holds] a trident, an arrow, a sword, an axe, a shield, a noose, and a club.

I bow to the Black-throated One, the Death of Time, who holds a needle in his right hand and a multitude of axes in his left, whose lotus-foot destroys the left [side], and who removes the death of the sage-born [Brahmins]. 35.
The Enemy of Desire.

His body is smeared with ashes, he wears the moon, and is adorned with matted locks and a single braid; holding a chisel and a black antelope, he is stainless and seated in the heroic posture (vīrāsana),
having placed his right palm upon the left and his left palm upon the right in supreme yoga.
I worship Śambhu, who wears a tiger skin, whose forehead is like [the moon], and who has burnt the God of Love.
Lakulīśa.
With a crimson body, he holds a hand-drum and a trident in one pair of hands, while in another pair he displays the gesture of fearlessness and a small staff;
he bears a smiling countenance, his body is covered in ashes, and his tawny hair stands erect;
he has three eyes, a blue throat, wears great serpents as ornaments, and is radiant with necklaces and other jewels.
In my heart, I meditate upon Lakulīśvara, the lord of the gods, seated upon a lotus throne.
Bhairava:
Wearing matted locks of red flames, possessing three eyes, and endowed with a terrifying fanged countenance,
he holds in his right hands a noose, a skull-cup, a trident, and a *ḍamaru* drum, while in the other [left] hands he bears a bell and a garland; he has clean shanks.
I worship that Kṣetrapāla. [p.
183] [This is] the Deliverance from Calamity.
With three eyes resembling the rising sun, adorned with a radiant skull-cup, holding a fruit and a staff in his pair of hands, with earrings on both ears,
clad in a tiger-skin garment, with a smiling face, and possessing ears as beautiful as the moon, the ender of the world.
I perpetually bow to the one who wears a sacred thread made of strings of bells and who delivers one from calamity.
Vaṭukaḥ.
May Vaṭukanātha be victorious— he who holds a skull in his hand, wears earrings, carries a staff, has a dark-blue serpent as his sacred thread like fresh darkness,
and who, having performed his ritual worship, is the cause of the destruction of obstacles and the bestower of success upon practitioners. 40.
Kṣetrapāla: The Guardian of the Field.
One-faced, four-armed, and three-eyed, he is dark blue with beautiful, wide-open eyes;
holding in his hands a trident, a skull of Brahmā, a hand-drum, and a serpent;
with hair like flames, terrifying, wearing the crescent moon, and a face formidable with fangs.
I worship the Lord of Śrī Bhairava, adorned with a garland of bells and accompanied by a dog. || 41 ||
Vīrabhadra.
May the form of Vīrabhadra, blue-hued and clad in red garments, manifest before me. 42.
The Aghora Weapon Mantra.
I meditate upon Him who resembles a dense mass of clouds, who has terrifying fangs and three eyes, and who bears [the crescent moon] upon His brow. (43) (p.
The Destroyer of Dakṣa’s Sacrifice.
One should meditate upon the Hero, who bears a form fashioned by the enraged Vīrabhadra; who stands firmly with his excellent left foot placed forward upon the ground,
while his radiant lotus-like left foot remains well-set behind it.
With a sword, he struck the one standing in the east, who was joined by two right hands and possessed a large, excellent face.

Upon his head he bears the five [arrow-heads] along with the ear-ornament of flowers; clad in a tiger-skin garment, his belly is adorned by bound serpents—I should meditate upon me, the Great Kirāta. 44.
The Form of the Guru.
[One should meditate on him] whose complexion is like crystal, who holds a rosary of pearls, a jar of nectar,
and the *jñānamudrā* with the tips of his hands; who has serpents for his bracelets, the moon as his crest-jewel, and three eyes.
I bow to the divine Dakṣiṇāmūrti, whose form is the preceptor.
Mounted on a horse.
Red in color, possessing the form of a sixteen-year-old, with blazing red earrings, wearing a red-bound crown and bearing the moon, adorned with necklaces and other ornaments,
mounted upon a horse as green as palāśa leaves, pure, and accompanied by a vessel held in his right hand.
I worship him who holds a rope in his left hand, wears excellent garments, and is mounted upon a horse. || 46 ||
The Destroyer of Elephants.
Skilled, peaceful, serene, bearing the moon upon his crown, his body illuminated by earrings,
with a khaṭvāṅga staff in his right hand and a skull-topped staff (huṃ) hanging from his left, possessing two arms.

I praise the elephant-demon who, possessing the beautiful form of a young elephant resembling the rising sun, swiftly approached with his trunk extended, his body swallowed by Indra’s thunderbolt. 47.
The Enemy of Jalandhara.
Reddish in hue, with a fierce gait, enriched with three eyes, and with hands beautified by a *ṭaṅka* and a black antelope skin upon the head—
this is the Earth, supported by Cakradharaṇa and Gajalāndhara.
He who has the form of the slayer of Jalandhara, who struck down Karṇa.
Meditation on the Threefold Form with One Foot

One lotus-foot is placed upon the middle of the waist; Brahmā and Viṣṇu are joined there for the sake of pleasure, immersed in that water. On the beautiful waist, he is endowed with two bent feet, holding three red threads, granting boons and fearlessness, and bearing an axe in his hand.
May the Trimūrti worship the radiant Lord of the Gods, who bears the moon upon his crest and possesses three feet.
One-footed.

I worship Śiva, whose feet are honored by the worlds, who bears a single form yet has many faces, who stands on a single foot, who is endowed with the trident, the chisel, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness, who has a dark throat, and who is exceedingly terrifying.
Meditation on the Bestowing of the Boon by Gaurī.
I worship him who has three red eyes, whose crescent moon shines, and who holds in his three hands an axe, a deer, and a trident;
with his right hand he holds ashes and offers a gesture of salutation (*añjali*) to Gaurī as the cause, while bestowing boons upon Gaurī. (51)
The Gift of the Wheel.

One should meditate on the peaceful [deity] with three eyes and four arms, bearing the moon, joined by the Goddess; holding an axe and a black antelope in the left hands, and bestowing boons and a lotus in the right;
with the right foot hanging down and the left foot resting peacefully upon a lotus.
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu at the foot, worshipped by the deer, accompanied by Brahmā, and bestowing the discus. || 52 ||
Meditation on Gaurī endowed with her playful grace.
Joyful, endowed with three eyes, possessing the luster of coral, with blazing red earrings,
holding an axe, a black antelope, and the gestures of granting fearlessness, standing upon the broad thigh of Gaurī,
he embraces her with his left lotus-foot; this [form] has been attained by the face [of the poet].
In the sky above the women's garden, I worship Gaurī’s graceful play within her celestial chariot.
The Remover of Poison.
Holding the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*) and a black axe, wearing the moon as his great ornament,
clad in yellow garments, and possessing three eyes; white in complexion yet with the luster of a dark throat— that god mounted upon a bull, whose form is capable of neutralizing poison.
His form is enriched with a parasol and a peacock-feather fan. || 54 ||
The Meditation on the Burning of Garuḍa

One should meditate on him mounted upon Garuḍa, holding a serpent, a trident, and the gestures of boon and fearlessness, adorned with a serpent as a sacred thread, and attended by the best of sages, Siddhas, and others.

I worship the son of Tarkṣya, who burns the serpent with his own wings and eyes, holding a staff and other weapons in his hands, possessing a left hand joined with a spear, seated in a firm posture, and consuming the serpent. 55.
The Severing of Brahmā’s Head.
One should meditate on the dark blue deity with three eyes of a bluish hue, joined with the moon, his face terrifying with the syllable *huṃ*,

his limbs smeared with ashes, holding a trident and an axe in his three hands, and manifesting as a black deer; he wears fine sandals upon his feet and, while laughing with human cries, seizes Hara by the chest with his left hand.
One should always meditate upon the blood-glistening bodice and the severing of Brahmā’s head.
Meditation on the Reabsorption of the Tortoise (Kūrmasaṃhāradhyāna)
May the white-rayed moon protect you this moment— the moon-crested Lord who stands upon level lotus-feet, who bears a black boar’s tusk,
and who, with the tips of his hands, grants fearlessness while resting his left foot upon the back of a tortoise.
The left hand is joined with the earth, and he is the deity Kūrmasaṃhāra. || 57 ||
The Fish-Destroyer.
In Tryaikṣa, [he is] blue-black in body, bearing a multitude of serpents, and holding with his right and left hands a sword adorned with a parasol-line, a shield, a bell, and also an axe;
having struck the fish with the sword and drawn it out with the axe placed [there], he removes the distress from its eyes.
Bearing the lotus-feet worthy of worship, may this Lord, the destroyer of the fish-demon, grant you prosperity. (58)
The Enemy of the Boar (Varāhāri)
Golden-hued, with flaming hair and curved, reddish eyes, his body possessing a terrifying form;
in his [four] hands, he holds a noose and a trident in the left, while from the excellent right hand he displays a *ḍamaru* drum and a skull-cup (*bhindipāla*).
With his lotus-like arm, he strikes a boar with a trident and uproots its tusk.
May Narahari, who dwells nearby, serve him who maintains [the vow]; I praise that slayer of the boar. || 59 ||
Meditation on the Form of Prayer (Prārthanāmūrtidhyāna)
May he protect you— he who resembles a jasmine flower, who has three eyes, who bears the moon,
and who holds an axe; whose matted locks are tied at the right side and rest upon his knees, and who, embracing Caṇḍī with one hand, holds her chin with his other beloved hand.
May Śiva, who embodies our prayer, protect us as he speaks.
The Blood-Seeking Beggar.
One should meditate on him holding the lord of serpents at his hip with his right hand, a noose in his left hand,
and a begging bowl in his left [other] hand; having raised a trident with the lotus-like hand of another,
he bears a stream of thick, spreading blood as it is proclaimed by Viṣṇu.
I bow to the Lord Maheśa, praised by sages and gods, who wanders for alms in red robes.
Meditation on the State of a Disciple

Having fashioned [the deity] with a jasmine-like complexion and a gentle smile, wearing a crown of the moon and illuminated by earrings, with his right hand placed upon his chest; ||| p. 189) ||| and having placed his left hand upon his chest; O Goddess belonging to Viṣṇu!
Having visualized her with two eyes, four arms, peaceful, dark-complexioned, and in the full bloom of youth,
holding a conch and a discus, and endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
Having made Garuḍa her vehicle, adorned with all ornaments— [this is] Vārāhī.
She has four arms and three eyes, is clothed in yellow garments,
is endowed with the form of a boar, and is possessed of a red complexion.
She is endowed with a crown and diadem, possessing a golden and blue form;
she is likewise adorned with a jewel-encrusted crown and has a swan as her vehicle.
And likewise Hasalāmusala, as well as Abhaya and Varada; and Māhendrī,
who has two eyes and four arms, who is peaceful, bestowing the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons, endowed with the thunderbolt and the spear, and possessing a golden-blue form.
She is adorned with a crown set with jewels and has an elephant as her vehicle. || 6 ||
Cāmuṇḍī
The wise one should cause Cāmuṇḍī to be fashioned with four arms and three eyes, having the form of a dark cloud and possessing a luster equal to a dark cloud.
She is joined with a skull and a trident, as well as a noose and a hand-drum.
